# UI.md

> **Carried over from Ballarc (Last Wave) on 2026-11-20.** The method, the engine facts and the measured lessons
> apply here; the old game's look does not. Kill All The Monsters is not pixel art and not anime: maps are stud-style
> (LEGO-like bricks at real scale), UI is sleek and modern (`UIMatt.md` is the designer's spec). Sections named after
> a Last Wave weapon, boss or screen are worked examples. A path that does not exist in this repo (`Assets/...`,
> `tools/vfx/...`, a `src/Survivors/...` module) is in `../Ballarc`; `../Anime Zombie Survival` holds the enemy rig,
> map and burst pipelines this repo's `tools/` came from.

## Kill All The Monsters: the UIMatt look (read first: it overrides anything below)

Learned porting the In-Game HUD (`HudController`, 2026-11-20) over four rounds of the user's corrections. Where an
older section of this file disagrees, this section wins; the "Superseded here" list names the known conflicts.

### The look is his art, measured, with our content

- **A UIMatt screen looks exactly like his render.** The STYLE is his; the CONTENT is ours (our defenses wear his
  ability cards under his ABILITIES title). What he drew that has no system yet is drawn and does nothing. Nothing
  he did not draw is added: no key badge on SKIP WAVE, no colour change on the countdown's last seconds, no "IN X
  WAVES" on the boss strip, no extra segments.
- **Measure, never eyeball.** His layout boxes include each PNG's shadow bleed, so a box is not the panel. The
  drawn rect is the PNG's opaque bounds (alpha > 200) mapped through the `Art` ImageLabel's placement. His text
  sizes come from rur's `scene.json` for the original (the user's `gamehudui.luau` export with his ids swapped for
  the local PNGs). Then render ours with `tools/uimatt/Hud.story.luau` through the same renderer and diff crops side
  by side, before calling a screen done.
- **His look, as the components draw it** (`Components.Panel` / `Card` / `Slab` / `Plaque`; numbers in the `Look`
  table). Every size handed to them is his OUTER drawn rect: the edge is the frame's own background and the face is
  inset over it, because a `UIStroke` draws outside the frame and his rects include the edge.

| Piece | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| Dark panel (plates, boss strip, AUTO-SKIP, money plate, Squad, Settings) | 2 px muted pink edge, darker at the bottom; a darker lip under the top edge; a light pink line inside the bottom edge; the streak texture; his black drop shadow, blur 20, 4 down, at 0.6 |
| Card (items, upgrades, abilities, hotbar slots) | 3 px accent edge, darker at the top; dark face warming toward the accent at the bottom; a 35 px name band on the tall cards; faint corner marks low in the face on the tinted ones; the accent's glow at 0.7 |
| Slab (SKIP WAVE, the countdown, the money packs) | 1 px dark rim, 2 px hot pink edge, a glossy green or gold face with a dark line under the edge; dark corner marks inside where he drew them; a pink glow |
| Plaque (keys, the vote count) | grey edge round an ink square |
| Corner brackets | white, 1.5 px, the bend ROUNDED (a rounded outline's corner seen through a window a leg square), only where he drew them: not on Settings, the vote count, AUTO-SKIP, the countdown or the money plate |

- **The streaks on every face are one texture** (`Icons.PANEL_TEXTURE`, drawn by `tools/uimatt/icons.py` to his
  measured statistics), each panel looking into it at a different place. His faces were too small to tile from.

### Engine facts found here

- **A UIGradient blends its keys in squared space at 8 bits** (rur's `docs/images.md`, measured against Studio), so a
  dark key's channel under about 16 renders as 0: a face keyed at (18, 11, 34) came out (16, 0, 36), a magenta cast
  beside his flat PNG. `Components.Gradient` puts the brightest of each channel on the frame and lets the keys only
  scale it down. Every dark ramp goes through it.
- **His TextScaled boxes are cut to the glyphs**: the TextSize is the box's height, and a cap is about 0.6 of it.
- **TopbarPlus clips its icons** (the widget and the button, for its dropdowns) and clips the button again on every
  deselect. An icon wearing the HUD's panel is unclipped, and unclipped again after each deselect, or its shadow is
  cut off.
- **An atlas glyph is fitted inside its cell**, so to land his glyph at its measured size the icon is drawn in
  `Components.GlyphBox(longest)`.

### Motion in this style

- **One ring.** A shockwave is a single outline growing by pixels at one weight. The two-ring echo this file
  describes for Last Wave is not used here.
- **Never hide a moving thing with Visible**, a fill included: turned Visible it is drawn for a frame where it last
  stood. The countdown's ring snapped at full size for exactly this reason. Fade it (`Transparency` 1) instead.
- **A sweep rides an envelope** (`Components.Sheen`): nothing at either end, so it never pops off at a flat alpha.
- **One element changes shape rather than two swapping.** The WAVE plate becomes his NEXT WAVE IN plate, the
  countdown square pops out under it and is swallowed by it when the wave starts, the boss strip slides out from
  behind it.
- **Juice is motion; at rest the screen is his render.** Punches, slides, rings and sweeps are welcome; a colour or
  a part that changes his look at rest is not.
- **A readout written every frame is written at the resolution it draws at** (SKIP WAVE's cooldown is rounded to
  the fill's pixels), since any write redoes the ScreenGui ("What a frame of UI costs" below).

### Cards in the world (the upgrade pick, `UpgradePickController`, 2026-11-21)

- **A ScreenGui always draws over the world**, so UI on parts cannot sit over a screen dim or the HUD. The pick's dim
  is a part behind the cards (depth-tested, just past the lens; the cards are `AlwaysOnTop`), the HUD's ScreenGui is
  disabled while they are up, and a black curtain on the screen fades it out and in round the swap.
- **`SizingMode = FixedSize`, or `CanvasSize` is ignored**: the default is PixelsPerStud, and the part showed a zoomed
  corner of the card. The canvas is his card plus a margin for the glow and brackets, drawn at 1.5x for a card held
  close.
- **Tell a body where it is in the SCREEN's terms** (design px from the middle, and a zoom) and let the stage solve the
  part's place from the lens (`Stage.Step`): it lands on his rect at any field of view, and a FOV punch does not move it.
- **Hit-test the REST rect, in 2D**, never the leaning part: a card that tilts away from the hand must not lose it.
- **One SurfaceGui a card**: past a quarter turn the part is turned the other half and the canvas shows its back, so
  the swap happens edge-on, where nothing can be seen.
- **Position on a low-damped spring, turn on a wobbly one** (0.72 against 0.3-0.42): a card that overshoots where it
  is reads as loose, one that rocks as it lands reads as a card.
- **Give a show its own clock.** The count ticks once a second; on the header's clock it would run the pick's 22 sparks
  for a third of every second. With the clocks at `math.huge` a hand at rest writes nothing on the screen.
- **Filming it offline**: `tools/ree/UpgradePick.luau` runs the real controller (its header has the command), then
  `ror video --no-service` with `ROR_RUR` set, or the warm service keeps an environment without rur and skips every
  GUI. ror draws the ScreenGui at its own size, so the header is checked flat with `tools/uimatt/UpgradePick.story.luau`.

### A screen for both places: Settings (2026-11-21)

`src/Global/Client/UI/SettingsUI` (the view) and `Controllers/SettingsController` (the sources, the clock, what each
setting does). Rendered by `tools/uimatt/Settings.story.luau`; previews in `Assets/ui/settings/preview`.

- **A view that starts a gesture by itself must keep the clock ticking.** `Now` is written only inside the owner's
  motion window, so a stamp a view writes on its own (the name field's pencil on focus) animates nothing unless it
  also calls `actions.Stir()`. Stamps the controller writes go through its `stamp`, which does both.
- **Anything read off `Now` is a `derive`.** A binding that reads `state.Now()` reruns on every tick of the window,
  whoever opened it. Derived, it reruns only while its own value changes (a reset arrow's turn, a row's sheen, the
  saved flash).
- **A glide is drawn in the steps it shows.** A slider's fill is derived in whole pixels and its number in whole
  percents, so a spring's hundred steps write each a few dozen times.
- **A drag listens to the whole screen only while it holds.** `InputChanged` / `InputEnded` are connected when the
  knob is taken and dropped when it is let go; connected for the session they run on every mouse move in the arena.
- **Words fade by their own transparency.** A CanvasGroup is for a piece built of many parts (a panel, a slab, a
  dimmed reset button); a lone label under one is a screen-sized texture for nothing.
- **A stamp may be in the future.** `Motion.Progress` clamps to 0 before its start, so RESET ALL staggers its rows by
  stamping each one a beat later, with no timers.
- **His art missing is rebuilt from its sibling, and said so.** The Settings header image is private; the Daily
  Rewards header has the same layout (a pink glyph, the title, a rule under it), so that is what is drawn.
- **A state he drew only one of** borrows the nearest thing he did draw: a row with nothing to reset wears his dimmed
  reset button, and RESET ALL with nothing to reset wears the `Off` slab.
- **A saved setting is stored only while it is not its default** (`SettingsCore`), so adding one needs no migration
  and a default changed later reaches everybody who never moved it.

### Superseded here

- The pixel kit: pixel-snapped Slabs, the bezel, Silkscreen, stepped glows, row sheens, blinking square particles,
  gold edges on hover. Those are Last Wave's look.
- Two rings or an echo thrown 70 ms behind the first: one ring.
- `pixelMotion`, `UiSpring` and the `GlobalShared.Utils.Vide` wrapper named below are Ballarc's; this repo uses vide
  directly (`Packages.vide`) and the HUD's own `Motion` curves and `Now` clock.

## Start here for Last Wave (updated 2026-11-05)

This file contains both imported BeACastleLord reference material and Last Wave's later review history.
**Ballarc currently uses Vide and the pixel Slab kit.** The original introduction below describes the other
game's cut-face style; it is not an instruction to replace Last Wave's chrome or restore Fluid. Read the
latest round for the element being changed, then verify its current source. A dated "unjudged" or "not
playtested" note describes that round's evidence, not every later change to that element.

### Decisions to carry into the next session

- Keep this file for UI quirks, fixes, rejected approaches, style and reusable implementation lessons. Put feature
  proposals and non-UI planning in a separate document.
- Preserve the user's selected look and tuned values. Apply the specific correction they requested; do not
  reopen approved choices or restyle the whole HUD. Read files immediately before a targeted edit because
  another session or the user may have changed them. Keep existing history when adding new findings here.
- (Last Wave's look; this game draws the UIMatt look above.) Reuse existing icons and `KeyImages` input glyphs. The active shared kit is
  `src/Global/Client/UI/Components`; many run-specific drawings live in
  `src/Survivors/Client/UI/Components`. Inspect the actual owner before creating another helper or controller.
- Make meaningful events satisfying: anticipation, an immediate response, a readable payoff and a clean
  settle. Frequent events need bounded light/position/pitch feedback; do not stack large scale kicks or
  make every event as loud or elaborate as a completion. Success, cancellation and ordinary hiding are
  distinct states. Preserve existing confetti and attack voices when adding another feedback layer.
- For a substantial redesign, make a UI Labs story for the element with the real drawing component,
  synchronized Before/After states and selectable variants where a taste choice is open. Default the bench
  to the state being judged. An experiment is not the selected live design merely because it compiles.
- Keep kills/souls fire **inside the number wells**, clipped behind the digits. Outer flames were rejected
  near the screen's top. The accepted bright kills band is restrained peach-gold `(255, 194, 100)`; a third
  RGB value must also read as a distinct band to the eye. Keep the separate milestone feedback intentional.
- Legibility and input come first: label ambiguous numbers, reserve room for hover growth, use the themed
  scrollbar, and test small screens and long content. Touch selects without persistent mouse hover; pad
  selection uses the component's own highlight and brackets. Move focus before destroying its old target.
- **Remaking a lobby page (or any page with a map, a count of purchases or a ceremony)?** Read
  [What the skill tree rounds taught](#what-the-skill-tree-rounds-taught-read-before-remaking-any-lobby-page) first:
  hover by events, centring, links under boxes, no round shapes, text that fades out, looped sounds, count pickers
  and skip.
- **Changing a screen's controller or touch behavior?** Read the
  [Controller and touch contract for Last Wave](#controller-and-touch-contract-for-last-wave) before editing.
  It consolidates the required behavior, rejected fixes, source owners and regression cases from the lobby
  controller rounds. It takes precedence over their earlier implementations, including the shifted scroll glyph.
- **Changing spectating, mirrored HUDs, UI replication or claiming a UI is fully optimized?** Read the
  [Spectator UI and replication contract for Last Wave](#spectator-ui-and-replication-contract-for-last-wave).
  It consolidates the user's corrections, current source owners, rejected approaches, retention/cache rules and
  required evidence. The earlier top spectator strip and displaced clock/quest layout were rejected.
- Keep drawing components fed by their owning wrapper, so stories can mount them without live gameplay.
  Services decide outcomes. A reward sound or celebration follows confirmed success, not an optimistic click.
- Objective reminders must stop when their objective is complete, even for players who never contributed.
  Check eligibility where the event is emitted, using the owner's existing state; see
  [altar reminder completion](#last-wave-altar-reminder-completion-2026-11-05).
- Before changing rewards, minimap discovery or loading, read
  [loading, reward and map reliability](#last-wave-loading-reward-and-map-reliability-2026-11-05).
  Reward expiry must grant an offered reward; image availability must not gate discovery. Cosmetic loads need
  deadlines, and terrain/party readiness needs stored completion, bounded recovery and a clear failure path.
- Keep server/client communication on Blink. Do not use Roblox Attributes or CollectionService tags as a network
  protocol. Prefer ordinary Lua state for client UI bookkeeping too; retain engine metadata only where an existing
  integration needs it. ECS component/tag state is ordinary Lua state, separate from Roblox instance tags.
- For sound selection, gain, timing, pooling and rejected candidates, read [Sounds.md](Sounds.md). The latest
  UI-specific lessons are at the end of this file under "score, reward and sound feedback". Do not infer that
  the combat rule against musical power-up cues bans positive coin, score or UI confirmation sounds.
- Use the shared `GlobalShared.Utils.Vide` wrapper (`defaults = false`, `defer_nested_properties = false`).
  Use `UiSpring` for the existing native Vide scalar/Vector3 spring path; its translated coordinates let
  zero-target springs settle. Preserve the `pixelMotion` clock for the kit's timed effects. Reactive teardown
  must also explicitly destroy owned Instances and disconnect external subscriptions.
  Before adding or rebuilding UI, read [UI lifetime and cleanup](#last-wave-ui-lifetime-and-cleanup-2026-11-05),
  including world anchors, delayed callbacks, pooled UI and the required teardown checks.
- Cache drawn state, skip unchanged writes and let settled/hidden effects sleep. Recheck all inputs to a
  draw gate, invalidate after layout/palette changes, and include the final frame that hides an ended effect.
  Pool recurring particles and counter sounds. Assignment counts are not measured Studio frame-time gains.
- Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) before implementation. Preserve the connected Studio/Rojo session and the
  user's running playtest unless interruption is authorized. Report source checks, offline simulation,
  controlled Studio probes, visual review, listening and performance profiling as separate evidence.
- **A readout more than one screen shows (tickets, a currency), or things flying into it?** Follow "Recipe: a
  readout every page shows, and the payout that flies into it" after the tickets rounds near the end: one mounted
  instance, a grid that keeps its shape at every size, the picked gold-and-glints look, and BeACastleLord's sprite ids.
- **Drawing or resizing anything with a border?** Follow "Pixel fidelity: one bezel, and chrome derived from it"
  near the end. Every Slab takes `pixelSlab.Bezel`, every inset is `pixelSlab.Edge` / `pixelSlab.Chrome`, the lit
  and shaded rows are as thick as the bezel, and a part with words in it grows instead of losing its well.
- **Restyling a lobby page?** Follow "Recipe: a lobby page in the pixel style, in one round" under the Codex
  section near the end. It lists every correction the user made across the Codex, stash and Quests rounds, so they
  can be right the first time.

The detailed Last Wave history begins at **"Last Wave: the retro run UI"**; that first experiment is marked
parked. The later vitals and individual-element rounds explain the selected direction. Latest corrections
take precedence over earlier candidates; verify that any named branch, scratch harness or module still exists.

---

How the interface is drawn, and why. This is the file you open before touching a screen, and the file you
update when a rule here stops being true.

The style has a name: **the cut face**. It is implemented by `src/Global/Client/UI/Components/facet.luau` and
it replaces `panel.luau`. The skill tree (`src/FeedTheCore/Client/UI/SkillTreeUI.luau`) is the reference
screen; the **HUD chrome** — the hotbar slot, both health bars and the Core's panel — is converted too. The
**build bar** (`UI/BuildBarUI.luau`) is the first whole *screen* to follow them, and it is the worked example
of a **round run end to end**: four candidate slots drawn, benched, judged, one picked, the losers deleted
(§5e). **Every other screen in both games is still on the old chrome and is meant to migrate.**

How a surface **answers a cursor** — hover, press, and the light that follows a pointer — is §5f, and what
that reaction costs on a screen full of them is §5g. Both are in the game.

How a **readout** stays legible while the surface under it changes is §5h: the special attack's cooldown
badge, which is in the game on both weapon slots. It is the first thing here that has to be *read* rather
than looked at, and almost every rule that lets a decoration be approximately right failed on it.

The **down** and the **waking caption**, the two times the Core puts a lord back on his feet, are the
`Keystone` and the `Gem`, picked from a round of four drawings each and benched on `Stories/Revive`. §5i
is how they are built.

How to make **things fly from one element into another and feel satisfying** (a payout into a purse, a heal
into a bar, a stream of pieces into a gem, an explosion that pays out) is §5j: the recipe the Keystone took
five rounds of feedback to reach, general, with the numbers that shipped and a table of what was rejected.
Read it before building any collect, burst or payoff.

The **world prompt** (`UI/PromptUI`, the mark over a thing you can press) is §5k: `Gem` is in the game and
`Lit` is kept on the bench. It is also the place to read before any object that changes STATE: how to
change without turning into another thing, why a settle into a smaller state is not a leave, and why a
keycap's letter vanishes on a light surface.

The **loot screen** (`UI/PackUI`, the pack) is §5l: what a loot or inventory screen needs, decided once; how an
icon in a tile's corner is made of the corner's own art; what comes and goes and how; and a table of every
pitfall it hit with the fix. Read it before building any grid of items, cards that compare, or a help key.
How that screen is put up in the GAME, out of the pack in his hands, with his own body in the doll and a tool
picture for a thing with a front, is §5n.

How the **marks** on the skill squares are drawn, and how to draw another one in the same style, is §8b, with a
recipe for taking a new icon set from a script to the screen in one pass.
They are a third art family beside the faces and the blooms, and the one you are most likely to need to add
to: nineteen are authored and eighteen are wired, and every new square wants one.

How a **whole screen** comes on — the pack's panels rising in one after another, the skill tree shattering open
and building itself, four rounds of what "modern, not cartoonish" meant, and the fade that has to run on its own
clock — is §5o. Read it before giving any screen an entrance.

How a thing **arrives and leaves** — the three curves, why a spring is the wrong tool for an entrance, and
whether to open by size or by transparency — is §5c. It is the part of this style most likely to be got
wrong twice, because every mistake in it looks like a taste problem and is arithmetic.

How to **bench** any of it is §10c (a slider page in a browser, for a number that is a matter of appearance)
and §10e (a UI Labs story with a settings panel, for the component's own behaviour, drawing the real thing).
How a **variant round** runs from four candidates to one shipped slot — and what deleting the losers is
actually worth — is the top of §5e.

## 1. The idea, in one paragraph

The Core is a crystal and the shard is a cube stood on its corner. The ground the skill tree is drawn on is
already made of that (`SkillTreeBody`: planes of light at the angles the cube's own faces are cut at,
fractures through them, dust near the eye). The panels were the one surface still speaking a different
language — a cozy-mobile pixel sticker with a two-pixel pure-black outline, a two-pixel corner radius, a hard
black lip along the bottom, and the whole thing doubled with a band of coloured plastic showing between the
two frames. On a 91px skill square that chrome ate 22px a side: **about half the square was frame.** The cut
face is the fix, and it is three rules.

### The three rules

1. **Corners are CUT, not rounded.** How MANY is the face's business, not the style's: the default `Cut`
   face takes the top-left and the bottom-right, the skill tree's four faces take all four, and
   `SquareTable` keeps its corners and lights them anyway (§4). "Two rather than four, because a symmetric
   octagon reads as a sci-fi HUD" was a real argument and it lost to a bench. What never changes is that a
   corner is cut or lit, never rounded.
2. **The outline is LIGHT, not INK.** A 3px edge in the surface's own hue. A facet edge catches light; it
   does not get drawn round in black.
3. **Depth is a SHADOW, not a LIP.** A cut stone casts shade. It does not wear a black bar along its bottom.
   **With one hard limit:** Roblox's `UIShadow` feathers a *box* whatever it is hung on, so a visible one on
   a cut face grows back the corners the cut took off. Nothing in the HUD casts one; light that has to be
   seen comes off the bloom art instead (§3, §5d).

Everything below is consequence.

**Rule 2 is the one that keeps catching things.** It is not only about panel borders: *nothing* on these
screens is outlined in black. The link wires between skill nodes were a 12-unit bar inside a 4px near-black
stroke — about 20 screen px of connection, most of it ink — drawn that way so they would "read as drawn onto
the sky rather than glowing". They are now a 6-unit filament with no stroke at all, and the colour took back
the shade the outline was worth. When something looks wrong and you cannot say why, check whether it is
outlined.

## 2. `facet` — the component

```lua
local facet = require(StarterPlayer.StarterPlayerScripts.GlobalClient.UI.Components.facet)

facet({
    Name = "Tip",
    FillColor = PALETTE.Paper,     -- the plane's own colour
    EdgeColor = PALETTE.Divider,   -- the cut edge, the bevel and the join
    Padding = 20,                  -- content inset, design px
    Size = UDim2.fromScale(1, 1),

    someChild,                     -- array entries land inside the padding
})
```

It builds **two ImageLabels**, not four:

| Child   | What it is                                                                   | Tinted by   |
| ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| `Plane` | the solid cut face; children and the `UIPadding` live here                    | `FillColor` |
| `Edge`  | the cut edge at full strength, plus the plane behind each cut and their join  | `EdgeColor` |

### Reserved keys

| Key                | Meaning                                                                   |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `FillColor`        | the plane's colour                                                        |
| `EdgeColor`        | the hue the surface is lit in                                             |
| `FillTransparency` | the plane alone, for a face over something worth seeing through it        |
| `Transparency`     | fades the chrome together, for a panel that comes and goes                |
| `Padding`          | content inset in design px; defaults to `Cut + 4` = 20                    |
| `AspectRatio`      | adds a `UIAspectRatioConstraint`                                          |
| `Glow`             | a colour for the bloom the face throws, or nil                            |
| `GlowTransparency` | how strong that bloom is                                                  |
| `Shadow`           | `false` to drop the shade it casts                                        |
| `Face`             | which cut it is drawn on (`facet.Faces`); the two-cut `Cut` by default    |

**`Face` takes a table OR a getter**, and so does `facet.Light`'s. Every screen passes a table and that path
is unchanged — the pictures and the slice are read once and written as plain properties, so a static caller
builds no effect nodes at all. A **bench** passes a source, which is what lets a surface be redrawn on
another cut while it is being looked at instead of being torn down and rebuilt (`Stories/BuildBar` sweeps
the build bar's sheet and its slots separately). The light's *margin* is the light's and not the face's — every
face falls away over the same 24 or 84 — so a swept face never resizes the layer.

Anything else goes on the root Frame. Array entries become children inside the padding.

### Numbers

| Thing                | Value                            |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Cut                  | 16 design px (`facet.Cut`)       |
| Corner cell          | 34 design px (`facet.Cell`)      |
| Edge                 | 3 design px (baked into the art) |
| Default padding      | 20 design px (`Cut + 4`)         |
| Skill-square padding | 18 design px (`SQUARE_PADDING`)  |
| `SliceCenter`        | `Rect.new(102, 102, 114, 114)`   |
| `SliceScale`         | `scaleNumber(1/3)`               |
| Fill image           | `rbxassetid://140261849228744`   |
| Edge image           | `rbxassetid://96352919074263`    |
| Bloom image          | `rbxassetid://106996112505139`   |
| Bloom slice          | `Rect.new(228, 228, 240, 240)`   |
| Bloom margin         | 42 design px (`facet.BloomReach`)|
| Crystal image        | `rbxassetid://104027632398122`   |

`facet.Faces` holds the cuts a surface can be drawn on and `facet.Light` draws the light one throws — both
are §4. The numbers above are the default `Cut` face; another face carries its own slice and cell, because a
deeper cut needs a bigger corner cell.

The last two are not part of a panel and `facet` does not build them; they are exported (`facet.Bloom`,
`facet.BloomSlice`, `facet.BloomReach`, `facet.Crystal`, plus `facet.Plane` / `facet.Edge` / `facet.Slice` /
`facet.SourceScale`) so anything that has to draw the same silhouette can. See §5d.

`facet.Inset(padding)` is the chrome reservation, **both axes** (unlike `panel` there is no bottom lip), and
it now covers the padding too.

## 3. Rules that will bite you

These are all things that cost real time to find. Read them before you debug them again.

### If it looks wrong, check these first

| Symptom | Almost always |
| --- | --- |
| A panel draws nothing at all, no error | a **Decal** id in `Image`; it wants the Image inside it |
| A whole animated thing draws nothing, no error | a **0 sentinel** that a clock starting at 0 can now hit |
| Some layers vanish and the rest animate fine | they read a **source nothing writes any more** (see below) |
| One mirrored half of a pair is not clipped | it is **rotated**, and `ClipsDescendants` skips those |
| Something reads heavy or muddy and you cannot say why | it is **outlined in black** somewhere (rule 2) |
| A glow is a soft **box** round a non-box thing | it is a **`UIShadow`**, which always feathers a box (§3) |
| ...and it is hung on the object itself | then it is the **cell** around it, not the object |
| A halo is huge on one element and fine on another | blur/spread are **shares of the caster** |
| A tooltip lands on top of the thing it describes | a **rotated** frame reports its unrotated rect |
| Text has holes between the letters | a proportional face on a **fixed-width grid** (`typewriter`) |
| Text is ~20% smaller than it used to be | the face changed; multiply sizes by **1.236** |
| A word in a button is tiny | the **default panel padding** on a control-height slab |
| A shadow is sliced off along a straight line | a `CanvasGroup` cut to the element's own size |
| A gradient's step or ramp lands nowhere near where you asked | it is **rotated** on a non-square element |
| A swept band stops in a corner and then pops off | its reach is a share of the **width** and it has width+height to cross (§3) |
| ...and the last of it hangs there before vanishing | a **flat alpha** on a spring's exponential tail; put the band on an envelope (§3) |
| A click off a panel does not close it, or closes it from inside | the panel is not **`Active`**, or something floating over it is not (§3) |
| An effect node exists for a property nothing will ever write | a **getter** was handed where a constant would do; resolve and branch (§10b) |
| A face's outline looks dimmer on a bar than on a panel | the **corner cell** is shrunk to fit and the edge with it (§3) |
| A border is thicker on one screen than another | a Slab given its **own bezel number**, not `pixelSlab.Bezel` ("Pixel fidelity") |
| A shine or shadow row reads as **half a pixel** | the lit/shaded row is one unit on a two-unit bezel ("Pixel fidelity") |
| Icons resize a moment after a page or tab opens, the **first time only** | an **async measure** (`imageBounds`) landing after the picture was shown whole; hide it until measured, warm on open (shop rules, 2026-11-02) |
| Words or arrows sit a unit off centre in a Slab | the chrome is a **literal** (`4 * p`) from an older bezel ("Pixel fidelity") |
| A pressed button sinks and its word (or badge) stays put | the press handler moved only the **Slab**; everything on it must move through one `place` function ("A pressed part moves as one") |
| Two screens read the same sentence at different speeds | each set its own copy of a pace the component already had (§7) |
| A panel has more air on one axis than the other | something was **reserved on one axis** — headroom, a lift, a grow (§5e) |
| A bloom reads as a thick coloured **stroke** | a **step** in its alpha at the shape's boundary |
| A halo is thin at the **corners** and full along the edges | it was **blurred**, not distance-fielded (§5d) |
| A halo pokes out past a CUT but looks right on a square | the bloom was **scaled** to set its reach (§5d) |
| A lit edge is uneven along a run, or thicker than the file says | the element is **rotated** and resampled (§3) |
| A highlight sits somewhere senseless on a turned element | the turn **turned the light** with it (§3) |
| A glow is sheared off flush along one edge | its mask stops **on** the fill instead of past it |
| A lit edge is the wrong colour against what it sits on | the ramp was sampled at its **head**, not at the edge |
| A pattern stops short of an element's ends | it was **inset** to clear a cut; taper it instead |
| A glow reads as heavy and diffuse | its **tail**, not its peak — compare in bar-heights, not px |
| A glow is brighter at the fill's end than above it | its mask ramp **starts** at the fill instead of straddling it |
| A pattern comes out as smeared slivers | `ScaleType.Stretch` on art authored at another aspect |
| A gradient on a frame does not reach what is inside it | a `UIGradient` only ever affects **its own parent** (§5f) |
| Two gradients refuse to multiply | one of them has to sit on a **`CanvasGroup`** (§5f) |
| A 90°-turned gradient will not move when you set `Offset.X` | `Offset` is in the **element's** space, not the ramp's (§5f) |
| A press feels soft although everything on it moves | the press-in is sharing the **pop's** underdamped spring (§5f) |
| A soft light has a clearly visible end | its mask is a **triangle**; a slope jump reads as an edge (§5f) |
| A hover "ticks" instead of lifting | one spring is doing the **rise and the light**; they want opposite answers (§5f) |
| A button feels like one more upgrade | it is being **lifted** and lit from outside; a control does neither (§5f) |
| Two frames meeting at 0.5 leave a hairline between them | their edges round **independently**; tile them in whole px |
| ...and overlapping them left a **bright** line instead | semi-transparent layers **compose** where they overlap |
| Everything measures as zero in a probe | the playtest's **ViewportSize is 1×1** (§11) |
| A hover's light answers a cursor that is somewhere else | a GUI mouse event is **raw screen** and `AbsolutePosition` is not (§3) |
| A readout is fine on the bench and gone in the game, top left | the **Roblox unibar**, 208 × 58; a plugin widget has no topbar (§3) |
| ...and near the top of the element it stops answering at all | same thing: the point is a whole inset low and pinned to the clamp (§3) |
| A click on a scrollbar's empty track jumps to the wrong place | same thing; a **drag** hides it because the error cancels (§3) |
| A gap written in px doubles the zoom on a scaled map | a `UIScale` carries a descendant's **offsets** with it (§3) |
| One label's drop shadow reads heavier than another's at the same px | the **letter** differs; a gap in px is not one shadow (§6) |
| Motion feels toy-like | **rotation**, or low damping over a long period |
| `Out of local registers ... exceeded limit 200` | a scope has **200 locals**; group constants into frozen tables (§5g) |
| The screen is smooth, then quietly is not, and nothing looks wrong | a spring that **never settles**, stepping its layers forever (§5g) |
| `attempt to index nil` on a local you can see declared | it is read **inside its own initializer**; the local is not in scope until the statement ends (§5g) |
| An effect fires but the value it reads is stale by one event | a probe (or a handler) **sampled once** where it had to poll (§11) |
| A bloom reads as a flat **plate** rather than a light | the face in front of it is **see-through**; a bloom is full peak inside its own outline (§5d) |
| A thin **blue line** along one edge of a dark frame, only in the lobby | the engine's **default 1 px border** ((27, 42, 53)) on a frame whose background was turned on later; the lobby's correction makes it bright. `BorderSizePixel = 0` on every frame you create raw (`pixelSlab.Frame` already does) |
| A wider hit area does nothing past a panel's edge | the panel's **well clips input** as well as drawing; a grab area can only use the empty space inside it |
| ...and tightening its reach made it **worse** | a crop keeps the flat inside and throws away the soft outside (§5d) |
| A fill draws at FULL when it should draw nothing | its gradient was **disabled** at the empty end; that stops the mask, not the layer (§5h) |
| A number over a rising fill vanishes as the fill reaches it | one ink, two grounds. It wants **two copies cut by the same line** (§5h) |
| A readout is legible when measured and invisible on screen | something is **drawn over it**; the readout belongs at the top of the ladder (§5h) |
| A part shows its **default look** (lit, bought, full) the first time only, right after re-entering it is fine | it is **made by the layout**, which runs after `paint`; whatever makes a part paints it ("Lazy parts and late text") |
| A mark, badge or glyph is missing on things that **loaded** already on, but appears once toggled | it is **built lazily on a change** and the load path snaps the state without building it; one entry point (`setMark`) builds then sets |
| Words grow **up** into a picture, or the picture is off centre in its room | the line count was an **estimate** that came up short; measure the drawn label's `TextBounds` and lay out again ("Lazy parts and late text") |
| A pixel glyph touches its badge's bezel | the badge's well is exactly the glyph's 8 texels; size it with **`pixelSlab.WellTexel`**, a unit of air each side (well >= 10 units) |
| A glyph has a unit and a half of air on one side, half a unit on the other | it was centred on its **drawing**, not its box; centre the box (drawing + shade) so it stays on the unit grid |
| Two cards' icons differ by a whole size | a **whole-texel floor** across a cliff (8 units a step); let a glyph reach into the gaps round its room |
| Tickets bought fast: the number runs ahead, a spend plays with no pieces, the wallet freezes ~2.5 s | a **single** hold or a **single** pending record per key; holds count, each flight pays its own slice, presses queue ("Tickets in quick succession") |
| A letter in a diamond is far too small | it is being held inside the **picture's** box; a letter's box is not an icon's (§5h) |
| A layer measures right and looks wrong, and the art is "obviously" fine | the probe measured the **layer** and assumed the **picture** (§11) |
| A drawn shape sits off-centre in its own image, or is clipped at one edge | a **mitre runs past the vertex it was written at**; solve the box from what it draws (§8b) |
| A key's letter is unreadable on a light surface and fine on a dark one | the keycap art's **letter is a hole**; fill it from behind (§5k) |
| A state change reads as the object turning into another thing | the two states are **different drawings**; keep the pieces, change size, colour and light (§5k) |
| Growing into a state bounces and shrinking into one does not | the shrink is on the **leaving** curve; a settle is an arrival (§5k) |
| Stepping in and out of a state mid-move makes the object jump | two curves share one travel; run **legs from the current value** (§5k) |
| A story works in UI Labs and fails "already registered" in a playtest probe | the template copy **re-registers an Ignis module**; swap the running module in (§5k) |
| A variant set is judged "exactly like the old one" | the candidates were given the **control's motion**; each variant moves its own way (§5k) |
| Something flashes at its resting place for a frame, then snaps to where its animation starts | it was hidden with **`Visible = false`** and turned visible on the frame it moved; the engine draws its **last layout** first. Park it off-screen instead (§3) |
| A screen's title and buttons are huge with one item and tiny with fifty | the chrome **follows the content's unit**; give it its own (§3, the win box's round 5) |
| A big grid leaves a lot of room and its cells are still small | the fit was **floored to a whole px a unit** (3.27 -> 3 is 9%, 4.6 -> 4 is 13%); size the cell from the exact fit, round only its pixel (the win box's round 5) |
| Text overflows or clips its box on a phone and fits in Studio | the player's **Text Size** setting enlarges fixed-`TextSize` labels; `TextSizeController` caps them (§3) |
| A lobby page runs off the right edge (~6% too wide) and fixes itself only sometimes | its size was divided by a `UIScale` that is **not on the frame it measured**; a layout mid-grow went wide and nothing re-laid it out at rest ("The gift picker and the lobby pages' size") |
| Every button on a page stops answering after a popup closes | the popup never reached **Hidden**: its clock reported busy for the whole leave, so its invisible full-screen dim stayed up and sank every press ("The gift picker and the lobby pages' size") |
| The page under a popup ignores presses for ~0.5 s after the popup closes | the popup's dim and panel stay **Active** for the whole leave animation. Set the popup's root `Interactable = false` the moment the leave starts, `true` on open; the leave is only a picture ("The gift picker and the lobby pages' size") |
| Buttons light up under a modal's dim in the lobby | the lobby is a **SurfaceGui**: covered buttons still get `MouseEnter`. Set the page under it `Interactable = false` while it is up |
| A click inside a modal's panel closes it | the panel is a plain Frame, so the press falls through to the dim's cancel. Put a handler-less `ImageButton` under the panel, as `CodesUI` does |

### Lazy parts and late text

- **Whatever makes a part paints it.** Cards build pips, chips, glyphs and badges on first need, usually from the
  layout, and the layout runs after `paint`. A part made after the paint keeps its creation colour (gold pips = "all
  bought") until something repaints. The `ensureX` that makes it calls the matching `paintX`.
- **One entry point for a state that builds things.** If turning a mark on builds its glyph, every path that turns it
  on (load, refresh, toggle) goes through that one function. A "snap without playing" path is a flag on it, not a
  second function that skips the build.
- **Text line counts are estimates until drawn.** `TextBounds` reads 0 before the first draw, so layouts guess from a
  character advance; for the pixel faces the guess can come up a line short, and bottom-aligned words then grow up
  over what is above them. Measure after the draw (`TextBounds` changed: `round(Y / TextSize)` lines), remember it by
  text, size and width, and lay out again (`shopCard.remeasure`). Skip a truncated label.
- **Never fit text by writing sizes in a loop that immediately reads `TextFits`.** It can describe the previous
  layout, so another interaction changes the result. Lobby `questCard` did this: achievement pip previews reran the
  fit and changed the title size. Its title now uses `TextScaled` with a `UITextSizeConstraint` set from the card's
  unit, so first display, new text and resizing all fit without input. `Layout` owns the font limits and outline;
  tier previews only update the text and its available room. Keep manual measurements event-driven where
  they also place surrounding content (`shopCard`, `inspectCard`, `pauseBanner`, `teammateCard`).
  Regression cases: open Daily/Weekly/Achievements without hovering, preview a tier and return to the same title,
  switch short/long titles, resize in both directions and reopen. Check mouse, touch previews and pad focus.
- **Centre a picture in the room it really has** (between the title's bottom and the words' top), never the card.

### Pixel glyphs (tick, cross, star)

- One drawing each, in the kit: `pixelSlab.TickRows`, `CrossRows`, `StarRows`, built with `pixelSlab.Glyph`, never
  per-screen cells or images. The codex marks and buttons and the shop's Codex cards use them (`codexButton` takes
  `Glyph` + `GlyphPalette`; shop cells take `Glyph`). The accept check image stays an image (the user's call).
- The box is 8 texels: 7 of drawing, 1 of shade down and right. **Centre the box**, not the drawing.
- Card banish overlays (`upgradeCard`, `rewardCard`) fit their full square glyph to 75% of the shorter card side.
  These use `FitWithinMaxSize` so wide level-up rows and upright ability/augment cards both retain air around the
  mark; sizing from width alone made the new cross fill or overflow the row's height.
- In a badge: `pixelSlab.LayoutGlyph(glyph, pixelSlab.WellTexel(wellW, wellH, unit))`, a unit of air on every side.
  The well must be at least 10 units: a 16-unit badge at `pixelSlab.Bezel`, or 14 with a 1-unit bezel.
- A texel is a whole number of units, so sizes step 8 units at a time. Where a glyph is a card's picture, let it reach
  into the gaps round its room so a card with a unit less room does not draw it a whole step smaller.
- The run's tools are glyphs too (2026-11-06): `SkipRows` (gold), `RerollRows` (blue) and `CrossRows` for banishes
  (red), on the reward screens' `actionButton` (`Glyph`, required now), the mobile `touchButton` (`Glyph`, a source),
  `codexButton` (the box shop's auto-skip, the skill tree's skip), the cards' banish hover and the shop's TOOLS cards.
  `ChestRows` (lifted from the codes screen) is a box. The old skip / reroll / banish images remain only where they mean
  something else: the top bar's restart and the settings reset (TopbarPlus takes an image), and the lobby's kick.
- The ticket (`pixelSlab.Ticket`) wears the glyphs' shade: a unit down and right, outside the body, so a caller that
  recolours `BackgroundColor3` still recolours the face; `PaintTicket` recolours every part. A pile needs no ink box
  behind each ticket: each one's shade parts it from the one under it (two ZIndex steps a ticket). Its full bounds
  are `TicketWidth` x `TicketHeight` (8 x 6), including shade; use those for layout, not the 7 x 5 face. The two
  centre perforation dots were rejected (2026-11-06); keep the side notches and shade, with a plain centre.
- A compact action's unit must reserve the chrome **and** the full glyph **and** its air: at least
  `pixelSlab.Chrome + pixelSlab.GlyphTexels + 2` units across. `actionButton` caps its pixel size against that
  minimum before calling `WellTexel`; `touchButton` reserves the same space when it takes a `Glyph` source, even
  while that source returns nil. A minimum-one-texel clamp cannot make an undersized well fit. See the fitting
  correction at the end of this file.

### Tickets in quick succession

Every tickets moment must survive the player buying or claiming again before the last one has finished.

- `ticketsCounter` holds **stack**: `Hold()` once per purchase or payout, `Pay(amount)` for each slice a flight moves,
  `Release()` once when that flight is done; the last release hands over to the real balance. Never let one flight's
  end release another's hold.
- Every press that holds must be released on **every** answer: success with nothing flying (0 tickets), refusal,
  screen closed. Otherwise the counter waits out its 2.5 s deadline and looks frozen.
- A pending record per press, **queued** per key (`ShopUI.remember` / `takePending`), not one per key: a second press
  overwrote the first, so one purchase played with no spend.
- A repeat press before the answer prices the **next** level and checks the balance less what is already in flight.
- The card holds once per purchase and strikes once per landing, each with the state that came in for it.
- Labels ("+N", "-N") add up while still on screen (re-pop +9%), flights land a piece taken by a newer throw instead
  of dropping it, and repeated chimes climb a pitch chain instead of stacking.

Daily deal purchases (2026-11-06): `ShopUI` owns the mapping from drawn cards to the deal slots mirrored by
`ShopController`; `ShopService` checks and charges the stored slot's price. Carry the slot through `dealsTab`'s
`add` into `shownDealSlots` on every refresh, and use it for both ticket purchases and Robux intents. Never send
the card's page index: flash, free, milestone and weekly cards precede daily deals, so a weapon click could request
a different item at its higher price or a nonexistent slot. A daily deal already awaiting its ticket answer ignores
repeat presses before the affordability check; utilities still queue their next level. Check all five slots with
and without a weekly bundle, both currencies, insufficient tickets, and repeated presses before the answer.

Quest claims (2026-11-06): `ProgressionService`'s one-second request gates discarded distinct daily/weekly claims
and achievement claims made quickly. These two listeners now rely on their claim functions' authoritative guards:
the reward must be complete and unclaimed, and its `Claimed` flag is written before any payout. Other actions keep
their rate limits. `questCard.Set` clears pending when the shown tier key changes, even when the next tier is also
ready; a card-wide pending timeout must not delay the next reward. Keep the existing animation timing.

`ticketsFlight` samples the wallet's current anchor once per active frame and moves both the curve endpoint and its
incoming control toward it. Capturing that anchor only when a piece turns misses a wallet that moves during flight.
Keep each overlapping burst's own payout and hold release, including when the fixed piece pool is reused.

Regression cases: rapid daily and weekly claims, repeated ready tiers in one achievement ladder, duplicate claims,
moving the wallet mid-flight, exhausting the piece pool with overlapping rewards, and closing mid-flight. Checked
with actual function bodies in offline probes, compilation and lint; **not playtested in Studio or on touch/pad**.

### The player's Text Size setting, and `TextSizeController`

Roblox's **Text Size** setting (`GuiService.PreferredTextSize`, Medium to Largest) enlarges every label that is not
`TextScaled`. On mobile it follows the phone's font size, so it is on for players who never opened a menu. The pixel
kit sizes its boxes from the designed `TextSize`, so the enlarged text spills out: on a phone (2026-11-01) the end
screen's chips read "LED BY SLI", the buttons "ESTART", the debug lines ran into each other, while the `TextScaled`
"ACTIVATE ALTARS" stayed tiny. Studio is usually at the default Medium, so nothing shows there. Roblox has no opt-out property. Only
`TextScaled` and a `UITextSizeConstraint` on the label stop it.

`src/Global/Client/Controllers/TextSizeController.luau` (loaded in both places) handles it for the whole game. It
watches `PlayerGui` and gives each fixed-size `TextLabel` / `TextButton` / `TextBox` a `UITextSizeConstraint` with
`MaxTextSize = ceil(TextSize)`. It follows the label's `TextSize` writes, so the cap is always the size the code asked
for, at any resolution (4K included: `MaxTextSize` defaults to 1000; the 100 limit is `TextScaled`'s). It skips
`TextScaled` labels and labels that already carry a `UITextSizeConstraint`.

- **New UI needs nothing.** Set `TextSize` as usual and parent into `PlayerGui` (billboards included).
- **Decided once, on arrival.** Turning `TextScaled` on later, or adding your own constraint after the label is in
  `PlayerGui`, leaves two constraints fighting. Create your constraint with the label, or set `TextScaled` up front.
- **Outside `PlayerGui` is not covered**: a `BillboardGui` / `SurfaceGui` parented into `Workspace`, or anything in
  `CoreGui`. Give those their own constraint.
- **Not verified on device:** rich-text `<font size="N">` runs (the small `x` after counts). A DevForum report says a
  constraint overrides the markup; a run smaller than the cap should be unaffected. Check it on a phone with Text Size
  at Largest.
- **Testing it:** set Text Size to Largest in the Roblox menu (or the phone's font size) and open the end screen and
  the debug readout. Without the controller, both overflow.

### Three silent ones: a module that draws NOTHING, and no error anywhere

These share a signature and it is the worst one there is — the code runs, `selene` is clean, the Output is
empty, and the screen is blank. All three were found by reading, not by debugging.

- **A 0-as-absent sentinel that a new clock can now hit.** A title tracked "is it up" as `shownAt`, with
  **0 meaning not up** — safe for exactly as long as the clock was `os.clock`, which is never 0. The moment
  it kept its own `elapsed` so a bench could slow it, the first announcement of the session set `shownAt` to
  precisely the value meaning *not shown*: the step returned on its first line every frame and the whole
  thing drew correctly and completely transparent. **When a timebase changes, grep the file for what it
  compares against zero**, and prefer a boolean for a state — it cannot collide with a measurement.
- **A `source` nobody writes any more.** Two opacity numbers were collapsed into one; the sweep was rewritten
  to write the survivor and stopped writing the other — and the layers that had been reading it went on
  reading it, drawn at `1 - (1 - base) * 0`, which is *gone*. Everything else animated on over nothing.
  Nothing errors and nothing is unused, because the dead source is still **read**. **When two numbers become
  one, grep for the old one's READERS, not its writers.**
- **A rotated descendant of a `ClipsDescendants` frame.** It is simply not clipped — so one mirrored half of
  a pair ignored the window that was revealing its twin. A `CanvasGroup` clips it; see §5c.

### A GUI mouse event is in RAW screen space and `AbsolutePosition` is NOT

**Measured in a playtest, both directions, so this is not a guess.** Cursor at raw `(400, 400)`, inset
`(0, 58)` in Studio:

| What you asked | What came back |
| --- | --- |
| `MouseMoved` / `MouseButton1Down` args | `(400, 400)`, the real top-left of the window |
| `UserInputService:GetMouseLocation()` | `(400, 400)`, the same |
| `InputObject.Position` | `(400, 342)`, a whole inset higher |
| `Mouse.X` / `Mouse.Y` | `(400, 342)`, the same |
| `AbsolutePosition` of a button at `fromOffset(200, 200)` | `(200, 142)` under `IgnoreGuiInset`, `(200, 200)` without it |

So `AbsolutePosition` is **always** measured from under the topbar, whatever the gui's own `IgnoreGuiInset`
or `ScreenInsets` says: a gui that ignores the inset simply reports its own top edge as a **negative Y**.
There is no gui setting that makes the two spaces agree.

**The consequence.** `(y - element.AbsolutePosition.Y) / AbsoluteSize.Y` reads the cursor a whole inset LOW,
36px in a game window and 58 in Studio. On the skill tree's 91px square that is most of the way down it, so
the bearing pointed at a light below the hand, the three depths tipped the tile toward it, and anywhere near
the top of a square the answer pinned to the clamp and stopped moving. Nobody could say what was wrong with
it, only that it felt wrong, which is the signature of this bug: **the reaction works, it just answers the
wrong place.**

**The fix is `UITools.GuiEventInset(element)`**, which returns what to subtract from the event's coordinates
and returns **zero under a SurfaceGui**, whose canvas has no topbar to sit under. Callers: `pointerIn` in
`SkillTreeUI` and the scrollbar's drag.

Two more things that follow from the table:

- **An `InputObject` needs no correction at all.** It is already in `AbsolutePosition` space. The skill
  tree's wheel-zoom anchor subtracts `screen.AbsolutePosition` from `input.Position` and has always been
  right; "fix it too" would have broken it. **Check which of the two spaces a number came from before
  correcting anything.**
- **A DRAG hides the bug**, because the same error sits in the offset taken at mouse-down and in every read
  after it, so it cancels. The scrollbar's thumb was always correct and its click on empty track was always
  36px out. A drag working is not evidence that the space is right.

### An ACTIVE frame is a hit test you never have to write

**"Clicking off the panel closes it" needs no coordinates.** Set `Active = true` on the panel's root: an
Active GuiObject sinks the input that lands on it, and Roblox reports that to every `UserInputService`
listener as **`gameProcessed`** — which every listener in this game already drops at the top. So a click on
the panel, on the gaps between its children, on its padding, is *not your click*; a click anywhere else is.
The dismissing branch becomes `if open then close() return end` and there is nothing to get wrong.

**That is the point, not a convenience.** The alternative is comparing a click's position against the panel's
rect, and the section above is 40 lines about how those two numbers are in different spaces. Whether a point
is inside a box is a question the renderer has already answered; asking it again is asking to be a whole GUI
inset out.

Three things that follow:

- **Buttons inside it keep working.** `Active` sinks what *reaches* it, and anything drawn above is reached
  first — so a slot's own `Activated` fires and the frame never sees it.
- **A click that dismisses should not also act.** The build bar returns before `place()`: a player who clicks
  off a menu to get rid of it has not aimed at anything, and doing the thing under the cursor would be the
  menu charging them for closing it.
- **Anything you did NOT make Active is outside.** The build bar's description card floats above the bar and
  is not Active, so a click on it closes the menu. That reads correctly here (the card only exists while a
  slot is hovered) but it is a decision, not a default — check every floating child.

**The same mechanism is why a menu can live on a mouse button at all.** The build bar opens on right click,
which the game already spends on a weapon's alt-fire; they never collide because that listener resolves the
weapon in hand and no-ops without one, and a Hammer is not a weapon. The cost of putting a menu's button on
the mouse is that a right click *on* the bar is sunk and so cannot toggle it shut — which is right anyway:
it is the same press that opened it, landing on the thing it opened.

### A `UIScale` carries a descendant's UDim OFFSET with it

**Measured:** a child at `Position = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0.5, -8)` under a `UIScale` drew its offset at
**8 / 4 / 2 px** at scale **1 / 0.5 / 0.25**, with the letters at 68 / 34 / 16.

So under the skill tree's zoom, a number written as an offset is multiplied by the zoom before it is drawn.
Anything meant to stay a fixed **share** of something else there has to be written as a ratio, not as pixels:
a share of the box is scale-invariant because both halves carry the zoom and it cancels. That is why
`textShadow`'s measured gap is a `Scale` and not an `Offset` (§6).

**What is NOT known: whether a `UIScale` scales `UIStroke.Thickness`.** It was not measured, there is no
numeric readout for it, and the devforum reports contradict each other. Until someone settles it, an outline
under a zoom is the one number here you cannot reason about.

### A page laid out from `AbsoluteSize` must divide out its OWN `UIScale`

`AbsoluteSize` includes every `UIScale` above it **and on it**. Every lobby page opens by growing from 94.5% with a
`UIScale` on its root, and five of them (shop, boxes chrome, quests, stash, codex) re-laid themselves out on the
root's `AbsoluteSize` change. So each frame of the grow placed everything for a smaller page, and the scale then
shrank that again: the contents drifted in toward one corner (the ITEMS BOX plate came "from the middle left")
instead of growing from the middle. Seen 2026-11-02.

- Lay out from `AbsoluteSize / scale.Scale`, rounded (`unscaledSize` in each page).
- Hook the resize to a guard that lays out only when that unscaled size changed (`onResize` against `laidSize`).
  Without it the page still did a full layout on every frame of every grow, for nothing.
- A layout that reads a PARENT's size is safe: the parent does not carry the child's `UIScale`.

### `<font size='N'>` in rich text is PIXELS, not a share

A rich-text `<font size='6'>` is 6 px whatever the label's own size. The data had `5<font size='6'>s</font>` and
`2<font size='6'>x</font>` all through weapon, augment and item text, written for a small label. In the shop's canvas
(text 20 px and up) the letter was a speck: "2. LUCK" for "2x LUCK". Never put a fixed size in data text. A suffix
drawn smaller is computed from the label at draw time (`cornerRibbon`, `inventorySlot`, `pixelDropdown` do
`math.round(label.TextSize * share)`). Changing a data string makes Roblox's cloud translation see it as a new string.

### A ROTATED UIGradient's ramp spans the element's HEIGHT, not its length

**Measured, off a screenshot of a 544x35 bar.** A `UIGradient` turned 45 degrees does keep a true 45 degree
edge in *screen* space — the edge in that shot ran at exactly 1:1 — but its nought-to-one ramp spans
something close to the element's **height**, about 45px, rather than its 544px length. So:

- a hard step asked for at `t = 0.983` landed at **57% of the bar**;
- a `ColorSequence` across it crushed itself into a ~50px band at the middle, with flat colour either side;
- and the tell was unambiguous — the wrong band's colour was `#FF399A`, which is `facetBar`'s own
  `lift(ember, NIB_LIFT)` to the byte.

**So a turned gradient is only safe on a roughly SQUARE element.** The one long-standing user of the trick
is `hotbarSlot`'s cooldown sweep, on a 97px square, where it has always been correct — which is why this
went unnoticed until a bar was drawn with one. Every mask in `facetBar` is now rotation 0.

Nothing was lost by squaring them up: the slanted **ends** that read as "cut" are the plane image's own
corners, not the fill's leading edge.

### A SWEPT band's travel is a share of the WIDTH, and it has width PLUS height to cross

The other half of the same trap, and it shows up as a band that **stops in a corner and then pops off**.

`UIGradient.Offset` is in fractions of the element's **size**, so `Offset.X` of 1 walks the ramp one *width*
along X whatever the element's height is. A band turned 45° has to get across a face that is as long as its
width **plus** its height. So the reach that carries the band's centre corner to corner is `(w + h) / w`,
half of it either side of nought — **1 on a square, and 1.273 on a 150×232 tile.** The build bar's glint was
a flat ±1.15 for both, which is 10% short on the tall one: the band ran out of travel in the bottom-right
corner and sat there.

**And then it popped, which is the spring.** The sweep is a critically damped spring struck to zero and
easing back to one: it crosses in its 0.26s and spends **another 0.16s creeping the last half a percent**
before vide retires it. A band at a flat alpha is parked for the whole of that and then vanishes on the frame
the spring settles.

**So put the band on an ENVELOPE rather than trusting it to leave.** `sin(π · swept)` is nothing at both ends
and full where the band is over the middle of the face, so it grows in off one corner and dies into the
other. At the end of the visible crossing it is at 4% of peak and at the settle it is at 0.1% — there is
nothing left to park and nothing to pop. It also stops the whole gesture depending on a geometry this side of
the screen can only estimate, which is the deeper reason: **an effect that has to be carried off the element
to stop being seen is an effect betting on a number you have not measured.**

A nine-slice never scales a corner, so a bevel authored inside one is the same size on a 91px square and a
520px tooltip. **It was tried as a `UIGradient` first and that is the trap:** gradient offsets are fractions
of the element, so the crease grows with the panel and a big tooltip wears a bright wedge across its own
text. Below about 68px the corner cells shrink together, so the cut settles at a constant *fraction* of the
element instead of eating it — which is what carries the shape through the skill tree's 0.3–1.6 zoom without
knowing anything about zoom.

### The top-left corner is the PLATFORM'S — measured, 208 × 58

The Roblox unibar (the logo, chat and player list in one pill) is hard against the top-left corner, and
every HUD gui here sets `IgnoreGuiInset = true`, so nothing stops you drawing under it. **Measured in a
playtest rather than guessed:** `GuiService.TopbarInset` returns `min=208,0 max=1918,58` at a 1918×1080
viewport — the chrome owns the first **208 px across and 58 down**, and the rest of the strip is free,
which is why the Core's panel has always been fine sitting in it at x 730–1190.

**58 is the Studio figure and it is the bigger one.** `UITools.GuiEventInset` records the pair for the same
reason — **36 px in a game window, 58 in Studio** — so clearing 208 × 58 clears a real client with room
spare. Use the larger number: a guide should over-state an obstruction.

Two things follow:

- **`GuiService.TopbarInset` is the thing to read**, not `GetGuiInset()`. The latter gives only the strip's
  height; the Rect gives the horizontal extent too, which is what tells you the *centre* of the strip is
  usable and the left of it is not.
- **A bench cannot see this.** A UI Labs story draws in a plugin widget, which has no topbar, so the corner
  looks free — `Stories/Hud` had two arrangements put in it before anyone noticed. That bench now draws the
  measured footprint on its backdrop as a red block marked ROBLOX. **If a bench is being used to place
  something, it has to draw what the placement has to avoid.**

And one thing the measurement does *not* cover: **the pill expands.** Opening chat drops a window out of
that corner far bigger than 208 × 58, over anything down the left edge. Clearing the block is the floor,
not the whole argument.

### A caller must NOT add its own `UIPadding`

`facet` owns the padding. Two `UIPadding` on one parent is undefined. When migrating from `panel`, delete the
caller's and pass `Padding` instead — and remember the old `panel` callers reserved chrome *and then* padded
inside it, so the height arithmetic loses a term.

### Pad a CONTROL less than a PANEL

The default 20 is cut for a tooltip. On a 91px-tall button it ate more than half the interior and the word
came out at **46% of its old size**. Use ~14 for a button-height slab. It still clears the 16px cut because
what sits there is a few centred letters, not a paragraph reaching into the corners.

### A frame turned `Visible` draws where it was LAST laid out, for a frame or two

Setting `Visible = true` and a new `Position` in the same frame does **not** show it at the new position: the engine
draws the frame's previous layout first, then catches up. Anything hidden at its resting place and shown on the frame
its animation starts elsewhere flashes at the resting place and snaps. `task.defer` does not help (it resumes in the
same frame, before the render).

Seen twice: the SkillTree tooltip (old position, empty text) and the win box cards (2026-11-02), where every card
waited hidden at its grid slot and was shown on the frame it was thrown from the chest's mouth. With fifty cards, each
one flashed at its slot and snapped into the chest. A probe reading `AbsolutePosition` does **not** show it; the
numbers are right and only the drawn frame is wrong.

**The rule: never hide a moving thing with `Visible`.** Keep it visible and park it off-screen
(`UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0.5, 100000)`) until it is shown, with a boolean (`isThrown`) for what `Visible` used to mean, and
draw it in place the moment that flips. Check `Selectable` first: an off-screen selectable is still a gamepad target.
`Visible` stays fine for things that do not move when they appear (a flash, a face swapped in place).

### What a frame of UI costs: one write redoes the whole ScreenGui's VISIBLE elements

Measured 2026-11-09 (`performance/runui-2026-11-09/RESULTS.md`, with the probes that measured it):

- **Any write to a ScreenGui makes that frame redo every visible element in it**, even a write that moves nothing (a
  BackgroundTransparency). About 0.5 us an element on PC, fully transparent frames included. On a Samsung A13 each
  written ScreenGui also costs about 0.25 ms on its own, and a run frame wrote about 7.
- **Hidden (`Visible = false`) elements cost nothing**, and **writing a property its current value costs nothing**.
  So a closed screen is free for layout, and a draw that rewrites unchanged values is free.
- **A frame parked off-screen is visible**: it is redone every time its ScreenGui is written. Park only what needs it
  (the rule above), not a whole screen.
- **Touch input walks every ENABLED ScreenGui** each frame (1.26 ms on the A13). A screen that closes wraps its
  ScreenGui in `enableWhileShown(gui, { contentFrame })`: on in the frame the content turns Visible, off 2 s after it
  hid, so the close and its puffs finish first.
- **An ambient loop (a breath, drifting motes) draws at `pixelMotion.AmbientHz`**, 12 Hz: take
  `pixelMotion.AmbientGate()` when the element is built, call it once per step, and update the drawn pose and spawn
  motes only when it says so. Particles spawned steady (`isSteady`) already are. Hits, thumps, sparks and sheens stay
  every frame.
- **Moving an effect into its own ScreenGui helps only if it is that gui's only writer**; otherwise it adds a second
  written gui and its 0.25 ms on the phone.
- **Do not judge this from a forced read.** Reading `AbsolutePosition` after a write shows a cost per sibling (51 us for
  200 hidden pooled labels) that the real frame does not pay. Time the frame instead (`bench.lab2.client.luau`).

### Rotation: three traps, and why nothing on these screens turns any more

Nothing on the skill tree rotates (§4). These are why, kept because the next person to reach for `Rotation`
will meet all three.

1. **A rotated frame LIES about its size.** Roblox reports the **unrotated layout rect**, so a 96-unit square
   turned 45 measures 96 and *draws* 136. Anything positioning itself off its edge has to multiply by √2, or
   it lands on the point. That is what `VERB_REACH` was.
2. **A rotated `ImageLabel` is RESAMPLED, and a rotated nine-slice is nine quads resampled separately.** A
   3px lit edge is 3px measured square to itself in the file; sampled at 45° it spreads over four or five and
   does so unevenly along a run, the diagonals stair-step, and each of the nine seams rounds its own way.
   **Nothing the art can be authored against**, because what reaches the screen is no longer what is in the
   file. If a shape has to be drawn at an angle, author it AT that angle and draw it at `Rotation` 0: turn
   the geometry before it is rasterised, not the picture afterwards.
3. **A TURN TURNS THE LIGHT WITH IT.** Any art with a light direction in it, which is all of this art, states
   where the light comes from. Turn the element and the statement turns too: the streak across a cut corner
   lands somewhere that makes no sense, and on a diamond it landed at the left and right points, parallel to
   the flat and a few px inside it, so a tip read as an edge growing a second edge out of itself.
4. **A turned frame turns about its MIDDLE, whatever its AnchorPoint says.** A line anchored at one end and turned
   swings its far end AND its near end off where they should be: every diagonal wire on the skill tree's bench sat
   off both its squares. Place a turned line by its midpoint, with AnchorPoint (0.5, 0.5) (§5o).

### Uploading art: Decal id ≠ Image id

Open Cloud `asset_type: "Decal"` returns the **Decal's** id. `ImageLabel.Image` wants the **Image inside it**,
and handed the wrapper it **silently draws nothing** — no warning, no error, just an absent panel. Recover the
real id by `insert_model`-ing the decal and reading `Decal.Texture` from a playtest print. See
`reference-tripwire-asset-upload` in memory.

### The bevel is absolute UNTIL the element is thinner than two cells, and then the CELL sets the edge

A nine-slice never scales a corner — that is why the bevel lives in one (§8) — but Roblox does scale the
borders **down**, proportionally, the moment the element is smaller than the sum of them. A health bar always
is. So the lit edge, which is authored *inside* the corner cell, renders at

```
3 design px × min(1, height / (2 × cell))
```

and on anything short **the face's cell is the dial on how bright its outline looks.** Measured on the Core's
readout at 1080p (its HP bar is 37.8px tall and its shield strip 18.3):

| cell | HP bar | shield strip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 34 (`Cut`, `Table`, `SquareTable`) | 1.67px | 0.81px |
| 18 (`SquareCrown`, `Square`) | **3.00px** | **1.52px** |

The edge pictures are **identical along a straight run** — same profile, same peak, checked out of the PNGs —
so all of that difference is the shrink, and a line under a pixel wide loses brightness to coverage as well
as width. This is why the Core's bars are on `Square`: not for anything the face draws, for the cell it
carries. It is also why the shield strip still reads quieter than the bar under it at the same cell, which
happens to agree with what that readout wanted anyway.

**The same arithmetic is what `facetBar`'s crystal taper is worked out from**, and the reason a bar's cut
lands at about 8px rather than the authored 16.

**And it scales the CUT by the same factor**, which is the half of this that cost a round (§4): the whole
corner cell shrinks as one, so a face whose cell is halved to brighten its edge draws its corners twice as
deep along with it. Brightness and cut depth are one dial through the cell. Moving them apart means
re-authoring the cut, since the rendered cut is `height × cut / (2 × cell)` and the rendered edge is
`height × 3 / (2 × cell)` — equal ratios of `cut/cell` draw the same chamfer at any cell.

### A UIShadow feathers a BOX, so nothing with cut corners may wear a visible one

This is the rule that supersedes "depth is a shadow". A `UIShadow` is cast from its parent's rendered alpha
and then **feathered as a rectangle**, so on any shape that is not a rectangle it grows its own square
corners as soon as it is strong enough to see - which is the one shape this whole style exists to stop
drawing. Nothing in the HUD casts one: the hotbar slot, both health bars and the Core's panel all pass
`Shadow = false`, and none of them cast one before the conversion either.

**It is only safe where nobody could find a corner in it:** a slow breath in one colour on a dark screen.
Two survive on that basis — the hotbar's gold "something waiting here" pulse and the health bar's low-health
alarm — and both are faint and moving.

**"Faint" is a standard, not a feeling.** Both were first set at strengths that read as a square on a dark
screen: the alarm at transparency 0.35 with two pixels of spread, against a bloom whose own peak is 0.52.
They are held at **0.48–0.58 at their brightest, with no spread and a tight blur**, which is well under the
art that replaced every other glow in the HUD. If you can tell what shape a `UIShadow` is, it is too strong.

**To throw real light off a cut face, use the bloom art instead** (§5d). A blur authored into the silhouette
has the silhouette's shape by construction, which is the only way to get a halo the shape of the thing.

### Two frames that must meet have to be cut from ONE number — not positioned at a half, and not overlapped

Every edge of every frame rounds to a whole pixel **independently**, so two halves placed at 0.5 of a 97px
slot are asking to meet at 48.5 — and whether they do depends on where the parent's own box landed inside a
pixel. When they miss, the column between them is covered by neither and the world shows through it: one
pixel, the full height of the element. The hotbar's cooldown sweep wore exactly that down its middle.

**Overlapping them is worse, and it sounds obviously safe.** These faces are semi-transparent (the dark sits
at half alpha), so a strip covered by both is drawn twice and composites to three quarters. The bare hairline
became a *bright* one — the same bug in the other colour — and that one showed at rest as well as mid-sweep.

**Two things that touch cannot be made to touch by nudging them.** Take the element's own rounded pixel
width, floor half of it for the first, give the remainder to the second, and place both by **offset**. The
*arithmetic* is then exact at every width from 24 to 220px: nothing left over, nothing counted twice.

**But offsets under a `UIScale` are not integers either**, and that caveat is load-bearing. The hotbar's
selected slot carries one (1.1, plus the pick's pop), which multiplies both halves' offsets — so the
renderer is again rounding a position and a size independently and the boundary can land a pixel out on the
one slot you are looking at. If it shows there, the fix is not more arithmetic: put each sweep layer in a
**`CanvasGroup`**, draw the halves *opaque* inside it and let the group carry the layer's alpha. Overlap is
then free, because opaque over opaque is opaque, and one render target per layer is cheap beside the two
`ViewportFrame`s every filled slot already runs.

### A layer laid over another must answer every question that one answers

The crystal field added over the cooldown sweep took the gradient's half-plane mask but not the *other* two
tests the face beneath it passes — draw nothing at all until this half is reached, and switch the gradient
off once the half is wholly covered (the seam note below). With only the mask, it drew the sliver the
gradient's own edge leaves at its extreme: a lit line down the middle of a slot with nothing spent at all.
If you stack a layer on a layer, copy its whole state, not the obvious part of it.

### A `CanvasGroup` clips the shade off

A shadow lives outside the shape casting it, so a `facet` inside a `CanvasGroup` cut to its own size gets its
shade sliced off, leaving a hard line. Pass `Shadow = false` there (the skill tree's tooltip does).

### Don't give 54 nodes a shadow each

The skill tree's squares pass `Shadow = false`: the pool of light an owned square throws already lifts it off
the ground, and a second `UIShadow` each, to say a thing that is already being said, is the one place on that
map where the chrome is worth counting.

---

## 4. Shape is meaning

Every node on the skill tree is a square of 96 design units. What separates a cheap RUNG from a dear VERB is
which FACE it is drawn on, and nothing else: not its size, not its angle.

**It used to be the angle.** A verb was the rung's own art turned −45, which spans 136 and so said "dear" by
being half again as wide. That is gone, for two reasons that each cost a round of chasing the same artifact
(below). If you find yourself reaching for a turn to make something read as important, read those first.

### The skill tree is on FOUR faces, and none of them turns

A face is data — `facet.Faces`, a plane, an edge, a slice and the two lights it can throw — and a caller
picks one with `Face`. The default is `Cut`, the two-corner face every other screen still wears, so nothing
outside the tree moved. Picked from the bench in `Stories/SkillNodes` (kept, along with every candidate's
authoring code in `Assets/ui/authorshapes.py`):

| Surface | Face | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a cheap RUNG | `Table` | four corners cut, a lit chamfer behind every one |
| a dear VERB | `TableCrown` | the same face wearing the **stroke** |
