| the description | `SquareTable` | four corners **intact**, the corner art drawn across them |
| Back, and the points counter | `SquareCrown` | square and bare but for the stroke |

And four more, authored for the **Core's readout** rather than for the tree, in two rounds
(`Stories/CoreBars`, where the choice is still open):

| Surface | Face | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the Core's SHEET | `SquareTableLeft` | corners **square**, the corner art on the **left two** only |
| the Core's BARS | `TableBare` | `Table` exactly, with the corner art taken off |
| *(round one)* | `TableLeft` | cut on the left two corners, both lit; the right end square and bare |
| *(round one)* | `Square` | `SquareCrown` with the table line taken off — a bare lit outline at cell 18 |

**Both sheets answer the same question and the second one answers it more quietly.** The Core's mark stands
at the left end of that sheet and the mark *is* the crystal, so the light belongs on the side the crystal is
on; the end that holds the end of a bar is a straight line, and an angle there answers nothing. `TableLeft`
says it by **cutting** the two left corners, `SquareTableLeft` by **lighting** them and cutting nothing —
which is the distinction `SquareTable` already drew (is the corner gone, does the corner catch) taken one
step further: *which* corners.

**What comes off a bar face is whatever runs THROUGH the fill.** The table line came off `Square` because on
a bar it is not a second facet edge, it is two bright rules running the length of the fill 10 design px in
from each edge (10.0px on the HP bar, 5.1px on the shield strip, leaving 8.1px of clear fill between them).
The corner art came off `TableBare` for the same kind of reason: a lit chamfer is a statement about a corner,
and on a strip thirteen times as wide as it is tall the corners are most of what you see of the chrome.

**`TableBare` changes nothing else about `Table`, and that is the whole point of it.** Same 16px cuts, same
cell of 34, so the corner is cut exactly as deep as `Table`'s is — see the trap below, which is what the
first attempt at this face walked into.

**THE CELL SCALES THE CUT AND THE EDGE TOGETHER, so they are ONE dial.** §3 says the cell decides how thick
an edge draws on anything short; the half that is easy to miss is that it decides how deep the *cut* draws by
exactly the same factor, because the whole corner cell shrinks as one. `Chamfer` was this face's first cut —
`Table`'s 16px cuts at a cell of 20, to buy the brighter edge a small cell gives — and it drew a **15px
chamfer on a 37.8px bar against `Table`'s 9px**. It was deleted for that. The rendered cut is `height ×
cut / (2 × cell)` and the rendered edge is `height × 3 / (2 × cell)`, so the only way to move them apart is
to **re-author the cut**: a face cut at 8 on a cell of 17 draws `Table`'s own chamfer with twice the edge,
since `8/17 = 16/34`. Nothing does that today, and `TableBare` takes `Table`'s edge along with `Table`'s cut.

**Most of a new face is already uploaded.** A fill is the silhouette, a bloom is the silhouette's falloff and
a rim is the silhouette read inward, so a face that changes only which corners are *lit* changes only its
**edge** picture: `SquareTableLeft` is `SquareTable` plus one upload, `TableBare` is `Table` plus one, and
`Square` was `SquareCrown` plus one.
Check with a checksum before authoring — `md5sum` across `Assets/ui` after a run says exactly which pictures
are new and which came back byte for byte.

**A VERB IS NO LONGER A DIAMOND, and nothing on the map rotates.** §4 spent the *turn* to say "dear"; the
stroke says it instead — the table line of a cut gem, 10 design px inside the face's own outline, which is a
different picture rather than a different angle. Two things killed the turn, each of which cost a round:

- **A turn turns the LIGHT with it.** The streak across a cut corner is the second plane behind that cut, a
  statement that the light comes from the upper left. Turned −45 it landed at the diamond's left and right
  points, parallel to the flat and about ten screen px inside it, so a tip wore two parallel bright lines and
  read as an edge growing a second edge. Measured: fill `32/66/65`, the join `58/102/101` nine px inside the
  tip, the cut edge `120/190/189`, nothing outside the silhouette — and drawing the same shape as one
  seamless polygon reproduced it exactly, so it was the art, not the seams.
- **A rotated `ImageLabel` is resampled**, and a rotated nine-slice is nine quads resampled *separately*. A
  3px lit edge is 3px measured square to itself in the file; at 45° it spreads over four or five and does so
  unevenly along a run. Nothing the art can be authored against.

That retires the `GlyphTurn` trap below and the `VERB_REACH` fudge, and a verb is the same 96 units a rung
is, so the lattice keeps its spacing.

**The stroke stops at each corner facet rather than crossing it.** Drawn as a whole inset outline it runs
straight *through* every corner plane — the plane reaches the corner cell (34) and the line sits at 10 —
so each corner came out as a lit triangle with a line ruled across the middle of it. A table's edge on a
real stone ends where a corner facet begins.

**And a corner can carry the art without being cut** (`SquareTable`), which separates two questions that had
been stuck together: *is the corner gone* and *does the corner catch light*.

### A node's light is a PICTURE, not a `UIShadow` — and so is the hotbar's

`facet.Light` draws a bloomed copy of the face's own silhouette. Both of the tree's lights and the hotbar
slot's gold breath are on it; the rules it is built from are in §5d, and the two that bite are **blur
starves corners** (author the falloff from the distance) and **never scale a bloom to set its reach** (one
picture per light).

- It is a **sibling** of the face, never a child: it is bigger than the face on every side, and a child
  clipped to the face is no light at all.
- It sizes itself as `1 of its parent plus twice the margin`, so a caller hands it to a parent that is the
  face's own size and never restates that size.
- `Visible` says whether it is lit and the breath writes `ImageTransparency` — the split the `UIShadow`s had
  between `Enabled` and `Transparency`, kept so the per-frame pass writes only to lights that are on.
- The pool's 84 design px **is the lattice gap** (`GRID_STEP - NODE_SIZE`), so each square's light crosses
  the whole gap and two of them stack in the middle: that is what makes a bought arm read as one lit stretch
  of ground rather than a row of lamps. Move the step and it stops being true.
- The hotbar's light uses `Cut`'s, which is `TwoCrown`'s art: a bloom is the silhouette's falloff and the
  stroke lives in the edge picture, so a face cut on the same diagonal throws the same light.

### If you ever turn a node again

Nothing on the map turns any more (above), so these are kept as the two traps rather than as instructions.
The turn went on the node **container**, because a panel turned inside the tinted `CanvasGroup` has its
corners cropped — the group renders at its own size. And the glyph rode the turn back in its **own holder
frame**: `Rotation` must never be passed to `textShadow`, which draws the ink as a child of its own drop
shadow and hands both the same props, so the turn lands twice and the letters come out at ninety degrees to
the word they belong to.

---

## 5. Hierarchy — three surfaces, three voices

The panel was overused: the thing you buy, the thing telling you about it and the thing counting your money
all wore the identical face. A screen where those are one object has no hierarchy in it.

| Surface                    | Edge                        | Why                                             |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Nodes (rungs and verbs)    | the arm's own hue, + a light | the thing you buy; the loudest                 |
| Controls (buttons)         | `PALETTE.PaperRing`         | pressable, so legible                           |
| Tooltip                    | `PALETTE.Divider`           | a note held up in front of the map, not part of it |
| Persistent readouts        | `PALETTE.Divider`           | up all session, never asks to be pressed        |

**Colour is the thing being bought.** No unbought square has any: the map opens as a colourless lattice and
each square arrives in its arm's hue as it is paid for, so a lit arm is literally the shape of what the lord
owns. Keep that.

---

## 5b. Light, and how much of it

### A UIShadow glows the shape of what it is HUNG ON

This is the rule that matters, and it caused two separate problems here. A shadow is cast from its parent's
rendered alpha, so hanging one on a **cell** that merely contains an object gives you a glowing *box*, not a
glowing object — however small you make the numbers and whatever colour you paint it. The seed is a crystal
turning inside a square cell; recolouring its shadow fixed the temperature and left the shape wrong.

**To glow an OBJECT, cast from the object's own silhouette.** The fix is `modelPreview`'s trick: a second
picture of the same model, same camera, same turn, rendered flat (full ambient, black key, bodies opaque and
unlit) so the render *is* the outline, tinted on the way out and parked behind the real one. Hang the shadow
on **that**, and what gets feathered is the shard rather than the rectangle around it. See `SHARD_GLOW` in
`SkillTreeBody`. It costs a second ViewportFrame and a second set of parts — affordable for two cubes, and
emphatically not for a 200-part building, which is exactly what `modelPreview`'s own header warns about.

### Blur and spread are shares of the CASTER

**Historical: none of these three is a `UIShadow` any more** (§4, §5d). The rule is kept because it is true
of every `UIShadow` still in the game, and because it is the reason a light's reach is now stated in design
px rather than as a share: a share of the caster means the same light is a different light on every element
it is put on.

The same pair of numbers puts a far bigger halo round a big element than a small one. Two were badly out:

| Glow | Was | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Affordable (gold, per square) | blur 0.25 / spread 0.08 | 0.16 / 0.02 |
| Owned (arm hue, per square) | blur **1.05** / spread 0.22 | 0.5 / 0.05 |
| Hotbar slot | blur 0.35 / spread 0.12 | 0.2 / 0.03 |

The owned "pool" was a blur a whole square wide, so a lit arm read as fog with letters in it. What it still
has to do is **merge** — a run of squares should read as one lit stretch of ground rather than six lamps — so
it is set against the gap: a square is 96 units and its neighbour's middle is 150 away, so half a square of
blur still reaches the neighbour.

**Gold is what the points reach**, which is right on a square and wrong round the crystal the whole style is
derived from. The general rule: *an object that is the style's source lights itself; everything else may
borrow the shared signal colours.*

### Driving a silhouette copy

Pose the copy off **the same values as the original**, not off its own arithmetic — `SkillTreeBody` writes one
pair of CFrames and hands both sets of parts the same two. A silhouette that recomputes its own pose lands a
frame behind the thing casting it and reads as a smear rather than as its light. The copy also **dims with
its original**: the picture's `ImageColor3` is a multiplier on a lit render (so `WHITE` means "leave it
alone"), while the silhouette's *is* its colour (it is multiplying flat white), so the same state is two
different writes and the glow's is taken off its own authored tint.

### Connections

A link between two nodes is a **filament of light**, and the numbers are worth having because they are set
against the lattice rather than picked:

| | Was | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wire | 12 units inside a 4px near-black `UIStroke` | 6 units, **no stroke** |
| On screen at 0.3 / 0.95 / 1.6 zoom | 15.6 / 19.8 / 21.2 design px | 3.8 / 5.9 / 6.6 |
| Dash length / gap | 16 / 16 | 10 / 14 |
| Dash thickness | the wire's own | 0.6 of it (`DASH_THICKNESS_SHARE`) |

A dash drawn at full wire thickness on a **diagonal** link is a rotated square — a chip of gold rather than a
dotted line, which is what the old map was strewn with. `PALETTE.LineStroke` is deleted; do not reintroduce
one.

### Light on the STATE, not on the balance

The hotbar's shard slot glowed whenever the player *had* a point. Those come apart the moment someone saves:
one point toward a three-point verb lights the slot for as long as it takes to earn the other two, and a bar
that says "spend me" while nothing is buyable is a bar players learn to ignore. It now asks
`SkillTreeCore.CanSpend` — is anything on the frontier actually affordable — rather than reading the purse.
Ask the same question of any "you can act now" light.

## 5c. Motion — serious, and still juicy

The old motion was authored for an arcade feel: a 10-degree rotational knock on hover ringing out over 0.4s
at 0.2 damping, a hover lift that sailed well past its mark, a 13-unit refusal swing with three passes in it.
Modern and serious does **not** mean still. It means:

- **Rotation is the cartoon channel.** Spend almost none of it. The hover knock is 1.5 degrees over 0.2s, a
  glint rather than a wobble. Lift, scale and light carry the rest.
- **Fast attack, firm settle.** Shorter periods with much higher damping (0.6–0.85) reads as responsive; long
  periods with low damping reads as floaty and toy-like. The hover is 0.17s at 0.82.
- **Spend the flourish on the one moment that earns it.** The purchase keeps a real overshoot (0.26s at 0.58)
  because it is the only thing on the screen worth a flourish — a screen with no flourish anywhere is not
  restrained, it is dead. Everything else is restrained so that one reads.
- **A refusal is a jolt, not a swing.** One short hard knock that stops dead (7 units, 0.14s, 0.7 damping)
  reads as the control refusing; a wobble reads as the control playing.

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hover knock | 10°, 0.4s, 0.20 | 1.5°, 0.20s, 0.62 |
| Hover lift | 16, 0.30s, 0.30 | 14, 0.17s, 0.82 |
| Purchase pop | 0.34s, 0.42, squash 0.84 | 0.26s, 0.58, squash 0.88 |
| Refusal | 13, 0.26s, 0.18 | 7, 0.14s, 0.70 |

Things that FLY between elements (collects, bursts, payouts, a stream filling something) have their own
recipe, with its numbers and what was rejected, in §5j.

### A thing that ARRIVES and LEAVES is not a hover, and a spring is the wrong tool for it

A reaction to a cursor is a spring: it is interrupted constantly, it has no end, and easing toward a rest is
exactly right. **An entrance is not.** Both of its ends are the point — it has to start at nothing and land
on nothing — and a spring can only ever approach, so it spends its last frames on a hair of movement. That is
a thing *dissolving* rather than a thing being taken away. Drive it by hand over a stated number of seconds
and land it ON its number. `SkillTreeUI`'s shutter has done this since it was written; the wave title was
moved onto it, and the two now leave the same way.

**Three curves, and they are not interchangeable.** Keep all three around; which one a layer takes is decided
by what that layer *does*, not by which gesture it belongs to.

| | Shape | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `easeOutBack` | sails **9.9% past** its mark at 60% through, settles back | anything that MOVES, arriving |
| `easeInBack` | lifts **7% off** the mark, then runs out at **4.4× its average speed** | anything that MOVES, leaving |
| `1 - (1 - t)²` | away at once, gentle onto the mark, no overshoot | anything that APPEARS |

**BUT NOT FOR A WHOLE SCREEN OR ITS PIECES (§5o).** The back pair on the screens' own entrance, and on every tile
and square landing in it, was called "retro or cartoonish": one overshoot on a title is a flourish, and a window
plus forty tiles all sailing past their marks at once is a toy. A screen and everything that lands in it arrive on
Fluent's decelerate `(0, 0, 0, 1)` and leave on Material 3's standard accelerate `(0.3, 0, 1, 1)`
(`screenOpen.Ease`), and never pass their marks. The back pair stays for the single things this table was written
for (the wave title, the OPEN row's buttons) and for the purchase.

- **A curve that overshoots a POSITION leans; one that overshoots a TRANSPARENCY clips at 1 and stalls.**
  That is the whole rule. Running a whole gesture on the smooth curve reads **robotic** — it lands and leaves
  without ever going past. Running all of it on the back pair reads as a snap.
- **A reveal may be slow onto its mark and never out of the gate.** An ease-*in*-out is `2t²` at the start,
  which leaves at a dead stop: a wipe run on one sat still for three or four frames and the title read as
  arriving a beat *after* the wave it was announcing. The frame a reveal is asked for is the frame the thing
  it announces happened on.
- **Changing the gesture means re-picking the curve.** `easeOutBack` is 70% of the way through at a fifth of
  its time, so a *wipe* on it crosses in 5 frames of a 24-frame sweep — exactly the snap the wipe replaced.
- **One clock underneath, read through two shapes.** Keep the raw linear travel and derive both, so the
  sprung half and the swept half cannot drift.

### A SIZE is punchy and a TRANSPARENCY is not

Two ways to make a thing appear from its own middle, and they feel completely different. Neither is better;
**picking between them is a decision, not an implementation detail.**

- **Stretch it** — walk its `Size` out of nothing and clip what stands on it. Reads as a thing *snapping*
  open. Cheap, honest, and the only option when what is arriving has to look physical.
- **Wipe it** — a `UIGradient` whose opaque radius grows from the centre with a soft edge beyond. Reads as a
  thing *arriving*. Nothing moves and nothing changes shape.

Four things bite on the wipe, and all four cost a round:

- **Put it on the GROUP, not on the layers.** A `CanvasGroup` renders everything into one canvas and a
  gradient on it fades *that*, so a plate, its light, two ends and two lines of type are taken by one edge
  and cannot disagree about where it is. Per layer it is six gradients, each in its own element's space —
  and a mirrored element's space is turned 180.
- **Then SIZE that group to the content.** A gradient's fractions are of the element it hangs on. Left at
  full-screen width while the title was a fifth of it, the sweep spent its first fifth and its last fifth
  crossing empty screen: everything that could be *seen* happened in **9 frames of 24**, which reads as an
  animation that either did not play or was over before it started. Solve the radius's reach off the two
  boxes as well, or its last third clears a margin with nothing in it.
- **Leave a SHORT fade under it, not none.** Once the wipe takes the title away, dropping the alpha ramp
  entirely trades one pop for another, because anything near the middle of a centre-out window is uncovered
  inside a frame. Three frames of fade takes the edge off the frame the reveal starts on without being what
  anyone reads.
- **The kick has to live somewhere.** A `UIScale` outside the group means the canvas is rasterised at 1:1 and
  then scaled — a resample of the type while it moves. Inside, it clips at the canvas edge. Pick knowingly.

### Scale the SURFACE, not the announcement — and then clip what stands on it

When something opens by size: scale the **plate**, and keep the type and the ends as its **siblings** so they
hold their size and their place while the surface under them moves. A `UIScale` on the lot is the whole thing
zooming, which is a different and much cheaper-looking effect.

But **siblings are not carried by a scale either**, and that is the half that is easy to miss — the plate
opened past two ends and a line of words that were simply *there*, arriving and leaving on their opacity
alone. So the clipping window has to close on **the axis the gesture opens on**, at the plate's own width,
locked to the same number. Then everything on the plate is uncovered exactly as the plate reaches it.

- **`ClipsDescendants` DOES NOT CLIP A ROTATED DESCENDANT, and a `CanvasGroup` does.** A mirrored half of a
  pair — one picture turned 180 — was the one thing the window could not uncover: it arrived and left on its
  opacity while its twin was revealed properly. A group renders into a canvas of its own size, so what falls
  outside is not drawn whatever angle it is at. Keep `GroupTransparency` at 0 or the children are flattened
  first and faded together, which is a different picture from each carrying its own.
- **A window has to clear everything the thing draws AT REST** — the plate, its light's `BloomReach` on both
  sides, and the tallest a live knob can push the type — or it crops while standing still.

## 5d. Lit surfaces — the bloom and the crystal

Two images exist for surfaces that are **lit** rather than merely drawn. Neither is part of a plain panel.

### `FacetBloom` — light in the shape of the thing

The octagon with a soft falloff authored **outside** it. It exists because `UIShadow` cannot be used here
(§3): a blur authored into the silhouette has the silhouette's shape by construction.

**A BLUR OF A SILHOUETTE STARVES ITS CORNERS; author the falloff from the DISTANCE instead.** At a corner
less of the shape is nearby than at the middle of an edge, so a blurred halo is weaker there and dies
sooner. Measured off a bench screenshot of a square node: one pixel out reads 21 against an edge and **8**
against a corner, and the corner's glow is gone by 4px where the edge's is still going at 6. A halo that
thins at every corner does not *wrap* the thing it comes off — it reads as light leaking out of the flat
sides, which is the same complaint a `UIShadow` earns from the other direction.

Taking the signed distance to the outline and running `GLOW_ALPHA · ½ · erfc(d / σ√2)` over it gives one
profile that holds all the way round — the same band at an edge, at a 45° cut and at a right angle, rounding
off at a corner because distance does. **It is the same profile a blur gives against a *straight* edge** (a
Gaussian's own integral), so nothing about the strength on the face's own edge moves; it just stops falling
apart where two edges meet. `authorshapes.py`'s `distance_field` does it exactly, for convex shapes, as the
smallest point-to-segment distance over the outline's edges. **The node blooms are authored this way and
`FacetGlow` is not yet** — it is a long bar, where the corners are a small share of the outline, but the
same swap is waiting for it.

**AND ONE BLOOM PER LIGHT: never scale a bloom to set its reach.** Scaling the art scales *everything* in
it, and the silhouette is in it. The nodes ran two lights off one picture — a tight gold offer and a wide
pool — by drawing it at `k` times its authored margin, and at the offer's `k` of 0.37 the halo's cut came
out **3.5px deep against the face's 8.5**: the light poked five pixels past the cut at every corner, glow
sticking out exactly where the shape has no corner. A plain square never showed it, having no cut to
disagree with, which is how it was finally caught — the bug was invisible on the shape it was blamed on and
obvious on the shape used as the control.

So each light's falloff is baked at its own reach (`authorshapes.py`'s `LIGHTS`: 24 design px of margin at
σ 7 for the offer, 84 at σ 26 for the pool) and **both are drawn at the same `SliceScale` the face is**. At
that scale one design px of art is one design px on screen, so the silhouette inside the bloom is the
face's silhouette to the pixel and its cut is the face's cut. The caller grows the layer by twice the
light's margin and nothing else. Verified on the art: the face's cut begins 6px along the diagonal and both
blooms' cuts begin at the same 6, inside a pixel of sampling.

**What it is.** One Gaussian, σ 12 at peak 0.52, inside 42px of margin — and it was two. It was authored as
a tight core over a long tail, and what the bench came back with had the tight pass at a twentieth of the
long one's strength. Checked across the whole image, the tight pass decides **zero pixels**: the long one
sits above it everywhere it has any value at all. A pass that never shows is not a subtle pass.

**Drawing it.**

- Authored **inset by `BloomReach` on every side**, so a caller draws it at the face's size **grown by twice
  that** and the octagon inside lands exactly on the face.
- **A GLOW SCALES WITH ITS BAR; the rest of the cut face does not.** This is the one place the absolute rule
  breaks. Everything else is absolute because a nine-slice never scales a corner — the cut is the same pixels
  on a slot and on a tooltip, which is the whole reason the bevel lives in a corner cell. Light is not a
  crease: light off a bigger object is bigger. At a fixed 42px the glow is a fifth of a tall bar's height and
  a third of a short one's — one file, one set of numbers, two looks. Measured: dialled on a 72px bar and
  drawn on the game's 35px one, the same art read 16% of the bar's brightness a fifth of a bar-height out on
  the bench and **40%** in the game.
- **So the layer's growth AND its `SliceScale` both ride the bar's own rendered height** (`BLOOM_TUNED_HEIGHT`
  = 72, the height it was dialled at). The viewport's scale cancels out of both — the bar's height in screen
  px already carries it — so neither needs a `scaleNumber`. The art's inset then lands on the bar at every
  size and the corner cells always just fit, because the whole geometry is proportional.
- The margin has to hold **3σ** or the tail is cut off square at the image's edge.

**Authoring it.**

- **Do not paint the silhouette back in at full strength.** The first cut did, to make the bloom "light
  coming out of the face", and it put a *step* in the alpha at the boundary — opaque inside, half the peak
  one pixel out. A step in an alpha is an edge, and the bar wore a thick coloured stroke instead of a glow.
  The blur alone has no step anywhere, and the part falling inside the face is hidden by the face. A Gaussian
  sits at **half** its peak on the shape's own boundary, so the authored peak is twice what shows there.

**Masking it to the fill** — three separate bugs lived here, and all three are worth knowing.

- **The mask is a RAMP, not a step.** A step is right for a fill, whose end is a real edge, and wrong for a
  glow, whose end is the whole point — masked with a step, a bar at two thirds has its halo sliced off down a
  razor-straight vertical line.
- **The ramp is CENTRED on the fill's end, not started there.** Arithmetic, not taste: the art is flat at
  0.85 through the middle of the bar and falls to 0.42 at its own edge, so a ramp still at full strength
  where the fill ends would glow twice as hard there as the same bar's top and bottom. Run from one reach
  before to one reach after, it sits at half where the fill ends — `0.85 × 0.5 = 0.42` — and all three edges
  agree.
- **How deep the ramp cuts walks to nothing over the last reach of the bar.** Two things are both true: in
  the middle of a bar the art has no falloff to lean on, so the mask must supply the whole of one; at a full
  bar the fill's end *is* the bar's end, where the art's falloff already lives, so a mask there attenuates
  twice. Answering that with "a full bar is not masked at all" makes it a **step** — everything up to 0.999
  carries the ramp and 1.000 throws it away, so a bar healing to full snaps its glow on in one frame. Blend
  instead: `depth = clamp((1 - fill) · w / reach, 0, 1)`, which is 1 in the middle of the bar, walks to 0 over
  the last reach, and reaches "not masked at all" **continuously**. Checked over the last 4% of fill in
  thousandths, the biggest single step is 0.037.

### A BLOOM IS FLAT AT PEAK INSIDE ITS OWN SILHOUETTE, so it needs an OPAQUE face in front of it

The line above — "the part falling inside the face is hidden by the face" — is a **requirement**, not an
observation, and reading it as an observation cost two rounds of tuning the wrong number.

The picture is a Gaussian of the distance to the outline: half its peak **on** the outline, dying away
outside, and **full peak everywhere inside**. Put one behind a face you can see through and what shows is
that interior: a flat plate, brighter in the MIDDLE of the thing than at its edge. Measured on the special
badge's gem, through a face at 0.32 transparency: **0.260 in the middle against 0.130 on the outline.** It
reads as a second object sitting behind the first rather than as light coming off it.

**And tightening the reach makes it worse, which is the tell.** A crop throws away the soft outside and
keeps the flat inside, so the halo gets HARDER the tighter it is asked to be. If a glow is going more
plate-like as you shrink it, stop shrinking it and go and look at what is in front of it.

So: the face over a bloom is opaque, and it runs out to the **outline** rather than to the inside of
whatever sits on the outline. Leaving a band between the face and a ring exposes a strip of the interior,
which is the same bug wearing a smaller coat.

### A DIAMOND'S BLOOM IS A SQUARE'S, TURNED — and that is one of the two places a turn is allowed

`SquareTable`'s silhouette is a plain square with its corners left intact, so its bloom turned 45 is a
diamond's bloom **exactly** rather than approximately. Every one of §4's three objections to turning art is
about something a bloom does not have: there is no 3px lit edge in it to spread unevenly, no light direction
baked in to be turned with it (a bloom is one falloff measured from the outline, the same all the way
round), and no nine-slice seam — because it is drawn **stretched**, not sliced. Slicing it and turning it
would be nine quads resampled separately, which is the thing the rule forbids.

**Stretching a bloom is not the rule it looks like, either.** "Never scale a bloom to set its reach" is
about a halo whose cut stops agreeing with a face's ABSOLUTE cut, and what makes that cut absolute is a
nine-sliced corner cell. A diamond has no cut and no corner cell: it is one angle at every size, so a
uniform scale keeps the silhouette exactly on the gem and carries the falloff with it.

The geometry is the picture's own: it spans `(cell + margin) * 2 + 4` design px with the silhouette inset by
the margin on every side, so drawing it at `gem × image / silhouette × share` lands the silhouette at
`share` of the gem. Read both numbers off `facet` rather than writing them down, or a re-authored light
leaves the caller behind.

**A share of 1.0 is the CEILING and not a round number.** At 1.0 the silhouette sits exactly on the face's
own outline, so the glow leaves the face at half its peak — where a Gaussian sits on the boundary it was cut
from — and everything flat is behind the face. Past 1.0 the flat middle starts coming out from under the
face and the plate comes back.

### The REACH and the WEIGHT are two dials and they FIGHT

Dropping a light's alpha dims the edge of the thing **and** pulls the tail in with it. Raising the
silhouette's share pushes the tail out **and** brightens the edge. So "flatter, over the same footprint" is
a PAIR of numbers, and guessing at one of them walks the other. Solve for it: of every pair that holds the
reach where it was, take the one that puts the least light on the object's own edge. On the badge that was
share 1.00 with the layer at 0.24, which held the footprint at 7px and took the edge from 0.132 to 0.060.

### `FacetCrystal` — the light breaks

A field of low-poly facets, white and nothing else, laid over a lit fill and masked to the same edge.

- **`ScaleType.Crop`, not `Stretch` and not `Tile`.** Tiled, a 128px tile repeats four and a half times
  across a health bar and reads as wallpaper. *Stretched*, the authored field is squashed onto whatever the
  caller asked for — 280x64 onto a 544x35 bar is three and a half times flatter than it was drawn, and what
  comes out is a row of slivers with the resampling showing in them. Crop scales it to **cover** the box at
  its own aspect and discards the overflow, so a facet is the shape it was drawn at on every bar.
- **It is the one layer that is not the plane's octagon**, so its square corners would hang over the two
  cuts — and **Roblox has no alpha mask for UI to cut it with.** `ClipsDescendants` clips to a rectangle and
  nothing else, and the `AlphaMask` feature request has been open on the forum for years. So the shape has
  to come from the art or from the gradient.
- **Fade it out at both ends; do not hold it in.** Holding the rectangle in by the cut's width was tried and
  is worse than the problem — both ends of the bar lose their facets outright and read as bare. A taper in
  the gradient the layer already carries puts the pattern all the way to both ends and leaves nothing to
  hang over them, because there is nothing left by the time it arrives. It costs no art and no second pass.
- The taper is **1.6× the cut's *rendered* width**, which is not `facet.Cut`: a nine-slice shrinks its corner
  cells to fit an element under two of them, and a bar always is — `Cut · min(1, w/2·Cell, h/2·Cell)`, about
  8px on a 35px-tall bar rather than 16.
- **Every facet catches light; none is painted dark.** A dark facet is an outline with area, and rule 2 has
  not changed.
- **No line between two facets.** There was one — a hairline along every edge, brighter than either plane,
  on the reasoning that a break in a crystal is a line. That is not how a low-poly field reads: what
  separates two planes is that they sit at different angles to the light, so the only thing between them is
  the **step between their two values**. Drawn as a line as well, the field reads as a wireframe laid over
  the bar. No facet goes fully dark either, or the field breaks into islands.
- The lattice is drawn one cell **past** the frame and cropped, so the facets meeting the edge are whole
  triangles cut by the frame rather than triangles that stopped short of it.

## 5e. What was picked, and what the losers taught

The hotbar slot was drawn four ways, the health bar five, the badge five and the build slot four. They lived
in one file apiece behind a single word, were drawn at once on one bench driven off one event, and were
looked at side by side — because a variant judged on its own is judged against a memory of the last one.
**The choice is made and the losers are deleted**, which is what picking one means here; this section is the
record.

### How a round actually runs

The build slot is the one that went end to end in one stretch, so it is the shape to copy:

1. **Draw the candidates so they differ on the OPEN QUESTIONS and nothing else.** Everything that is not
   being chosen — the entrances, the springs, the state colours, the box the picture gets — is held identical
   across all of them, or the bench is comparing amounts of juice. The build slots varied on *what is cut*
   and *where the light comes from*, and gave the building the same 150 design px whatever chrome they
   wrapped round it.
2. **Include a do-nothing control.** `Shelf` cut nothing and lit almost nothing. It lost first and earned its
   place by losing: it is what the screen already *was*, so beating it is the minimum any candidate has to do.
3. **Draw them at the size and place the game draws them**, on one bench, off one clock — one pick picks in
   all of them, one purse drains all of them (§10e).
4. **Expect the winner to be ASSEMBLED, not chosen.** `Niche` is `Socket` plus `Plinth`'s blooms at
   `Ledger`'s size. Each loser was the control for exactly one half of it, which is why the round is worth
   running at all — a straight vote on four finished things would have picked the least wrong one.
5. **Then delete them, and shrink the bench to the winner.** A bench that outlives its round goes on
   inviting a comparison that is over.

**What deleting is worth is more than the lines.** Taking the three losers out was 94 lines of component and
85 of bench — but it also took a `Variant` word, a `BOXES` table, a `TSlotBox` type and a `CostInside` branch
that every piece of slot arithmetic had to be written *through*. One shape is one number. The wrapper frame
and list layout each slot carried so a price could hang under it went too, because the winner's face holds
the price. **The abstraction a variant set needs is a real cost, and it is only paid back while the round is
open.**

**The node faces went the other way, on purpose** (§4): `Stories/SkillNodes` and every candidate's authoring
code were kept. The difference is that the four winners are four *different* surfaces rather than one, so the
bench is still the only place they can be compared against each other and against the ones that lost.

**The bench survives it**: `src/FeedTheCore/Client/UI/Stories/Chrome.story.luau` now draws the three bars the
game actually has at the three heights it draws them at, plus the hotbar row, with buttons for Hit, Bleed,
Heal, Refill, Low, Overshield, Pick next, Spend, Recover, Add / Drop a tool and Fade. That comparison still
matters: **the bloom scales off the bar's own height**, so a glow that reads right on the player's bar has to
read right on the Core's thin shield strip too.

### The slot — `Socket`

Each of the losers put "this is the one you are holding" in one place: `Cut` on the cut **edge** (the face
stays dark, the edge walks to white), `Well` in the **face** (a recess that fills with light from the floor),
`Glint` on the **cut itself** (a darker resting edge, and a band of light crossing the face on the press).

What was asked for was all three at once, and that is `Socket`: the slot is a **hole cut in the face** with
the tool standing in it, and picking it lights the hole from the floor, walks the cut edge to white, and
strikes a band of light across the face along the same 45 degrees the corners are taken off at.

### The bar — `Crystal`

`Cut` was flat colour; `Ember` added the bloom; `Crystal` added the crystal field over the fill. Two others
were not merely beaten, they **failed**, and those are the ones worth keeping:

- **`Bevel` — a lit leading edge.** The last 2% of the fill in a brighter version of the fill's colour, so
  the edge would read as a cut catching light. It does not: on a 35px bar it reads as **a patch of a
  different colour stuck on the end**, and it read that way both when it was pink against orange (a real bug
  — it sampled the ramp's *head* instead of the edge) and after that was corrected to a lifted orange. **A
  highlight has to be both the colour of what it highlights *and* narrow enough to read as a line**, and at
  any width that survives on a bar this short it is neither. Without it `Bevel` was `Cut` exactly.
- **`Vein` — the light living inside the fill**, dim at the tail and blazing at the edge. It reads as a bar
  that is half unlit rather than as light in stone: on a health bar, *dim* is a state the player already has
  a meaning for, and spending it on decoration fights the reading.

**The colour is the caller's, not the face's.** `facetBar.EmberRamp` is the crimson-to-orange walk measured
off the reference; the Core's bars wear the same bloom and the same facets in their own ice blue.

**And so is HOW MUCH OF THE CRYSTAL FIELD SHOWS** (`facetBar.CrystalTransparency`), because the field is
white and what white does to a fill depends entirely on the fill. At the 0.6 it was dialled at — 40% white
over the colour — it lifts the lord's crimson head by **70 points of luma**, the Core's ice head by 30, and
the Core's shield strip by **16 on a base of 215**, which is under a tenth. The field is drawn on every bar
in the game; on the pale ones it may as well not be. That is not a bug in the number, it is a number that
was set on one bar and used on three, and the fix is that the strength travels with the colour.

**The Core's two bars carry 0.2**, which is 80% white over the fill: the HP head lifts by 60 and the shield
strip's by 32, so the planes in the stone read on ice the way they already read on fire. The lord's bar keeps
the 0.6 it was dialled at.

**And which CUT a bar is drawn on is a caller's too, as of `facetBar.Face`** — a table or a getter, exactly
as `facet`'s own (§2). It reaches the track, the fill and every layer between them, because the whole reason
a cut-face bar works is that the fill is a second copy of the track's octagon. **Two things do not follow
it:** the bloom is `facet.Bloom`, one picture authored at the shipped two-cut silhouette and the only
bar-sized glow there is (the per-face lights are the tree's, at 24 and 84 design px against this one's 42),
and the crystal field's end taper is worked out off `facet.Cut`. So a sweep compares the plane, the lit edge
and the shape the fill ends in; at the corners the halo stays the two-cut one. `Stories/CoreBars` (§10e) is
the bench that sweeps it, and `CoreHealthUI` takes all three of its surfaces' faces the way `BuildBarUI`
takes its two.

### A bar's LENGTH is free, and on the lord's bar it is now the body

`facetBar` draws the fill as a *share* of the track, so what the track's own **length** says is the caller's
to decide — and every bar in the game was saying nothing with it. A fixed-length bar cannot tell twenty
points of health from a hundred and seventy without the number printed on it, and worse: **a square that
raises the maximum registers as the fill sliding backwards**, which is the opposite of what was bought.

`HealthPlayerUI` spends the length on the maximum, which is Valheim's bar. It is 0.09 of the screen at the
body a lord stands up with and 0.30 — what it has always drawn at — once the whole Constitution arm is
bought, walked linearly between. Both ends are real states rather than picked (`Data/Passives/MaxHealth`'s
BaseValue of 20; that plus the Shard's 10 and seven rungs at 20 = 170), and the floor is set against the
readout printed on it, not against the ceiling: at 0.09 the bar is 173 px on a 1920-wide screen and "20/20"
wants about 73. The two ends are a slider pair on `Stories/Hud` while the arrangement is being picked.

Three things fall out of it, worth knowing before putting growth on another bar:

- **The anchor point decides which way it grows**, and that is the whole of it — pinned by its left edge it
  grows rightward, pinned by its middle it grows out of the middle both ways. Do not compute a direction.
- **`facetBar` already survives a track that changes length**, because its bloom and its crystal field read
  the *rendered* size off the layout rather than off what the caller asked for (that is what `barSize` is
  for). A hit's shards come off wherever the cut actually is on the frame of the blow.
- **The growth gets a little overshoot and the fill under it does not** (14 / 0.7). A square being bought is
  one of the few things on this HUD that earns a flourish (§5c); the fill is a *reading*, and a reading that
  wobbles is lying.

**The Core's bar deliberately does not do this.** Its maximum moves by 250 a fortress level, so the same
rule would want a bar several screens wide — and the Core's panel is the one object on the HUD whose size is
not up for negotiation.

### The Core's MARK — four were drawn, the drawn diamond shipped

The thing at the left end of the Core's readout says *this is the Core and not a boss's bar*. Four answers
were drawn in `CoreHealthUI` behind one word and swept on `Stories/CoreBars`; **`Diamond` shipped and the
other three are deleted**, which is what picking one means here.

| | What it was |
| --- | --- |
| **`Diamond`** ✔ | a square Frame turned 45° with a paler square inside it, drawn rather than pictured |
| `Mark` | the game's own **Shard mark** — a cube on its corner *is* a hexagon, three faces meeting in a gap |
| `MarkLit` | the same mark with the light it throws, as its own blurred picture |
| `Model` | the **real Neon crystal** in a `ViewportFrame`, at the size the server spawns it, turning |

**The winner changed on the way through, and rule 2 is what changed it.** The diamond wore a **white
`UIStroke`** — an outline drawn round it in paint — and it wears a **white bloom** now: the same statement
made by what a crystal *does* rather than by a line round where it ends. Set at **0.2** off a ladder of five
drawn at 4× (§10c), which is the loud end of it: the art bakes its own peak at 0.52, so that is 0.42 of white
on the brightest pixel of the halo. The mark is the one thing on this readout that is a light rather than a
reading, and it is what says the bar belongs to the Core at all, so it is allowed to be the brightest object
on the sheet. A quieter rung was tried first and lost by eye in Studio, which is where a number like this
gets settled (§10c: the eye beats the measurement, and by a lot).

**A diamond's bloom is a square's, turned** (§5d), and it is hung as a **child of the turned gem** rather
than as a sibling: a child rides its parent's rotation, so a square bloom parented there comes out at the
same 45° and lands on the gem exactly, with no second `Rotation` to keep in step. `ZIndex = -1` puts it
behind the gem's own face, which is where light coming off something has to be.

**What the losers were worth keeping a record of:**

- **The Shard mark already existed and had never been hung.** `authoricons.py` draws nineteen marks and the
  tree uses eighteen; the seed draws the shard's own model instead, so `Shard` was authored, uploaded and
  left out of `Marks.luau`. It is still there, and so is the **glow** authored for it in the same pass
  (`authoricons.py`'s `glow` — a blur rather than the faces' distance field, because a mark is one picture at
  one size with no corner cell to match a neighbour's, and a glyph with holes has no silhouette to measure a
  distance to). Decals `76252588243663` and `109820379148288` if the question ever reopens.
- **`Model` was cheap to build and expensive to leave on.** There is no Core model to clone —
  `CoreService.buildCoreModel` assembles a Neon `Part` at `CORE_SIZE` and stands it on its corner with
  `AwakeningCore.DIAMOND` — so the variant built the same part the same way, and pinned the Model's
  `WorldPivot`, because `modelPreview` pivots what it is handed to the identity and a Model's default pivot
  is its bounding box. The real cost is that **a `ViewportFrame` renders every frame it is `Visible`**,
  whatever else is true, and this readout is mounted for the whole run rather than built when it comes up.

### What no variant ever touched, because it is what the object DOES

- **The slot:** the arrival and the exit, the neighbours' flinch, the pick's spin and pop, the cooldown sweep
  (drawn on the cut silhouette, not a rectangle), the gold "something waiting" breath, and the **flash** —
  one wash of white on the frame of the press, the only part of the punch that lands on the press itself
  rather than three frames later when the springs have moved.
- **The bar:** two springs chasing one number with the band between them (white while it is taken, warm while
  it is given back), the flash, the **shards** thrown off the cut on a real hit, and the alarm.

### The build slot — four were drawn, one shipped

The build bar (`UI/BuildBarUI.luau`) is on the cut face, and converting it opened the one question the old
bar never answered: **what a slot IS.** It was an invisible hit area with a picture floating on the bar's
sheet, and every bit of "this is the one you picked" was carried by the picture growing, rising and washing
to white.

Four answers were drawn, lived behind one word, and were judged 2×2 on one bench off one clock over four
rounds. **`Niche` shipped and the other three are deleted**, which is what picking one means here.

| | What is cut | Lit by | Box |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`Niche`** ✔ | a **hole**, and the whole tile is it | the hole from its floor, the cut edge to white, a band across the 45 — **and** a bloom thrown outward on what the stores cover | holds the **price** |
| `Socket` | a hole in the bar, the hotbar's own slot | the hole, the edge, the band | the picture's square |
| `Plinth` | a **tile** on the bar | **outward** only | the picture's square |
| `Ledger` | a tile holding the price | **within**: the fill walks to white and dips under the thumb | holds the price |
| `Shelf` | nothing | a pool under the picked one | the picture's square |

**The winner was assembled out of the losers, which is the bench doing its actual job.** `Niche` is `Socket`
plus `Plinth`'s blooms at `Ledger`'s size — so each of the three was the control for exactly one half of it,
and none of them was wasted. `Shelf`, the do-nothing control, died first and earned its place by dying: a row
of pictures on a bare sheet is what the bar already *was*.

**The whole tile is the hole, price included**, which is a decision and not a consequence: a recess cut only
round the picture puts the plaque on a ledge *outside* the niche, which is two objects. The rule separates
the building from what it costs **inside** the one recess, the way a shelf does inside an alcove.

**What every candidate held identical**, so the bench compared the open questions rather than four amounts of
juice: the row assembling on its stagger, the grow, lift, turn and kick the picture takes, the grey drain and
reddened price line, the pop when the stores come to cover a slot, the card, the refusal, the bar's own face —
and **the picture's box**. Every one handed the building the same 150 design px however much chrome it wrapped
round it. A slot judged with a bigger picture in it wins for the picture; it is the rule the badge's five
shapes were held to (§5h).

**What deleting them was worth**, since the file kept them for one round after the choice was made: 94 lines
out of the component, 85 out of the bench, and — more than either — a `Variant` word, a `BOXES` table, a
`TSlotBox` type and a `CostInside` branch that every piece of slot arithmetic had to be written through. One
shape is one number; the wrapper Frame and list layout each slot carried so a price could hang *under* it went
with them, because the face holds the price.

### The boss bar — four were drawn, `Banner` shipped

The boss's bar (`UI/BossHealthUI`, GnG's bossHealthUI: shown only for a boss not yet beaten this run) was drawn
four ways, benched on `Stories/BossBar` off one set of numbers, and **`Banner` shipped**; the other three are
deleted and the bench is shrunk to the winner and the Core's readout beside it.

| | What it was | How it came and went |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`Banner`** ✔ | no sheet: the name spaced out and **centred** over a long thin bar, one small square per balloon at the left end of the name's line | unfurls out of its own middle, furls back into it |
| `Twin` | GnG's own: a sheet the Core's width, the Bloater's mark at its left end, one bar | dropped in like the Core's |
| `Sacs` | the Core's sheet with a plate per sac, going dark with a flash as each is shot off | plates lit one after another |
| `Tab` | a name tab over a narrower sheet, ticks under the bar at the thresholds | slid out from behind the Core's readout |

**Two changes came with the pick:**

- **The balloons, not the thresholds.** The banner first carried the brood thresholds (75/50/25%) as cuts across
  the bar; they crossed its number and were taken off for a square per balloon on the name's line (9 design px,
  5 apart), lit in the bar's bile while it hangs and fading to dark as it is shot off. That is `Sacs`' idea at the
  banner's size: shooting the balloons off is how the fight is won, and where the next brood drops is not.
- **The boss takes the TOP line and the Core's readout steps down for it**, which is GnG's stack the other way
  up: the boss is the fight while it is up. `CoreHealthUI.MakeRoom(share)` slides the readout down on a
  critically damped spring (`ROOM_PERIOD` 0.4, pinned before every move per §5g) and back up with 0;
  `BossHealthUI.Room` is what it asks for, and WaveController passes one to the other in an effect. **The two
  moves are staggered so they never cross**: the Core starts down 0.22s before the banner opens into the space,
  and the banner is furled 0.3s before the Core comes back up. Started on the same frame, the banner would
  unfurl across the Core's sheet while the sheet is still on its way down.

### A CROWN face has a table line inside it, and content has to clear it

`TableCrown` and `SquareCrown` carry the gem's table line **10 design px inside the outline, 2 wide** — so it
occupies 9 to 11 and anything drawn inside the face has to start at **11**. A caller that does not reserve it
runs its content straight through the line, and the one thing on the face that says *this surface is dear*
reads as a scratch across whatever is on top of it.

**It is a number on the face** (`facet.Faces[x].Stroke`, 0 on a face without one), not a rule about names:
"anything ending in Crown has a stroke" is true today and is exactly the kind of thing that stops being true
the first time a face is renamed.

**The box GROWS; the content does not shrink** — at least where the content is a fixed footprint. The build
bar's row is a fixed width centred in the face, so 2 × 11 more face is 11 more air on every side and nothing
inside has to know; a bar on `SquareCrown` comes out 828 × 282 against 806 × 260, and its bottom edge still
lands on 0.85 because the resting place is worked back from there. Where the content *is* a share of the box
— the building inside a slot — there is nothing to grow into, so that one gives up the 11: a 150px slot on a
crown face hands the picture 128, which is 73% of the area.

### A PANEL'S AIR IS THE SAME ON ALL FOUR SIDES, so reserve headroom on neither

This went wrong twice on the same number and the second time is the instructive one.

The build bar reserved the grow and the lift a picked slot spends — 24 design px — as **headroom over the
row**, and aligned the row to the bottom of it. That drew **36 px above the columns against 12 below**: the
reservation had become the thing you see. Centring the row fixed the top against the bottom and left the real
fault standing, because the sides only ever get the face's own padding — so it was then 24 top and bottom
against 12 left and right, and on a `SquareCrown` sheet (below) 35 against 23. *A reservation on one axis is
a reservation you can see.*

**The reserve is gone rather than balanced.** Nothing here clips, so it was only ever about the bar looking
like it contains its row — and on the two variants whose face holds the price, the picture already has
`LEDGER_PAD_PX` of air inside its own tile to rise into, which is the absorber the bar was standing in for.
The bar now reserves the column and nothing else, so the air is `padding + stroke` on every side: 12 on a
plain face, 23 on a crown one. A picked slot's art clears its face by 4 design px on the big box and crosses
it by 6 on the small one, which is stated where those two are built.

**On a crown face the air is measured from where the TABLE LINE ends, not from the edge** (`face.Stroke`, 11).
The pack's doll had its slots 20 in from the edge and 24 above its rule, which past the line is 9 against 24;
its header sat 24 in where its grid sat 40. Both read as the top being cramped. The doll now uses one air past
the line on all sides and down to the rule, and the pack puts its header at the grid's own inset.

**If a gesture genuinely needs room to spend, give it to the thing it belongs to** — the tile's own pad here —
not to the panel around it, where it lands on one axis and reads as a layout mistake.

### The card's juice: the knock went, the typewriter stayed

The build bar's description card arrived with the skill tree's **punch** — struck 3.5° off square and shaken
straight. That is gone: rotation is the cartoon channel and this interface spends almost none of it (§5c),
the same punch was deleted off the skill tree for the same reason, and a rotated nine-slice is resampled
besides (§4). It was the **last element rotation left** in either file — the only `Rotation` remaining is a
`UIGradient`'s, which is a ramp's angle and not a turned quad.

**What says "arrived" instead is a RISE and a FADE**, which is what §5c says to spend once the rotation is
gone. One target, **two springs** (§5f): the fade is an acknowledgement and is there on the frame the cursor
lands (0.12s), the rise is a movement and has to be readable (0.28s over 8 design px). Both critically
damped — a note held up in front of a menu that bounces is a note being cute about it. The card comes *up*
out of the row it belongs to rather than being hit into place.

**The typewriter was taken out in the same pass and put back, and that is the lesson.** "Rework the juice"
was read as *everything the card does as motion*, and the typing is not that: it is how the card **puts
itself together**, and a card that is simply there gets skipped by an eye that has already decided which slot
it wants. A rotational knock and a progressive reveal are both "retro" in a sentence and are not the same
kind of thing at all — **one is a flourish laid on top of the object, the other is the object arriving.**
Take the flourish; leave the arrival.

### A readout does not bounce when it is hit

The Core's readout (`CoreHealthUI`) kicked its whole sheet to 1.16 on an underdamped spring on every blow,
GnG's `DOPunchScale`. It was cut (2026-09-16): a persistent readout bouncing on each hit is the old toy
chrome, not the cut face. **A blow is a colour, not a movement**: the sheet stings red and falls back
(`Sting`), and the bar's own flash and chips say where it landed. The arrival's drop stays, because it is
critically damped: it slides onto its line rather than bouncing. The same holds for any bar or panel that
is read rather than pressed.

### A ceiling going UP is celebrated, and the sheet MOVES for it

A fortress level raises the Core's maximum by 250 and heals it by the same 250, so a full Core goes from
full to full. The readout came up, sat and left, and the only change was a number nobody was reading. The
raise (`CoreHealthUI.Raise`, tuning in its `RAISE` table) is the answer. The first cut was light, colour and
a number with the sheet held still, on the rule above, and it was sent back (2026-10-09): "I expect the
thing to move, shake or do other thing when the bar is being filled up and upgraded". **The rule above is
about a HIT. A reward is allowed to move the readout**, and a reward that is only light reads as a status
changing:

| Beat | What | Numbers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lead | only if the readout was away: let the drop finish first | 0.2 s |
| Charge | the sheet's edge lights and the sheet pulls in; the old numbers are still held | 0.12 s, edge to 0.55, size to 0.96 |
| Sweep | a comet of white crosses the track, the gain colour stands on the fill behind it, the numbers roll, the sheet trembles harder as the light goes | 0.5 s on `0.35t + 0.65t²`; a reach of 2 growing to 5 design px |
| Strike | the numbers land, the bar flashes, the sheet is thrown out past its size and jolted, an outline leaves it, `+250` is printed at the bar's end | size 0.96 to 1.09 in one frame, jolt 8 px; the outline 26 design px over 0.45 s |
| After | the sheet comes back with no pass under its size, the wash and the edge fall back; the chip stands, then lifts away | size `(1-t)³` over 0.35 s, jolt `(1-t)²` over 0.3 s; wash 0.6 s, edge 0.7 s; chip 0.2 in, 1.5 held, 0.3 out |

- **Roll the value and its ceiling by the SAME share.** `(c0 + dc·s) / (m0 + dm·s)` only ever moves from the
  old share to the new one, so a full bar stays full and a hurt one climbs. Re-basing first and filling
  after is the fill sliding backwards (above, "A bar's LENGTH is free"). The printed number rolls for free,
  because the bar is handed the rolled values.
- **The curve pulls INTO the landing.** An ease-out has the numbers crawl onto the new ceiling, which reads
  as a readout settling. This one is at 1.65 of its average speed on the frame it stops.
- **Only the SHEET moves** (a `Sheet` frame with a `UIScale`, about its own middle). The slot it stands in,
  the outlines leaving it and the chip beside it are not carried along.
- **A tremble is two sines a side at rates that never line up, read off the clock**, written in whole px.
  The reach is not what is seen: a reach of 5 is a shudder of 1 to 2 px ending at 3 to 4. Simulate it at
  60 a second before picking the number; the first pick (2.5) rounded to nothing for most of the sweep.
- **The chip is where the bar would have grown**, off its right end, since the Core's bar cannot grow. It is
  the one thing allowed past its mark: a single thing arriving once (§5c).
- **A ring is a STROKE on an empty frame, never a copy of the surface.** The first cut threw the sheet's own
  `Edge` picture twice, which is the sheet drawn again with its lit corners and bevel. The prompt's
  shockwaves (`PromptUI`) are a `UIStroke` with miter joins on a transparent frame, and these are now the
  same: 3 design px, one weight the whole way out.
- **Off a wide sheet it grows by PIXELS, not by scale**: `Size = (1, 2g, 1, 2g)`. A scale on a shape this
  wide runs off the screen sideways before it has moved at all upward.
- **The light is the bar's, the clock is the readout's.** `facetBar`'s `Surge = { Head, Wash }` is two
  getters, so a bar handed none builds no layers, and every source is written back to exactly 0 at the end.
- **A raise on top of a raise** restarts the roll from the numbers on the bars that frame, and the chip
  prints the sum.

The bench is `Stories/CoreBars`: `Core: a fortress level` is the server's raise (ceiling and heal together),
and `Show: time scale` slows it.

### Every light on the build bar is WHITE

Two of them were gold: the light pooling in a picked socket, and the bloom a building the stores cover
throws. Gold is what this interface says *you can act on this* in — the affordable skill square, the waiting
hotbar slot, the dotted wires — and carrying it onto a menu where **every** slot can be acted on was the
colour claiming something it could not deliver. White is what the picture's own tint already brightens to, so
a lit slot is one statement in one ink.

The cost is that the offer and the pool now differ in **degree** rather than in kind (0.72 against 0.36),
which §5f otherwise forbids. It is allowed there because neither is ever the only signal: a picked slot is
also grown, lifted, turned and washed to white, and a covered one is the only one whose price is not red.

### Ink round a letter is a SHARE of the letter, on the build bar too

The build bar pinned a flat `3` for both the outline and the drop shadow on every label it draws — which on
a 22px price is **13.6% of the letter against the HUD's own 6.25%**, so a two-digit cost wore more than twice
the ink anything else on screen wears and read as a sticker. §6 already had the rule; this screen had not
taken it.

It uses `STROKE_SHARE = 0.07` and `SHADOW_SHARE = 0.0625` now — **AmmoUI's and WaveUI's own numbers**, "2 at
32" — so the price comes out at 2 and 1 where it was 3 and 3, and the card and the refusal at 2 and 2. The
outline is still rounded pixels and still reads heavier on a small letter, which is §6's open problem and not
this screen's.

### An EMPTY band is louder than anything you could put in it

The X leads the build bar's row and has no price, so its price block was drawn **blank** — and on a tile that
rules a line and then shows a band of nothing, blank reads as *a slot whose price failed to load*, not as *a
slot that has no price*. The hole is the loudest thing in the column.

**What goes there is the fact a player actually hesitates over, not the fact the band is shaped to ask.** A
price band asks *what does this cost*, and the true answer for the X is "nothing" — but nobody hesitates over
that. What stops anyone pulling a building down is the fear of losing what it cost, and nothing is lost
(`BuildablesCore.DEMOLISH_REFUND` is whole), so the band says **`REFUND`**: one word, in the place, size and
colour a price line takes, on the row its neighbours' first price line sits on.

It is a field on the option (`Note`) rather than a branch on *is this the X*, and it is read only when the
cost is empty — so it can never quietly stand in for a price that does exist.

## 5f. How a surface answers the cursor

§5c settled how *far* things move. This settles what a surface does while a pointer is actually on it,
which is a different question and the one the chrome was still not answering: a skill square today lifts,
takes a degree and a half of knock, and shrinks to 0.92 while the mouse is down. All three are **state**
(and the knock is gone entirely — see below).
Nothing on the face answers *where* the pointer is, and nothing at all lands on the frame of the press.

**The bench is `src/FeedTheCore/Client/UI/Stories/SkillReact.story.luau`** and nothing below is wired into
the tree yet. It started as five reaction packages against the map's current behaviour; **that is decided
and the losers are deleted** (§5e), and what is left is three *kinds* of pressable thing and the question
of whether they read as three different kinds:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **RUNG** | the cheap half of the map — one number moved |
| **VERB** | the dear half — a new thing he can *do* |
| **BACK** | the way out |

Three rows: the **pair** side by side; a wired **run** at map spacing with the verb standing third in it;
and the way out beside the loudest upgrade there is.

### Before any of it: get the pointer's position right

Everything below is driven by one number, where the cursor is inside the element, 0..1 on each axis. **That
number is not `(event.Y - AbsolutePosition.Y) / AbsoluteSize.Y`**, because the two are in different spaces
and the answer comes out a whole GUI inset low (§3). Use `pointerIn`, which takes `UITools.GuiEventInset`
off first.

It is worth knowing what a wrong one looks like, because it does not look like a bug: every layer moves, the
springs are smooth, nothing errors, and the screen simply feels **off**. The whole of §5f was tuned on a
bench that had the same error in it, so the bench agreed with the game and neither was right.

### The reaction, now that it is one

Every specimen gets all of it; what differs is how much, and which gestures a kind is allowed at all.

- **The bearing** — one ramp across the face turned at the cursor. It beat a round spot, which reads as a
  lamp held against a gem rather than the gem catching anything.
- **The rim** — `FacetInner`, the inner shadow done as light.
- **The shine behind** — the face's own bloom, lit by the cursor rather than by the rules.
- **The cut edge** walking toward white, a little.
- **The press** is the light swelling plus the square going in, both on the fast spring so both land on the
  frame the button went down on.

### What makes a VERB dear

A verb already differs in its *face* — the same square wearing a gem's table line (§4). What it lacked was
a louder reaction, which is the half a lord actually feels.

**More of the same is not enough on its own.** A difference of degree is one he has to hold two squares in
his head to notice; a difference of **kind** is one he can see on the square in front of him. So a verb
gets both:

| | Rung | Verb |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every light | ×1 | **×1.35** |
| The lift | ×1 | **×1.25** |
| Overshoot | 1.06 | **1.10** |
| On commit | one band across the 45 | **two, on both diagonals, a beat apart** |
| Shockwave | one | one, further |

**A rung catches the light on one facet and a verb on two** — which is exactly what the extra line in its
art is there to say. The second band is a *beat* behind the first: two bands struck on one frame are one smear.
(A second, later shockwave was tried here and is not used in this game: one ring.)

### The reference was a glossy button, and two of its three lights translate

| It has | Here |
| --- | --- |
| a shine **behind** it | the bloom the face already throws (`facet.Light`), lit by the **cursor** rather than by the rules — and **faint**: on the reference you have to look for it |
| a shine **inside** it that follows the mouse | new; there is no radial gradient in Roblox, so it is built (below) |
| an **inner shadow** the shine stops at | drawn as an **absence of light**, not as ink (below) |
| the shine **expanding** on the click | the whole of the press signal; there is no flash |

### The bearing is not inset, and the spot was — the reason is what each one IS

- **A spot is a lamp shining ON a surface**, so it stops short of the rim and the band it leaves is the
  depth the reference's inner shadow draws.
- **A bearing IS the surface catching light**, so it runs all the way to the cut — inset, the face reads as
  a sticker with a lit picture on it rather than as a plane tipped toward something.

The bearing won on both objects, so **nothing is inset any more** and the whole spot — the `CanvasGroup`,
the two-bump product, the inset band and the pointer remap — is deleted. The paragraphs below are kept
because the *technique* is the only way to get a radial light in Roblox UI and the next screen that wants
one should not rediscover it.

### A BEARING on a non-square element

§3 says a rotated `UIGradient`'s nought-to-one ramp spans about the element's **height** rather than its
length. That makes a bearing a square's light by default — and the control row puts one on a 260×91 button
anyway, to see what a button wearing the square's light reads as. Two things are needed to make it usable,
and both are no-ops on a square:

1. **The boundary has to TRAVEL, not pivot.** With the ramp only ~91px on a 260px object, a centred pivot
   is one soft edge parked at the middle flipping sides as the cursor crosses it. An `Offset` of
   `(u−0.5, v−0.5) × 0.5` walks the whole front along the slab under the pointer.
2. **The angle has to be flattened toward the long axis** — `atan2((v−0.5) / aspect, u−0.5)`. A wide object
   has almost no vertical room for a ramp, so a cursor near the horizontal middle stands the ramp on end
   and the button goes flat. Dividing the vertical part by the aspect collapses the angle toward the only
   axis with room in it.

**It still goes quiet when the cursor is near the horizontal centre** — rendered, the lit share of the face
drops from ~0.26 at either end to 0.17 in the middle — and that is inherent to a one-dimensional light on a
wide object rather than something left unfixed. A blob does not have the problem, which is the argument for
keeping the blob on buttons.

### The inner shadow, drawn as absence

A dark band round the inside of a rim is an outline with area — the exact thing the old chrome was thrown
out for, so rule 2 will not let it be painted. **But what the reference's inner shadow actually does is
stop the glow short of the edge**, and that comes free from the light simply not reaching there: the spot
is drawn on the face's own silhouette **inset by a few design px** (10 on a square, 8 on a control), at the
same `SliceScale`, so the cut stays the same depth in px and a band of untouched face is left all the way
round. It reads as depth either way, and nothing dark was drawn.

The **rim** on top of that is the same statement said as light — a cut stone pipes light along the *inside*
of a facet edge — so the two stack rather than compete: a lit band at the very edge, then a band the spot
never crosses, then the moving light.

**The press is the shine EXPANDING, and there is no white flash.** There was one — a wash of white over the
whole face on the frame the button went down, on the argument that everything else in a press is a movement
and arrives late. Right about the problem, wrong about the answer: *a face that goes white has stopped
being the object for a frame.* The spot's growth is on the same fast spring and lands on the same frame.
A square with no spot at all still has the rim brightening and the press-in, both immediate.

### `FacetInner` — the rim, and it is the bloom's other half

A third art family beside the fill/edge pair and the blooms, authored by `authorshapes.py`'s `author_inner`
off the **same exact distance field** the blooms are cut from, read on the other side of the line: a
Gaussian at **peak on the outline**, dying inward over σ 10 design px. That stands it back to back with the
bloom — one band of light sitting *on* the cut edge, of which the bloom is the half outside the face and
this is the half inside it.

- **Authored at full alpha**, unlike the blooms, which bake `GLOW_ALPHA` in. A bloom is a *state*; a rim is
  a *reaction*, so its strength is a number the caller writes every frame and the picture is only the shape.
- **The cell has to hold 3σ.** A nine-slice stretches its centre cell on both axes, so whatever sits in the
  middle of the picture is what the middle of every face wearing it is painted with. Measured: 34 against
  σ 10 leaves the centre at **0.0000**, and the profile holds all the way round — one design px in reads
  0.996 at an edge *and* 0.996 down a corner diagonal, against the 21-vs-8 a blur gives (§5d).
- **One picture per SILHOUETTE, not per face**: three cover all six, because a verb is a rung wearing a
  stroke and the stroke lives in the *edge* picture. Decal ids `107300377138351` (Table/TableCrown),
  `107873372539354` (the square-cornered three), `75161145027754` (TwoCrown, which is `Cut`'s outline),
  plus `76701856276896` — `SquareCrown` at **σ 5**, the controls' hairline (below).
  **These are decal ids and `facet` needs the image ids** — the bench opens and prints them (§8).

### A mouse-following spotlight, with no radial gradient and no alpha mask

`UIGradient` is linear, and Roblox has neither a radial gradient nor an alpha mask for UI. The spot is
built out of what there is:

1. the face's **own plane picture**, masked by a bump along X centred on the pointer;
2. inside a **`CanvasGroup`** carrying a bump along Y.

The group flattens its child into one surface and its own gradient multiplies *that*, so what comes out is
the **product of two one-dimensional bumps** — a blob centred where they cross. Because what is masked is
the plane image, the light is inside the cut by construction and can never spill past a corner.

Three facts this rests on, each of which will otherwise cost an hour:

- **A `UIGradient` does not reach descendants.** It affects the object it is parented to and nothing else.
  That is the *only* reason the `CanvasGroup` is there; two gradients on one object is not a thing.
- **`Offset` is in the ELEMENT's space whatever `Rotation` is.** X moves the ramp across and Y moves it
  down, even on the one turned 90.
- **A turned ramp is only true on a roughly SQUARE element** (§3) — which a node is, and which the group is
  sized to. Do not lift this onto a bar.

It also **lags the cursor by 0.09s on purpose**. A highlight welded to the pointer reads as a decal stuck
to the mouse; one that arrives a breath later reads as light, which has somewhere to travel from. 0.09s is
under the ~100ms floor where a delay starts being read as lag, so it costs nothing in responsiveness.

### A soft light with a hard end: the mask must be a WINDOW, not a triangle

The first cut of the spot had a plainly visible boundary — "I can see where it finishes" — and **the cause
is not the strength**. A `NumberSequence` interpolates **linearly** between keypoints, so a three-point
bump is a *triangle*: constant slope out to the last keypoint, then zero. **A jump in the SLOPE of an alpha
reads as an edge** even where the alpha itself is continuous (it is Mach banding), so the light kept a hard
rim however faint the middle was made.

Use a **Hann window** — `0.5·(1 + cos(π·d/radius))` — which has zero slope at *both* ends and at the
peak, so there is no corner anywhere in it. Sampled at 8 steps a side it fits in **19 keypoints**, inside
Roblox's limit of 20. Measured, at radius 0.34: worst slope jump **1.79 against the triangle's 5.88**, and
what is left is sampling residue in the middle of the curve rather than a corner at its edge — which is the
half that shows.

**And a press must SPREAD a soft light, not tighten it.** The press used to narrow the spot *and* brighten
it — the two things that make a soft edge legible — so the one gesture the light had to survive was the one
that gave it away. It grows instead (0.34 → 0.62 on a square, 0.46 → 1.25 on a control) and lifts only a
little: the light floods out from under the thumb.

### A radius can be bigger than the element it is drawn on

A keypoint cannot sit outside `[0, 1]`, so clamping the window to fit caps the press at "half the element"
and the flood stops being a flood. Instead **sample the curve over the span it can reach and evaluate it at
its true radius**: past half an element the window comes out *truncated*, sitting at a real value on the
element's own edge rather than being shrunk to fit. Measured: at radius 1.25 the edge sits at 0.655 — light
running off the side of the thing, which is what the reference does on click.

**The endpoints must carry the evaluated value, not "transparent".** Forced to 1 they put a step back at
the very edge, which is the exact defect the window exists to remove.

### A round light on a wide object needs two different fractions

Each gradient's bump is a fraction of **its own axis**, so handing both the same number on a slab 2.84
times wider than it is tall asks for a blob 2.84 times wider than it is tall. The radius is stated in shares
of the **height**, and the X bump takes `radius × height / width`.

**And that aspect is the LIT box's, not the face's.** Insetting a 260×91 slab by 8 a side leaves 244×75,
which is 3.24 : 1 rather than 2.84 — a light made round against the wrong one of those is not round.

### The rise and the light are two different speeds

Hanging both on one spring is what made the hover feel snatched. A rise is a **movement** and has to be
readable; a light is an **acknowledgement** and has to be there on the frame the cursor lands. One target,
two springs:

| | Was | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The lift | 0.17s at 0.82 — arrives and **ticks**, because 0.82 still overshoots and settles back | 0.28s at **1.0**, critically damped, no overshoot at all |
| Every light on it | the same spring | 0.12s at 1.0 |

The travel stays the map's own 14. This is not a retreat from §5c's "fast attack, firm settle" — it is that
rule applied to two channels that were sharing one spring and wanted opposite answers.

### The three states must differ in KIND, not in strength

§5b set the hover *lift* by state (1 / 0.55 / 0.3) and left every other channel at full. That is not enough
once there are other channels: a reaction that is the same on a square he owns, one he can reach and one he
can actually buy has told him the thing he already knew — the pointer is here — and none of the thing he
was asking, which is whether this is a **decision**. Worse, a press wrote full strength on *all* of them,
so pressing an owned square lit it exactly like an affordable one.

| | Lift | Rim | Spot | Back | Edge | Commit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Affordable** | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| **Reachable** | 0.55 | 0.7 | 0.55 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Owned** | 0.3 | 0.45 | 0.45 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

**Only an affordable square throws light OUTWARD.** A square reaching past its own edge is a square asking
to be pressed, so the back shine and the edge ignition are affordable-only; reachable gets the rim and a
weaker spot, so it is alive under the hand without inviting a press that would be refused; owned gets a
