faint rim and barely any lift, because there is nothing to do there.

**But an owned square still blooms inside when it is pressed.** Its spot is faint on hover and real under
the thumb, because both the strength and the radius ride the press. *"You already own this"* is not the
same message as *"nothing happened"*, and a press that lights nothing at all is a press the screen did not
hear.

**What every state gets on the press is the light swelling and the square going in** — both immediate, both
true of any press on any square. The band, the shockwave and the overshoot say *something happened*, and on
a square he owns or cannot afford nothing did: a screen that celebrates a press the server is about to
refuse has told him he bought something. That is the `Commit` column.

### A saturated hue is a spotlight, not a field — and a bloom is a field

The affordable bloom read as "not part of this screen", and measuring the palette says exactly why.
**`SkillTreePalette` has three chroma tiers**, and they are what hold it together:

| Tier | Chroma | What wears it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | 0.014 – 0.076 | the sky, the paper, the lettering, the wires |
| The arms | **0.072**, every one | the six rings and sheets |
| Signals | 0.132 – 0.155 | the points, a gain, a cost — **all of them digits or single words** |

The offer bloom shipped at **0.100 — in none of them.** Three outliers at once: 39% more saturated than
any arm, lighter (0.908) than everything but the lettering, and **138° round the wheel** from the body's
own violet (306.9°, read off the crystal). The rest of the screen is a tight *analogous* family — every
structural colour sits between hue 268 and 307 — so the one thing 138° away is the one thing that reads as
borrowed from another game.

**And it is the largest area of colour on the map.** The offer light reaches 24 design px past a 96-unit
square on every side: `144² / 96² =` **2.2× the square's own area**. Every other colour at that chroma is a
digit. A saturated hue works as a spotlight and fails as a field.

**So the line keeps the gold and the light loses the paint.** `Dash` (a few px wide) stays at 0.100;
`Offer` is the same hue at **L 0.94, C 0.055** — *under* the arms' own chroma — which is also what light
that bright physically does: it whitens toward its core rather than getting more yellow. Derived with
`hueOf(Dash)` so the two golds can never drift.

| | rgb | L | C | vs sky | vs an owned Scavenging pool |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shipped | 255,220,146 | 0.908 | 0.100 | 12.8 | 0.134 |
| **`Offer`** | **252,233,194** | **0.940** | **0.055** | **14.1** | **0.162** |

That last column is the one real confusion this palette can have — Scavenging sits 23° from the gold on
purpose ("the furthest from gold that still reads as loot") — and the change moves them further apart, not
closer.

**The rest of the palette measured clean.** The analogous violet spine, the six arms locked to one
lightness and one chroma, and the three-tier chroma system are all doing what they say. The only other
thing near a line is `Xp` at C 0.095, above the arms — but it is a 8px strip, so it is a spotlight and it
is fine.

### One light colour per state, and nothing new ever appears

The rim, the spot, the shine behind and the shockwave all take **one** colour, and it is whatever light
that state is **already showing**. It used to be the arm's hue always, which put a *teal* rim inside a
square already throwing a *gold* offer bloom — two unrelated lights on one object — and a coloured halo on
a square drawn dark, which is a colour arriving from nowhere.

| State | Already shows | So it lights in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Affordable | the gold offer bloom | `PALETTE.Dash` |
| Owned | the arm-hue pool | `BranchRing[arm]` |
| Reachable | nothing | its own dimmed ring, `stone(BranchRingUnlit[arm])` |

**This retires "gold is not available to a hover."** That rule was guarding against the map saying *you can
afford this* about a square he cannot — but the light only goes gold in the state where he **can**, so it
is consistent rather than misleading. A control lights in its own edge (`PaperRing`) for the same reason.

### Nothing on the lattice moves except the square under the cursor

Two things were taken out here and neither should come back:

- **The knock.** A cursor used to knock a square 1.5° off square. Rotation is the cartoon channel (§5c),
  this was the last of it on the screen, and it resamples a nine-slice besides (§4).
- **The shove.** Neighbours moved out of the hovered square's way. A hovered square *rises*, which pulls
  its wires **into** it; neighbours moving outward push them the other direction, so the two gestures fight
  and the run reads as the map drifting. Moving the neighbours *toward* it instead would mean moving every
  square on the map to stay consistent — a map that will not hold still to be read.

One square rises. Nothing else moves.

### An UPGRADE and a BUTTON cannot wear the same reaction

They are different kinds of object, and a screen where they feel alike is a screen where pressing BACK
feels like buying something. The rule both are built on:

> **A thing you TAKE comes toward you and is lit from OUTSIDE.** It rises, it blooms past its own edge, it
> throws a shockwave when it is bought, and it overshoots coming back.
> **A thing you OPERATE holds still and is lit from WITHIN.** No lift at all, no bloom behind it, no
> shockwave, no overshoot — its own **fill** walks toward white, and the press goes IN.

One is a gem catching light; the other is a key with a lamp under it. In numbers:

| | Upgrade | Control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lift | 14 design px | **0** |
| Lit by | bloom behind, rim, spot laid over it | its own fill (`WASH_LIFT` 0.14, dipping to −0.08 on press) plus the spot |
| Rim reach | σ 10, dying at ~24 design px | σ 5, **a hairline, gone by 12** |
| Bloom behind | 0.34 transparency | **0.86** — present, and you have to look for it |
| State lights | pool and offer | none — a button is never anything but pressable |
| Press | 0.92 | **0.965** — a slab three times as wide losing 8% reads as the screen flinching |
| On release | shockwave, overshoot, band | nothing |

**A control gets no travelling band and no shockwave.** Both are *commit* gestures for a thing that was
bought; on a button they are flourishes on an object whose whole job is to be pressed and got past.

The control's rim is a **second picture**, not the same one drawn smaller: the reach is baked into the art
(§5d's one-bloom-per-light rule, in its other form), and `SquareCrown`'s own cell is 18 anyway. Decal
`76701856276896`.

### Split the press-in from the pop

The map writes `0.92` into the **same underdamped spring** an arrival pops out of (0.26s at 0.58), so the
press-*in* wobbles its way down over a quarter of a second. The channel whose whole job is to say "heard
you" is the slowest thing on the square, and that alone is most of why a click feels soft.

Two springs instead: the press-in rides a fast critically damped one (0.09s at 1) and is down and still
inside a tenth of a second; the overshoot is a second spring struck on release. **The only thing that ever
wobbles is the flourish that earned it.** It is the bench's `Snap` channel — turn it on and off on its own
before looking at any of the light.

### A scope gets 200 locals, and a constants block can hit it

Landing this in `SkillTreeUI` added about thirty module-level constants and the file stopped loading:
`Out of local registers when trying to allocate COST_HEX: exceeded limit 200`. **Luau allows any one scope
200 locals**, a module's top level is a scope, and neither linter can see it — only running it does.

The fix is the idiom that file already used for `POOL`, `PULSE` and `BACK`: group related constants into
one `table.freeze({...})`. One table is one register, and it reads better anyway. `ANSWER`, `BEARING`,
`RIM`, `TILT`, `VERB`, `BAND`, `WAVE` and `REACT` are that, and they took ~34 registers back to 8.

### The rest of the vocabulary, and what each one is for

| Channel | What it says | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Back bloom lit by the cursor | "this is under your hand" | none; art exists |
| Lit rim | depth, and half the inner shadow's job | one picture per silhouette |
| Bearing (a ramp) | where the pointer is, and the press. A flat facet tips to a light; it does not carry a hotspot | one gradient; wants a square, and needs two corrections anywhere else |
| Cut edge to white | the light on this square went up | none |
| Fill wash | a **control** lighting from within | none |
| Parallax at two depths (glyph with the pointer, back bloom against it) | the tile is tipping, with **no rotation**. Never the rim: a band inside the edge that moves either crosses the cut or leaves a bare strip | none |
| Glint at 45° | **the release**, said as the face catching light. Twice on a **verb** | none |
| Shockwave in the edge picture | something was bought | none |

**A shockwave is the EDGE picture, grown by the ELEMENT at a fixed `SliceScale`** — so the 3px line stays
3px and the cut stays the same depth in px while the octagon gets bigger. Scaling the art fattens both, and
the ring stops being the face's own shape on the way out (§5d's rule, in its other form).

**That goes for the PURCHASE ring too, and it was the last rectangle on the screen.** The burst's expanding
ring was a `Frame` wearing a `UIStroke`, which can only ever be a rectangle — so the one moment a lord is
actually watching a square, it fired a square ring off an octagon. It is the bought square's own edge
picture now, and *which* face is set when it is **fired**, because the ring is pooled and a rung, a verb
and the seed are not all cut the same. One `faceOf(node)` decides it for the square and for anything thrown
off the square, so the two can never disagree.

The line no longer thins as it travels, and that is a real loss taken knowingly: thinning a nine-slice
means shrinking its `SliceScale`, which moves the **cut** with it, so the octagon would stop agreeing with
the face halfway out. The fade carries the dying on its own.

---

## 5g. What a reaction costs when nobody is touching it

A reaction is paid for on every square, not just the one under the hand. The skill map draws ~54 of them, so
everything below is multiplied by 54 before it reaches a frame.

### A vide spring that returns to ZERO never settles

**This is the one to know.** Vide retires a spring when it is inside `|x0 − target| / 10000` — where `x0`
is the **last position WRITTEN to it** with `config{position=}`, *not* where it currently is. A spring
nobody has written has `x0 = 0`. So on the way **back down to a target of 0**, its tolerance is exactly
zero — and an exponential decay approaches zero without ever reaching it.

Measured against vide's own settle condition:

| | x0 written? | settles in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| press 0→1 | yes (0 vs 1) | 34 frames, 0.28s |
| press 1→**0** | **no** | **never inside a minute** |
| press 1→0, pinned | yes | 34 frames, 0.28s |
| lift 1→0, pinned | yes | 79 frames, 0.66s |
| rim 1→0, pinned | yes | 40 frames, 0.33s |

**And a stepping spring is not idle — vide re-runs every layer hanging off it, every frame.** A map where a
lord has brushed twenty squares is hundreds of property writes a frame that say nothing, and it only grows
as he plays.

**The fix costs nothing visible: write the position it is ALREADY AT before moving the target.**
`config{position = current()}` does not move the picture; it just gives the next leg a real tolerance. Do it
on **every** transition, not only the way down — `x0` is only ever what was written last, so the leg after
next needs one too. `SkillTreeUI` does it through one `motion.Pin()` per node.

**Three things about the pin the build bar had to learn separately.**

- **It belongs to whoever owns the SOURCE, not to the spring.** A skill square reads its own hover, so it
  pins itself. A build slot's emphasis reads *the row's* three sources — which slot is hovered, pressed,
  picked — so one write moves the target under **every** slot, the one being lit and the one being let go of.
  There the pin is `rowState.Pin`: a list the slots fill and every writer calls first.
- **An IMPULSE spring needs it too, and gets it in the same call.** `config` applies `position` before it adds
  `impulse`, so `config{position = current(), impulse = n}` pins and kicks in one go. `pickTurn` and
  `affordPop` rest at zero and are moved only by impulses, so without it they never retire after the first
  kick either.
- **Setting the source is NOT a pin.** Calling a spring's own getter with a value (`emphasis(0)`) writes the
  current position and zeroes velocity but leaves `x0` alone — read off vide 0.4.0's `spring.luau`. That is
  fine where the build bar uses it, snapping exactly onto a target, which retires by equality; it is not a
  substitute for the real thing.

This was pre-existing for the map's lift spring and is why `hintFade` already wrote both ends as a position;
the reaction multiplied it from one spring a square to four.

### A layer at full transparency is still DRAWN

Gate it on the value that drives it. The reaction adds seven layers to a square, and without gates all seven
are in the renderer on all 54 squares forever. `Visible = f() > VISIBLE_FLOOR` takes an idle square from
thirteen drawn objects back to seven, and costs one derive that only ever changes on the square under the
hand.

### 200 locals is a scope, and a module's top level is a scope

Landing the reaction added ~30 module-level constants and the file stopped loading:
`Out of local registers when trying to allocate COST_HEX: exceeded limit 200`. **Neither linter can see it
— only running it does.**

The fix is the idiom the file already used for `POOL` and `PULSE`: group related constants into one
`table.freeze({...})`. One table is one register, and it reads better anyway. `ANSWER`, `BEARING`, `RIM`,
`TILT`, `VERB`, `BAND`, `WAVE` and `REACT` took ~34 registers back to 8.

**`SkillTreeUI` is AT the ceiling, so treat a new top-level local there as a bug.** It happened a second
time on a change that looked far too small to matter: naming the square's padding, the box it leaves and
that box as a share of the square, three constants where there had been one, and the module stopped loading
again. Two things to carry:

- **The error names the wrong thing.** It is reported against whatever local happens to be allocated next,
  which that time was a helper seven hundred lines below the edit (`faceOf`) and the time before was
  `COST_HEX`. Neither is the cause. Do not read the line number as a clue; read what you just added.
- **A `do` block gives the derivation back for free.** Locals inside a block release their registers at its
  end, so building the table in one is the way to keep the arithmetic readable without keeping the
  registers: `local GLYPH do local padding = 18 ... GLYPH = table.freeze({...}) end`. The alternative is
  repeating the literal in each field, which is what drifts.

### A local cannot be read inside its own initializer

```lua
local hit = create("TextButton")({ MouseMoved = function() print(hit.AbsoluteSize) end })  -- hit is a GLOBAL here
```

The local is not in scope until the statement ends, so the closure captures a global and the handler sees
`nil`. Declare first, assign after — the shape `SkillTreeUI` already uses for `view` and `ui`. **This bit
twice in one session**, in the bench and again in the tree, because it lints clean and only fails when the
handler fires.

### Frozen groups, and what they cost

Nothing. A `table.freeze` lookup is a table read, and every one of these is read inside a closure that only
runs when something it drives changes. What they buy is the register budget and a file where the knobs for
one gesture sit together instead of scattered down 300 lines.

---

## 5h. A READOUT drawn on a surface that moves

The special attack's cooldown badge (`Components/specialBadge`, hung over the hotbar slot that owns it) is
the first thing in this interface that has to stay **legible** while the surface under it changes. Six
rounds went into it and every one found a real fault. They are all the same fault in different clothes: a
readout is not decoration, so every rule that lets a decoration be approximately right fails on it.

### The two extremes of a FILL are not the same extreme

A gradient that is switched off does not stop the layer, it stops the **mask** — so the fill draws across
its whole silhouette. That is the right answer at the FULL end, where the layer covers everything anyway
and a step sitting exactly on the element's edge is resolved by the gradient's sampling on one side and the
frame's pixel rounding on the other. It is catastrophically wrong at the EMPTY end, where the same switch
paints the whole face in a fill that has not arrived: an empty badge draws as a completely full one.

`hotbarSlot`'s cooldown sweep already had this written down and it was copied by half:

> a half with nothing to show is drawn fully **TRANSPARENT** (there is no edge to get wrong if nothing is
> being drawn), and a half that is completely covered has its gradient **DISABLED**.

Answer the two ends separately. One number cannot do both.

### A GLYPH over a rising fill needs TWO INKS, cut by the same line

A letter in the middle of a face that fills has **two grounds** under it, and the line between them climbs
through the letter. One colour cannot answer both, and while it tries, the count goes out exactly as the
fill reaches it — which is the one moment it is being read.

So the glyph is drawn **twice** at the same place, one copy in the ink for a lit ground and one in the ink
for a dark one, each masked to its own side of the line. The mask is the fill's own step **remapped from
the object into the glyph's box**: the line is stated against the gem and every layer that has to agree
with it is a different size. Miss the remap and the letter changes colour at the wrong moment.

**The ink for the lit ground must be a CONSTANT, and this is the retreat to remember.** An ink that tracked
the fill's own brightness — white while the fill is cold chrome, dark once it is gold — measures far
better: the dark ink clears gold at 8.8:1 and clears cold chrome at only **2.2:1**, and inverting holds
5.5:1 the whole way up. It was built, looked at, and taken out again, because both copies are then the same
colour for most of the climb and **the change stops happening at the line** — and the two copies changing
over IS the readout. What it bought in contrast it spent on the one thing the two inks exist to say. The
narrow band where the letter is dark on cold chrome is the price of a readout that reads as an event.

**And no fixed pair of inks can be made safe on a ground that sweeps.** A ground walking from near-black to
near-white passes every ink on its way, so wherever a switch is put there is a moment either side where the
letter is the colour of the thing behind it. Solved over the whole sweep, the best a fixed pair manages is
**2.4:1**, and darkening the ground does not move that number at all. Know the limit rather than chasing it.

### The COUNT belongs to the tool, the KEY belongs to his hands

One rule rather than two: **a readout speaks when it has something only it can say.** How long until a move
comes back is a fact about that weapon and is worth reading whichever one he is holding — a lord deciding
whether to switch is exactly the lord who needs the stowed tool's count. The KEY is a fact about what the
key under his finger does right now, and a row of badges all printing the same letter is a row all claiming
it. So a stowed badge counts down and then goes quiet; the held one counts down and then says which key
throws it.

The stowed one is dimmer for it, which is the reading rather than a loss: another tool's cooldown is
something to glance at, not something competing with the one in hand.

### Ink cut out of light is NOT the face's own colour

A face is near-black because nothing is over it. Ink on a LIT ground only has to separate from that ground,
and taking it all the way down to the face's value reads as a hole punched through the object rather than a
letter standing on it. The badge's is the face lifted toward the HUD's violet, still clearing gold about
eight to one.

### The READOUT is the top of the ladder, above even the flash

The count sat at ZIndex 5 under a press flash at 6, and the layer above was drawing into it — which is what
"not readable" actually was, twice, while it was being treated as a colour problem. **A flash is the object
saying it was pressed; the number is the object saying what it is for, and nothing gets to draw over that.**

State the ladder in one frozen table the way `hotbarSlot` does, and give the object's own root a place in
its parent's ladder too, so it does not depend on the order a caller happens to parent it in.

### A LETTER'S box is not a PICTURE's box

An icon has to fit the inscribed square or the shape takes its corners off. A single character is far
narrower than a full picture and can be half again as tall before its own corner reaches the face, so
holding it inside the icon's box leaves it unreadable — measured, capitals of **8.3 design px on a 52 px
gem, a sixth of it**. Give the letter its own box, and keep the box (which only has to hold it and carry
its mask) separate from the **size** (which is what the eye reads). Tying those two together makes every
change to one a change to the other.

The budget is the shape's corner: **half the string's width plus half its height** has to stay inside half
the face's span. That is why a wide string is expensive in a diamond — measured at the badge's type size, a
digit is 16px wide and lands 14.9 from the middle against a face of 23.3, `.8` lands at 17.9, and `0.8` at
25.9, outside it. Dropping a leading zero buys more than shrinking the type does.

### The numbers that decide legibility are MEASURABLE, so measure them

Every round of this that was settled by looking was settled wrong. Contrast is WCAG relative luminance and
it takes ten lines of Luau; the glyph's real width is one `GetTextBoundsAsync`; how far a glow reaches is an
`erfc` of a distance. Print the ratio and argue about the number. "Not visible" and "too black" are real
reports and they are not diagnoses — the diagnosis was a disabled gradient, a ZIndex, and a box, in that
order, and none of the three would have been found by staring harder.

## 5i. The two revives: Keystone and Gem

The last two screens on the HUD still on the old chrome were both the Core putting a lord back on his feet:
**the down** (`UI/DownedUI`, the ten seconds the Core spends lifting him) and **the waking caption**
(`UI/WakingUI`, which day this is and how far he held, after the Core went out and came back).
Both were TextScaled words outlined in black. Each was drawn four ways side by side on `Stories/Revive`,
and **`Keystone` and `Gem` were picked** (2026-09-16); the other six drawings were deleted, and the bench
now draws the two of them at full size with the real HUD behind.

| The down | The waking |
| --- | --- |
| **`Keystone`**: the Core's mark filling with its light, the count in two inks, and the Core's body seen pouring into it | **`Gem`**: the day cut in dark ink out of the Core's mark, already full of its light, over the score |

What lost, in case it comes up again: the old screens as they shipped; the plain conversion (a real
`facetBar` on `TableBare` for the down, bare type over a rolling number for the waking); and a ring round
the sight for the down against the wave title's dissolving plate for the waking.

The down still has **one field a bench can change**, `Frame`: what closes in from the edges (`Blood`,
`Bleed`, `Light`, `Clear`), and the game draws `Bleed`. **`Bleed` holds red until 45% of the lift** and
eases to the Core's light from there (smoothstep), because walking linearly it already read as blue at five
seconds left; the shade that showed there now shows between three and two (worked out in `lune`).

### The down tells its story with no words

**`THE CORE HAS YOU` is gone.** On the `Keystone` the effects say it:

It is a **collect animation**, and it is built the way the satisfying ones are: every piece has a LAUNCH,
a HANG and a PULL, nothing travels in a straight line, and the reward arrives in ticks you can count.

- **The stream.** While he is down, pieces of the Core (the cut face's own silhouette, a few px across, in
  a lifted ice, each trailing a streak along its own motion) are torn off the **head of the Core's HP bar**
  in clumps of one to three, about 12 a second. Each is **flung to one side by a share of the whole trip**
  and swung back in from a side, 40% of them from the other side (an S rather than a C).
- **The stream ends with the charge.** A piece is only thrown if it can land 0.05 s before the gem is full:
  its flight is cut to what is left (`DownedUI` reads the exact seconds from `SetProgress`), and under the
  shortest flight nothing more is thrown. Simulated over a whole down: 117 thrown, the last landing at
  9.95 s, **none in the air when the gem fills**. What is still flying on a stand that lands early fades
  with the gem; nothing of the stream goes on to his bar.
- **The gem swells while it is fed, it does not bounce per piece.** Every landing adds to a **pressure**
  (0.18 a piece, draining over 0.35 s, shown through a 0.08 s ease), which swells the gem by up to 5% and
  lights its rim. It replaced a loose spring kicked once per piece, which was built for one piece at a time:
  a dozen a second landed on each other's wobble and the gem shivered for the whole down. Simulated: the
  pressure holds near 0.7, and the swell ripples 0.6 px (std) on the 104 px gem, never more than 0.6 px in
  one frame.
- **No sparks at either end.** A little diamond popped where each clump left the Core's bar and where each
  piece landed in his; at a dozen a second both read as the bar itself pulsing, and they were cut
  (2026-09-16). The pieces arriving and the bar thumping are enough.
- **The lord's bar reads `0 / max`** for the whole down. It used to read FULL: the server hands a downed
  lord a pool of 60 and the bar clamped it to his 20. `HealthController.HoldEmpty` holds the bar at nothing
  while still tracking the pool.
- **The burst.** The gem **pulls in** over the last tenth of a second of the lift while it goes white, read
  off the down's own seconds left, and when he holds out it **blows on the frame the revive arrives**
  (`Stand`), so he gets up as it goes and not a beat before. It first pulled in AFTER the stand, which had
  him on his feet a tenth of a second early (2026-09-16); the squash is the only thing on the local clock,
  and a catch hides it under the blink. It swells and is gone in 0.14 s, in a white flash of its own shape
  and **two diamond shockwaves** a beat apart. Its two dozen pieces are thrown **out in every direction**
  150 to 300 px against heavy drag (half the reach in a tenth of a second), so they fly, slow and
  **hang**. Then each **keeps going the way it was thrown**, bows round in the direction it was already
  turning, and is pulled into **his bar**, faster and faster.
- **The landings are placed, not left to chance.** Who lands when is shuffled, then the landings are laid on
  a curve from 0.55 s to 1.45 s after the blast with the gaps closing (73 ms down to 31), and each piece lands
  at **the head of the fill the ones before it made**, carrying its slice of the heal. So the bar climbs in
  ticks, **thumps** on each (`HealthPlayerUI.Pulse`), and **flashes** on the last
  (`facetBar.Strike`). Left to random flights, all two dozen landed inside 0.41 s, a frame apart.
- **The blast is felt.** `DownedController` shakes the camera (3 swings over 0.3 s, a notch under the
  Core's catch) and punches the field of view by 3 degrees on the frame the gem blows.
- **A catch** is still the blink, and the bar is let go of under it.

**The motion was worked out offline before it was run.** The first cut threw a fixed 70 to 180 px mostly
downward, which on a 700 px drop is a lens of near-straight lines (widest stray 99 px); the burst's pull
bowed a fixed 110 px on a 900 px trip, so every piece turned on a point and came home in one cone. Both were
drawn with the module's own constants in twenty lines of Python (§10c), measured (strays now 86 to 257 px),
and redrawn as a six-frame strip of the burst before any of it went near Studio.

**How the two ends are found.** `DownedUI.SetAnchors` takes two readers, the Core bar's fill head
(`CoreHealthUI.HealthHead`, which reads the new `facetBar.Fill`) and the lord's bar rect
(`HealthPlayerUI.BarRect`), handed over by `DownedController` through `CoreController.GetHealthHead` and
`HealthController.GetBarRect`. Every point is worked out in absolute px and written as a **share** of the
flow frame, which is what keeps it right under a bench's `UIScale` and off UDim's whole-px offsets. A
distance added to a point uses the flow frame's own height per design px, not the viewport's, for the
same reason.

**`Stand({ Heal, Burst })`** is the handoff. `Heal(share)` is called once per landing, always rising, and
always ends on exactly 1 (at once on a drawing that throws nothing, and never later than 1.8 s after the
stand on one that does); `HealthController.RevealHeld` lets that share of his health through and thumps
the bar. `Burst()` is the frame the gem blows. `Show` settles any heal still in the air before the next down
empties the bar again.

### The shards texture on a diamond: `Components/crystalDiamond`

The facets every health bar wears (`facet.Crystal`) are now on the down's gem, the waking's gem and the
special attack's gems (`Keystone` and `Nib` in `specialBadge`). The field is a rectangle, Roblox has no
alpha mask for UI and `ClipsDescendants` does nothing for a turned frame, so the component is a
**CanvasGroup turned 45** (the diamond) with the field inside it **turned back −45** at √2 the size, cropped
at its own aspect: the facets stand upright on screen and only the silhouette is turned. **All three gems
carry it at full strength** (`CrystalTransparency` 0, asked for 2026-09-16), where the bars keep 0.2 on the
Core's ice and 0.6 on the lord's crimson.

**The sweep** is driven by hand on WaveUI's three curves, and the **stand-up** is its own exit:
`DownedController` tells a held-out down (`Stand`) from a caught one (`Hide`, under the blink). The waking
caption reads the alpha `WakingController` already drives as a sweep, and which way it is going off the
alpha itself, so nothing about the beat sheet moved.

### The waking says DAY, and says it to him

There are no hosts: the Core revives the same lord every time. A waking is the one time it puts the sun out
and brings it back, and the game has no other day since the day/night cycle was cut, so the count reads
**`DAY 2`** (the count is still WakingCore's host number in code). The score line is **`YOU HELD TO WAVE
12`**, and `YOU NEVER STARTED A WAVE` for a waking with nothing behind it.

**The `Gem` is already full.** It first filled from its bottom point as the caption came up, with the number
revealed by the light; a fill climbing under a number reads as a meter when there is nothing to wait for, so
the light now arrives whole with the rest of the caption (2026-09-16).

### What the shipped screens got wrong that the bench now shows

- **The waking caption landed ON the hotbar.** At 1080 its score line's box was y 957–987 and the slots
  start at 967; `HOST 2` stood over the special badges, which reach up to 903. The `Gem` keeps its ink above
  903, worked out in `lune`.
- **The lord's own bar read FULL while he was down** (the pool of 60 clamped to 20). It reads empty now; see
  above. The pool itself is still not on screen anywhere.
- **`THE LAST ONE NEVER RANG THE CORE`** was stale (the fight is rung on the target, not the Core) and
  spoke of a "last one" who does not exist. The `Gem` says `YOU NEVER STARTED A WAVE`.

### Benching whole screens side by side

While the round was open, `Stories/Revive` drew four whole screens at once, and the technique is worth
keeping for the next round. **Each cell is the whole screen, laid out at the widget's size and shrunk by a
`UIScale`**: the inner frame is `1/k` of the cell and the scale is `k`, so what is in a cell is the full-size
layout with the real HUD behind it, not a smaller layout. **Judge type and light at full size, not in the
grid**: `facetBar`'s bloom reads the bar's RENDERED height and then writes its reach as an offset, which the
cell's `UIScale` multiplies again, so every bar bloom in a half-size cell reaches a quarter of what it should.
Positions and sizes are exact in the grid. `DownedUI`'s flow still works in shares of its own frame and
divides the `UIScale` back out of its offsets, so it draws right under one.

**What has been checked, and how.** A playtest client mounted the bench with plain sources for the controls
and read back, frame by frame: the stream's last piece gone before the stand, the blast throwing exactly its
own 24, no pop before it, the gem's scale never moving more than 0.19 px in a frame while it is fed, the heal
ticking 1/20 to 8/20 between 0.67 s and 1.45 s after the blast, and the waking gem's light whole with no
mask. The same numbers came back off the game's own `DownedGui` with the server's down and revive events
fired at the client (last stream piece at 9.92 s against a stand at 10, 24 pieces on the blast, the bar
0 / 20 to 8 / 20 by 1.55 s after it). The screens have been looked at in UI Labs.

## 5j. Juice that satisfies: things that fly into things

The Keystone (§5i) went through five rounds of "not satisfying enough" and "that looks strange", and every
round taught a rule that holds for any effect where things travel from one element into another: a payout
into a purse, XP into a bar, a heal into a health bar, chips off a blow, a charge filling a gem. This section
is those rules in general form, with the numbers that shipped. `UI/DownedUI.luau` (`keystone`) is the code to
read next to it.

### The shape of a satisfying collect

Five things, and a collect missing any one of them reads as flat:

1. **Nothing travels in a straight line.** Every piece is on a curve whose bends are a SHARE of its trip.
2. **Every piece has a LAUNCH, a HANG and a PULL.** Out fast, slowing to a stop, then accelerating into the
   target. The contrast of speeds is the satisfaction; a constant speed is a conveyor belt.
3. **The reward lands WITH the pieces, one at a time.** The target is held at what it was, and each landing
   hands over its slice, so the number climbs in ticks you can count.
4. **The big moment has an anticipation.** Pull in, go white, then release. A release with no wind-up is a pop.
5. **The payoff is ON the gameplay frame.** The explosion is the revive; the last landing is the heal
   completing. A flourish that runs ahead of or behind the thing it celebrates reads as lag.

And one thing to keep quiet: **anything that happens per piece**, because per piece means a dozen times a
second (below).

### Paths: cubic curves with legs measured against the trip

A stream piece is a cubic from `from` to `to`. Its two control points are placed in the frame of the chord
(`d` its length, `along` its direction, `side` the perpendicular):

```lua
P1 = from + along * (d * rand(-0.05, 0.25)) + side * (fling * d * rand(0.25, 0.6))
P2 = to - along * (d * rand(0.10, 0.35)) + side * (swing * d * rand(0.15, 0.5))
-- fling is +1 or -1 at random; swing is -fling 40% of the time (an S) and fling otherwise (a C)
at = cubic(from, P1, P2, to, t ^ 1.1)
```

- **Shares, never px.** The first cut bowed a fixed 70 to 180 px on a 700 px drop and read as a lens of
  straight lines (widest stray 99 px). As shares, the same trip strays 86 to 257 px.
- **Warp time only a little.** A cubic with long legs already leaves fast, floats and arrives fast; `t^1.35`
  made pieces peel off slowly, which is not what "torn off" looks like. `1.1` is right.
- **Mix S and C.** All C is a fountain with one silhouette; 40% S breaks it up.
- **Jitter the source and throw in clumps.** 12 design px of jitter, one to three pieces a throw, the next
  throw `2 / rate * rand(0.6, 1.4)` later: the source reads as being pulled at rather than dripping.
- **Flights of 0.75 to 1.2 s** at 12 pieces a second leave 15 to 20 in the air, which fills the trip without
  becoming a solid beam.

### Bursts: throw, drag, hang, boomerang

```lua
-- THROW: evenly round the circle, then jittered, so the star has no gap and no pattern
angle = (i + rand(-0.4, 0.4)) / count * 2 * math.pi
-- FLY against drag: 1 - e^(-k t) of its reach, so half of it in ln(2) / k
at = origin + out * (1 - math.exp(-k * age)) -- k = 7: half in 0.1 s, 83% by 0.25 s
-- TURN once, at HangAt, onto a cubic into the target
P0 = hang
P1 = hang + heading * carryPx -- keeps going the way it was thrown, 90 to 200 design px
P2 = land + (hang - land) * 0.35 + across * (turn * dist * rand(0.15, 0.35))
P3 = land -- `turn` is the side the throw was already curving toward
-- PULL: from standing, faster and faster
at = cubic(P0, P1, P2, P3, s ^ 2)
```

- **24 pieces, 150 to 300 design px of reach.** Enough to fill the space round the gem, not so far that the
  pull is a second journey.
- **The turn is a boomerang, not a corner.** The first cut started the pull where the drift had died, with
  nothing carrying it on, and bowed a fixed 110 px on a 900 px trip: every piece turned on a point and the
  lot came home as one cone. Carrying past the hang and bowing by a share of the distance, the way it was
  already turning, is what makes them come home from everywhere.
- **Spin hard off the blast and let it decay**: 900 degrees a second times `e^(-2 age)`.

### Place the landings; never leave them to the flights

Random flight times put all 24 landings inside 0.41 s, a frame apart: a jump, not a count. So each piece is
told, before it flies, when and where it lands and what it carries:

```lua
shuffle(pieces) -- WHO lands when has nothing to do with where it was thrown
for rank, piece in pieces do
	local order = (rank - 1) / (count - 1)
	local arrive = 0.55 + 0.9 * order ^ 0.8 -- 73 ms between the first two, 31 between the last two
	piece.HangAt = rand(0.22, math.max(0.22, math.min(0.42, arrive - 0.3))) -- the pull gets 0.3 s at least
	piece.HomeFor = arrive - piece.HangAt
	piece.Target = barAt + barSize * Vector2.new(fillFrom + (fillTo - fillFrom) * rank / count, rand(0.35, 0.65))
	piece.Heal = rank / count
end
```

- **Gaps that close** read as a rattle speeding up to the finish, which is the feeling of a payout.
- **Each lands at the head of the fill the ones before it made**, so a piece visibly IS the slice it adds.
- **The reward is monotonic and it always completes.** A landing hands over its share only if it is more than
  what was given; the last share is exactly 1; a deadline (1.8 s) hands over whatever is left even if nothing
  flew; and a new event settles the old one's debt before it starts, or the old heal lands on the new down.

### What a piece looks like on its way

| | Rule | Numbers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Birth | pops into being, overshooting its size | `easeOutBack` over its first 0.08 s |
| Silhouette | the cut face's own plane, not a dot | `facet.Plane`, 7 to 12 design px in a stream, 9 to 17 in a burst, 0.72 as tall as wide |
| Colour | a LIFTED shade of what it came off: a chip at the exact colour of its source reads as a hole | stream `117, 245, 255` off the Core's ice; a burst picks per piece from lead, ice and white |
| Arrival | shrinks as it arrives, and a stream piece whitens as it is drunk in | stream to 30% from 60% of its life, colour `lerp(white, t³)`; burst to 45% over the second half of its pull |
| Exit | fades over its last frames and never pops out | weight `(1 - t) / 0.08`, a burst `/ 0.06` |
| Streak | a line along the motion it has just made, measured on screen | length `speed * 0.05 s` up to 80 design px, 35% of the piece wide, 0.35 transparency, a gradient to nothing at its tail, centred half a streak back because a frame turns about its middle |

### The receiver: hold it, feed it, thump it once per landing

- **Hold the target at what it was until the pieces arrive.** The lord's bar read FULL while he was down (the
  server's pool clamped to his maximum); it now reads empty, and `HealthController.HoldEmpty` / `RevealHeld`
  let the heal through a slice per landing. The same pattern fits any payout the server settles before the
  animation: hold the displayed number, release it on the landings.
- **Every landing thumps gently, and the last one strikes.** `HealthPlayerUI.Pulse(0.4)` a landing, then
  `Pulse(1)` and `facetBar.Strike` on the last. That thump is the one scale kick left on a readout (§5e: a
  readout does not bounce when it is HIT); it is a reward arriving, and if it ever reads as a bounce it goes
  the same way.
- **The source visibly pays.** The stream leaves from the head of the Core's fill (`CoreHealthUI.HealthHead`)
  while that bar drains, so the cost and the gain are one picture.
- **An indicator that is not a wait is drawn already full.** The waking's day gem filled as the caption came
  up and read as a meter with nothing to wait for; it arrives full now. A fill says "in progress".

### A reaction that fires per piece must survive the rate

A dozen pieces a second is the normal case, not the stress case, and two things that looked right with one
piece failed with twelve:

- **A spark where each piece leaves or lands** read as the bar itself pulsing. Cut; the pieces arriving and
  the landing thump are enough.
- **A spring kicked per piece** on the receiver: each kick landed on the last one's wobble and the gem
  shivered for ten seconds. It was replaced by a **smoothed pressure**:

```lua
-- on each landing
wanted = math.min(wanted + 0.18, 1)
-- every frame
wanted *= math.exp(-dt / 0.35) -- drains
shown += (wanted - shown) * (1 - math.exp(-dt / 0.08)) -- eased, so a clump is a surge and not a step
scale = 1 + 0.05 * shown -- and the rim lights by 0.45 * shown
```

Its level settles near `rate * 0.18 * 0.35`, about 0.75 at 12 a second. Simulated over a whole down it held
near 0.7 and rippled 0.6 px on the 104 px gem, never more than 0.6 px in one frame. **Before shipping any
per-piece reaction, simulate it at the real rate** (twenty lines, §10c), and look at the ripple rather than
the mean. Snap both numbers to 0 once they are tiny, or the scale is rebuilt every frame forever.

### Timing: the stream ends with the fill, and the payoff is the gameplay frame

- **A stream that fills something ends when it is full.** Cap each flight by the time left, and stop throwing
  once the time left is under the shortest flight:

  ```lua
  local room = secondsLeft - 0.05
  if room < FLIGHT_MIN then return end -- the stream is over
  piece.Life = math.min(rand(FLIGHT_MIN, FLIGHT_MAX), room)
  ```

  Without it, pieces were still flying when the gem blew and were carried on into the burst, which read as
  the stream not knowing it was done. Simulated: 117 thrown, the last landing at 9.95 s, none in the air at
  10. What still flies on an early stand fades with the gem rather than joining the payout.
- **The explosion IS the revive.** The first cut pulled in for 0.1 s AFTER the server said "revive", so he
  was on his feet a tenth of a second before the gem went. Now **the anticipation runs on the local clock
  toward the known deadline** (the squash is `clamp(1 - secondsLeft / 0.1)`, read straight off the seconds
  left with no state of its own) and **the release fires inside the event handler**. Only the cosmetic squash
  is predicted, never the outcome: a catch hides the squash under its blink.
- **Act in the handler, not on the next step.** A network event is handled after that frame's `PreRender`
  connections have run, so a flag left for the loop cost exactly one frame: a probe counted the revive on
  frame 599 and the blast on 600. Doing the work in the handler (after re-measuring the frame) put both on
  599.
- **A colour meant to change "near the end" has to be held, then eased.** The frame walked from red to blue
  linearly and read as blue at 5 s left; held until 45% of the lift and run through `smoothstep` after, the
  same shade shows between 3 and 2 s left. Work out WHEN a shade becomes visible, in `lune`, before picking
  the curve.
- **No caption for what the effect already shows.** "THE CORE HAS YOU" over the Core's body visibly pouring
  into the gem was a second, weaker telling of the same thing.

### The big moment

| Beat | What | Numbers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anticipation | pulls in and goes white | squash `1 - 0.2 c²` over the last 0.1 s, a white wash of `c` |
| Release | swells and is gone | +55% over 0.14 s, faded by the same share |
| Flash | its own silhouette growing off it | 0.3 to 1.9 of its side over 0.22 s, 0.25 transparency at peak |
| Shockwave | one outline of its own shape | 3.4x over 0.45 s; 3 px at 0.15 transparency |
| Felt | the camera | shake magnitude 3, roughness 0.4, over 0.3 s (swings = `duration * 4 / roughness` = 3); field of view +3 degrees, back over 0.3 s |
| Payout | the pieces | 24, on placed landings |

The three lights come from a fixed pool of 6 (room for two blasts overlapping) and are sized off the gem's
own side, so they are its shape at any size.

### What was rejected, so nobody draws it again

| Rejected | Why it failed | Instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A caption saying what is happening | the effect already says it | no words; make the effect explicit |
| Nearly straight paths | bends in fixed px vanish on a long trip | bends as shares of the trip, S and C mixed |
| A burst that homes at once | every piece turns on a point and they arrive as one cone | throw, drag, hang, boomerang |
| Landings left to the flights | all 24 inside 0.41 s | placed on a closing-gap curve |
| Spark diamonds at the source and the target | a dozen a second is a pulsing bar | nothing per piece |
| A spring kick per piece on the receiver | shivers at a real rate | a smoothed pressure |
| Pieces still flying after the fill, thrown on into the burst | the stream never ended | flights capped by the time left |
| A fill on an indicator that is not a wait | a fill reads as a meter | draw it already full |
| A readout bouncing on a hit | toy chrome, not the cut face | a colour sting (§5e) |
| Anticipation after the gameplay event | he is up before the gem goes | anticipation before it, release on it |
| A colour walk that starts at once | the change shows too early | hold, then smoothstep |

### Building it so it stays cheap and right under a bench

- **Work in absolute px and write SHARES of a full-screen flow frame.** A share is right under a bench cell's
  `UIScale` and is never snapped to a whole px: a UDim offset is an integer, so slow motion written as one
  visibly steps.
- **Two units, not one.** `screenUnit = flow.AbsoluteSize.Y / 1080` for any distance added to a point on
  screen (a bench cell's screen is smaller than the viewport), and `offsetScale = screenUnit / viewportUnit`
  divided back out of any on-screen length written as an offset under a `UIScale`.
- **Measure once per frame.** An Instance property read costs about ten times a local (CLAUDE.md), and a loop
  placing 24 pieces read the flow frame's rect up to four times a piece. Cache the rect, both units, the fade
  and the stand state at the top of the step; anything that places a piece outside the step measures first.
  The streak's on-screen motion is then just `(at - last) * flowSize`.
- **Fixed pools walked round-robin, fire and forget**: 48 pieces (a label and a streak each) and 6 lights.
  The oldest is the one reused and nothing is addressed again. Size the pool for the worst overlap, here a
  stream of about 20 plus a burst of 24.
- **Write a constant once.** A burst piece's colour is set when it is thrown, not every frame; only the
  stream's whitening is written per frame. Guard a source write with `if value ~= src() then` when the value
  sits still most of the time.
- **Early-return when idle, and keep the gui on while anything is out.** A `busy` source, written only when it
  changes, holds the `ScreenGui` enabled after the screen has faded, so the pieces still flying are drawn.
- **Anchors are READERS, not positions.** `SetAnchors({ Source = fn, Target = fn })`: both bars move and grow,
  so the flow asks where they are at the moment it throws.
- **One drawing, no hooks.** While the round was open the gem registered `OnStand` / `OnShow` / `SetBusy`
  callbacks so four drawings could share one screen; with one drawing it returns `{ UI, IsBusy, SetAnchors,
  Show, Stand }` and the screen calls it. The variant abstraction is only paid back while the round is open
  (§5e).

### Checking it, cheapest first

1. **Simulate the rates in `lune`**: the receiver's ripple, the stream's last landing against the deadline,
   when a colour becomes visible. Paste the constants straight out of the module.
2. **Draw the paths offline** (PIL, twenty lines, §10c): the fountain as a still and the burst as a six-frame
   strip. Measure the stray from the straight line rather than eyeballing it.
3. **Probe the bench in a playtest, frame by frame** (§11): pieces alive per frame, lights before the blast
   (must be 0), pieces on the blast frame (must be exactly the burst), the receiver's biggest scale step
   while fed, and the readout's text changes after the blast with their times.
4. **Play the game's own client path** by firing the server's events at the client from a server probe
   (§11), and count FRAMES between the gameplay event and the payoff.
5. **Then it gets looked at.** Every row of the rejected table came from somebody looking, not from a probe;
   the probes only prove the fix stayed fixed.

## 5k. The world prompt: Gem, and changing state without becoming something else

`UI/PromptUI` is the game's one press prompt: the mark over the Sword in the dead Core, a gift waiting to be
opened and a finished tool on the forge (three mounts of one file). It has three states, `Gone`, `Far` (the
**seed**, out of reach, no key) and `Near` (the **offer**, pressable), and two events, the take and the lost
press. It was redrawn in a round on `Stories/Prompt` (2026-09-16/17).

**`Gem` shipped** (`DEFAULT_VARIANT`). **`Lit` stays on the bench at the owner's word**, which overrides §5e's
"delete the losers" for this round, and `Iris` stays beside it as the old mark. Do not clean either up
unless asked.

| | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Iris` | the old mark: a lit stroke round a see-through hole, closing in and screwing itself square |
| **`Gem`** ✔ | a lit rim round an **opaque dark face** with the crystal field at 0.5, the Core's light behind it, the key standing off a drop shadow, and an **echo** of its outline as the offer opens |
| `Lit` (kept) | the same gem **full of the Core's light** (crystal at 0), the key on a dark fill and shade |

`Gem` and `Lit` share one driver (`cut`) and differ only in their body. A body draws its pieces at rest;
the driver scales the whole body with one `UIScale` (arrival × seed/offer × press swell × lost shrink).

### What lost, and what each one taught

Nine other drawings were made. Every one of these is a mistake worth not making twice.

| Rejected | Why | Instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A seed that is a **solid chrome chip** and an offer that is a **dark gem** | the owner read it as the mark disappearing and being replaced | the same face in both states (below) |
| A chip that **crossfades** into the key (`Cap`) | two things swapping, not one thing changing | what only the offer has grows out of the middle |
| Points that **snap out wide** when the offer opens (`Brackets`) | a jump in size reads as a new object | legs from the current value (below) |
| Every candidate given **the old mark's own motion** | "variants to replace it" means their own things; a reskin of the control is not a candidate | each variant moves its own way |
| Candidates made **still** because §5c calls rotation the cartoon channel and §4 puts the breath in the light | next to the old mark they read as dead; the owner wants life in a world prompt | animate, but in the variant's own vocabulary |
| A **heartbeat swell** on the opening (a double kick, light and rim flares) | only the ripple was wanted | `Gem`'s echo: the outline alone, 0.15 s after the opening starts, 0.7 s long, growing 1.9x |
| Closing on the **leaving** curve (`1 - easeInBack`) | no bounce going Far while Near had one | a settle is an arrival (below) |

The three animated candidates (`Orbit`, a shell of shards; `Pulse`, a heartbeat; `Split`, four quarters)
were removed, but **what they got right is in the two that stayed**: the seed look, the cold light warming,
and the ripple.

### A state change REUSES THE PIECES

The rule the owner asked for, in their words: "it looks more that it's reusing the shape and only changing
colors instead of being changed". So:

1. **Both states draw the same pieces.** Only size, colour, weight and light change. Checked by a probe
   listing the names of every drawn, not fully transparent `GuiObject` in the body on each frame of a
   change: the list must not change, apart from things that belong to the key (it only exists on an offer).
2. **The face keeps its material.** `Gem` is dark in both states; `Lit` is cold light (`FAR_COLOR`
   126/196/255) warming into the Core's (90/200/255). Grey turning into dark is a swap.
3. **The rim is already most of the way to the offer's colour on a seed**: `Gem`'s is `FAR_COLOR`, `Lit`'s is
   its lead white with 35% of `FAR_COLOR` in it. A grey rim turning blue reads as a new object.
4. **The light is there on a seed**, at `SEED_LIGHT` (0.35) of its strength, so it grows instead of
   appearing.
5. **What only the offer has grows out of the middle** (the key pops from 0.4 of its box) rather than
   fading in beside something that fades out.

### A SETTLE is an arrival, even when it shrinks

§5c's `easeInBack` is for a thing **leaving the screen**. A thing shrinking into a smaller state is arriving
at that state, so it settles with the same small overshoot a growing one does: `easeOutBack` both ways.

**But one curve per direction on one shared travel jumps on a reversal**: at half way, `easeOutBack(0.5)` is
1.09 and `1 - easeOutBack(0.5)` is -0.09, a jump of 1.17 when a lord steps back out of reach mid-move. So the
driver runs **legs**: each starts from wherever the value is (`openFrom = openNow`), takes its share of the
full time by the distance it has to cover (floored at 0.35 of it), and settles with `easeOutBack`. Worked in
`lune` and read back in a playtest:

| | Body scale | Biggest step a frame |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Far to Near, 0.26 s | 0.67 to a peak of 1.045, rests at 1 | 0.102 |
| Near to Far, 0.26 s | 0.87 down to 0.505, rests at 0.55 | 0.102 |
| In, out, in, 0.08 s apart | no jump | 0.123 |

The dip past a seed is the same 0.045 of the full body, which is **8% of the seed's own size**, so a close
can read a little bouncier than an open. Shorten the close's overshoot there if it does.

Colour and light still ride the plain linear travel through the soft curve: a colour must never overshoot.

### A keycap's LETTER IS A HOLE

The key art (Kenney's full faces, `Assets/ui/keys/art`) is white only where the cap is. **The letter is cut
out and shows whatever is behind it.** Measured off the files:

- every cap spans **0.75** of its picture;
- the keyboard cap's corners are rounded by about **0.14** of the cap; the pad buttons are full **circles**,
  and coloured.

So a key is only as readable as the ground behind its letter (WCAG contrast, worked in `lune`):

| Key on | Letter | Cap edge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a dark face (`Gem`) | 19 : 1 | 9.6 to 15.7 : 1 |
| pale ice, nothing behind (`Lit` as first drawn) | 1.5 to 1.8 : 1 | 1.5 to 1.8 : 1 |
| pale ice with fill and shade (`Lit` now) | 19 : 1 | 3.5 to 4.1 : 1 |

**The fix is two layers behind the key, both hidden where the cap is:**

- **The fill**: a dark disc 0.73 of the key's box. It sits inside every cap in the set (a keyboard cap's
  corner and a pad's circle both clear it), so the only part on screen is the part inside the letter. A
  `UICorner` is fine there because the roundness is never seen.
- **The shade**: `SquareTable`'s offer bloom tinted with the dark ink (`OnLight` 18/40/58), its silhouette at
  0.92 of the key's box, transparency 0. That puts the cap's edge 0.86 sigma inside the silhouette, 43% ink.
  **Any wider and its tail darkens the gem's rim**, about 11% at 1.0.

`Lit`'s bench setting `Lit: what the key stands on` keeps the alternatives: `Shade` (default), `Well` (an
opaque dark square 0.84 of the box, a dark ring round the cap) and `Bare`.

**Every key stands off a drop shadow** (`Components/imageShadow`, the `OnLight` ink). `Gem`'s key keeps its
ice tint; `Lit`'s stays near white, since a cap tinted toward the light it sits on disappears.

**Before putting any key picture on a light surface, check it for a hole and measure its cap share.**

### The billboard's box

- Everything is stated in shares of one **unit**, the old mark's 1.9-stud box. The candidates' billboard is
  `CUT.Room` (2.2) units across so the press has room, and the body sits in the middle unit.
- **Check anything thrown against 1.1 units from the middle, including the press swell** (x1.45). The first
  shockwave off a 0.42 face reaches 1.43 units of side, 2.02 point to point.
- The touch button is the unit, not the room. `Enabled` is off while nothing is drawn (a `CanvasGroup` is a
  render target).
- A billboard's `Brightness` pushes colours into HDR and **no bench can show it**: in the world `Gem` burns at
  1 on a seed, up to 1.35 under a held look and 3 on the press.

### A mount whose handle MOVES holds it through the press

The ruin's offer (`StrongholdController`) hangs the mark and its card on one `Attachment` that is moved from
site to site. Restoring the Workshop "disappeared instantly" (2026-10-10), and it was three things:

- **The press was played over the next site.** A lord at the Workshop is inside the Watchtower's seed range
  (offers 35 studs apart, a seed at 46), so the frame the server answered, the mark was free, the Watchtower
  took it, and the handle went 35 studs away a frame or two into the punch. **Hold the handle where the press
  was made for `PromptUI.TakeSeconds`** (`Tune.TAKE_HOLD`, counted on the offer's own clamped clock, since
  the restored building is cloned inside that window and a wall clock would end the hold early). Probed:
  the handle sat on the Workshop for 0.69 s, then the Watchtower's seed arrived.
- **A mark on an `Attachment` had no voice and no burst on the press**: `sayTake` only answered a `BasePart`.
  It reads the handle's place through `placeOf` now. A new kind of handle goes there.
- **The card only faded.** A paid press is the card PAYING (`restoreCard.Pay`, §5j "the source visibly
  pays"), in sequence and with no bounce:

| Beat | What | Numbers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The yes | a nod down toward the mark that stops dead: the refusal's jolt turned from a shake of the head | 7 design px, 0.14 s |
| The edge | goes white and falls back | the card's own `PaidFlash` |
| The price | each gauge struck white and emptied, its count running down to 0, one after another | from 0.05 s, 0.07 s apart, 0.2 s each; the last of three is empty at 0.39 s |
| Gone | drawn into the mark: shrunk about its bottom edge and carried down, on the standard accelerate, fading evenly | from 0.42 s, 0.22 s, to 0.6 of its size and 24 px down |
| Felt | the camera | 0.9, three swings over 0.25 s, under the mote's own 1.1 that follows |

The mark is thrown OUT on the same frame (its own take, untouched) while the card goes IN, which is §5j's
two things going opposite ways. A refusal that comes back from the server after all calls the paying off
(`Refuse`) and the gauges fill back from where they had emptied to.

### The bench: `Stories/Prompt`

- **A `BillboardGui` cannot sit in a widget either**: its children are lifted into a square cell. The cell is
  the billboard's studs times **px per stud = H / (2 · distance · tan(FOV / 2))**, with the game's 90 degree
  camera (`CameraController`) and the widget's height, so `Screen: distance in studs` draws the mark at the
  size the world does. Each cell hangs `PromptUI.Rise` studs over an aim marker; the sight view puts one mark
  over the real `CursorUI`.
- The module takes a **bench-only** `look` (`Variant`, `TimeScale`, `Key`, `SeedTurns`, `KeyGround`); the
  game passes nothing.
- **Springs a bench can slow are stepped by hand** with vide's own integrator: semi-implicit Euler at 120
  steps a second, `k = (2π / period)²`, `c = damping · 2 · (2π / period)`, snapped onto the target inside
  1e-4. `Iris` runs on these, so `Show: time scale` slows its whole clock.
- **A spring can run past zero**: the key's press (1.34 to 0.08) dips to -0.07. Clamp any size built on it,
  or the frame is drawn inside out for those frames.

### Probing a story in a playtest

- **A story that pulls in `InputTypeController` fails in a playtest** with `[Ignis] Module ... is already
  registered`: the StarterPlayer template's chunk name matches the running copy's. It works in UI Labs,
  where nothing is registered. In a probe, wait for the client to boot, **move the running `PromptUI` into
  the template's place** (require caches by instance) and require a `Clone()` of the story.
- **`FindFirstDescendant` is not enabled** in this place: walk `GetDescendants`.
- **`label.Image` is the PROPERTY**, not a child named `Image` (`imageShadow` names its picture that): use
  `FindFirstChild("Image")`.

---

## 5l. The loot screen (the pack): what it took, so the next one takes less

`Client/UI/PackUI` with `Components/itemTile`, `PackPalette` and `Stories/Pack`. It took about fifteen rounds
of "show me, change it". Most of the rounds went on the same few mistakes, so this section is the checklist to
run BEFORE showing a loot or inventory screen, and the reasons behind each item.

### What a loot screen needs, decided once

These were each asked for, researched or argued out on this screen. Start a new one here rather than from zero.

- **Rarity is colour AND shape.** The tile is lit from its floor in its rarity (EpicLoot's tile: a rarity
  light rising from the bottom under a black shade at the top, which is the hotbar socket's recess and well,
  recoloured), with a faint sigil in the middle whose number of sides climbs with rarity: triangle for Common
  up to octagon for Mythic. Shape is what makes it readable to a player who cannot tell the hues apart.
- **One picture per idea, everywhere it appears.** Better, worse, a trade, the same, and new are icons, and the
  tile's corner, the card's comparisons, the stats sheet and the help key all use the same five. Two pictures
  for one idea (or one word for two ideas) is the thing players get wrong.
- **A comparison is signed as well as iconed.** `Damage: 3 [down] -2.6`, never `[down] 2.6`, which reads as a
  second value. A line or number the worn thing does not have at all gets the NEW mark and no amount (an amount
  against nothing only repeats the number). With nothing worn there, the card compares nothing: every line
  would be NEW, which the tile's own icon already said.
- **Both cards say where their thing is**: IN BACKPACK over the thing under the hand (or EQUIPPED when the hand
  is on the doll), EQUIPPED over the one it would replace. An invented item name like "Worn Pistol" over a card
  headed WORN NOW read as the worn one; watch placeholder names for this.
- **Rolled lines print in the sheet's stat order**, not the order they rolled, so the two cards line up row for
  row (Diablo 4 made the same change). Verbs come last.
- **Unseen things wear a NEW mark until the hand has been on them and left**, because ten seals opened at once
  land ten things across a pack sorted by upgrade. It goes on the way OUT: taken off as the hand arrived, it
  left while it was the thing being looked at.
- **What the hand is on wears brackets, on every device** (`Components/focusMarker`, §5m). A cursor says where
  the pointer is, not which of forty things it picked. A pack item under the hand also puts a dimmer pair,
  breathing in time, on the worn thing it would replace, so both ends of the weighing are marked.
- **Putting a thing on is a button on its card, and ALSO a press on its tile, by device.** A touch screen has
  no hover to tell a look from a choice, so there a tap only PICKS the tile for the card, and EQUIP / UNEQUIP at
  the card's foot (bottom centre, inside the frame) puts it on. With a pointer or a pad the card has already
  answered on the way in, so a press on the tile equips (or unequips a worn one) at once. Decide by
  `UserInputService:GetLastInputType() == Touch` at the press.
- **An equip moves things IN PLACE and the pack stays sorted.** PackUI changes its state tables where they stand,
  bumps one revision source that every derived value reads, and re-lays the grid: the tiles are keyed by THING,
  so a tile that keeps its row slides to its new cell, one the order carries onto another row pops out and in
  there (sliding back across a row runs it over its neighbours), the thing coming back from the doll pops into
  its sorted place, and the doll slot that changed pops. Only opening and a sort button rebuild the grid.
  Rebuilding the screen on every equip was the first version and it was called out at once.
- **The card says WHICH thing before a word is read**: its edge in the rarity's ring, its own fill shaded black
  at the top lip and rising into the rarity at the foot (the tile's well and floor), and the rarity's light thrown
  round it. And the thing itself stands in it as a WATERMARK - its model, far larger than the tile's, with the
  rarity's sigil behind - on the card's plane, UNDER the words, clipped by the frame, grown out of its own middle
  on an underdamped spring and floating at rest. It is laid in a DARK ink (the rarity most of the way to black):
  light words over a light picture lose their edge wherever the two cross; over a dark one they gain it.
- **Weigh only what the hand is on NOW.** The card may keep the last thing the hand was on (so it does not go
  blank on the way to its own EQUIP), but the comparison - `now > after` on the sheet, the doll slot lit, the
  EQUIPPED card, the card's own arrows - follows only a live hover, point or pick. A comparison standing with no
  hand on anything read as a stuck hover. Likewise a PICK lights its tile only on touch; a mouse click that also
  picked left a tile lit with nothing under the hand.
- **One number answers "is this better", and it is printed.** Every thing has a POWER and so does he, his being
  the plain sum of what he wears, so a swap moves his by exactly the difference between the two cards and no
  arithmetic is hidden. The tile's arrow and the Upgrades order read the same number, so the three never
  disagree. On a card it stands IN the rule under the name (the rule opens in the middle for it): a row of its
  own cost 36 design px the card did not have, set into the rule it cost 8.
- **His numbers are put away.** Under his body is his power and a STATS button, and the panel ends there. The
  sheet is a drawer: the panel's foot comes down over it on a spring that does not pass its mark, and the rows
  stand still while the edge uncovers them (§5c). Eighteen rows always open were eighteen rows to step over.
  With it shut, a thing under the hand is still answered: the one number reads `now > after`.
- **A change in his power is paid in, not swapped** (§5j): an equip that raises it throws four to ten chips of
  the thing's rarity out of the slot, and the number is held and climbs as each lands (first at 0.42 s, last at
  0.92 s, the gaps closing from 86 to 45 ms), stinging green. A fall has no chips: the number runs down on the
  decelerate in the cost's ink. It never changes size (§5e).
- **A thing dropped falls.** DROP beside EQUIP on the card and the other mouse button on a tile. The tile lifts
  a hair and falls 84 px on `easeInBack` over 0.3 s, its light going on the square of the time, in a CanvasGroup
  the size of the CANVAS (one the size of the tile clipped the light it throws), with its hit button destroyed
  first so the tile closing up under it gets the hand.
- **Readable by someone who does not read cards.** Four things, each asked for after the power number landed:
  a thing WORSE than what he wears stands back 40% in the grid (not under the hand, not in a fight); a card opens
  on `BETTER +23` / `WORSE -105` / `SAME POWER` at 36 px with its properties and lines put away, and STATS under
  his power brings them out with his own sheet (ONE button for every number on the screen: the cards had a
  `DETAILS +` of their own for one round, and two switches for one idea was one too many); **EQUIP BEST** in
  the pack's header, there only while something in the pack beats what he wears, puts on the strongest thing per
  slot 0.14 s apart so every slot is seen to change; and the pack's hotbar slot wears the same green arrow off
  its corner while that is true (`hotbarSlot`'s `Upgrade`, bench: `Stories/Hud`).
- **Several payments into one number ADD.** EQUIP BEST is up to eight equips a beat apart. The first payment
  code restarted from the readout on each new one and called the last burst's chips off; now every chip carries
  its own amount, bursts overlap, and the last chip home lands the number on exactly what is owed. Only a fall
  calls the chips off. The pool is 48, six chips a slot.
- **A hover on a button that does a lot shows what it will do.** Under the hand, EQUIP BEST lights every thing it
  would put on and his power reads `now > after` for the whole of it.
- **A drop is HELD.** One right click dropped a thing at once, which is how a child loses a Mythic. The button is
  held for 0.5 s while the cost's red rises up the tile with the word DROP in it; letting go or sliding off
  drains it three times as fast. One fill for the screen, laid over the tile held, not one per tile. DROP on the
  card stays one press: a button is aimed at.
- **A queue is shown by brightness.** The seal row darkens one step per place, so the brightest (leftmost)
  opens first. The step is a share of the most the row can show, not of how many are held, so three seals do
  not already run to dark.
- **The slot being compared against is found at a glance**: while a pack item is under the HAND (not merely
  picked), its slot on the doll answers as if hovered and the other slots step back to 45%, eased.
- **Icon-only buttons say their word on hover.** Two ways were built: the button widens leftward with the word
  before the mark (the row slides over, nothing is covered), or a small label above. Measure the word, do not
  guess its width.
- **A help key, not a tutorial.** A `?` at the end of the header opens a panel over the grid with one row per
  thing on the screen that is not a word, each drawn with the same glyph in the same colour the screen uses.
- **What was researched and left out on purpose:** search and filters (for stashes of hundreds, not a pack of
  36), loot beams (a world-drop feature). What was researched and still to do: gamepad traversal (§3's DPad
  notes), a capacity readout with a warning before a full pack refuses a drop. (The lock before discard became
  the HELD drop, below.)

### The second pass: one number, and a screen a child can use

Asked for in five messages over one session, after the screen above was "done". Every item is something a
loot screen will be asked for again, so **run this list before showing the next one** and offer the lot up
front instead of waiting for each to be asked:

| Asked | What it became | The rule under it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Hide the stats unless expanded" | His POWER and one `STATS +` button under his body; the sheet is a drawer | A screen opens on the SHORT answer. Every row always open is a row to step over |
| "One number for overall power" | `TPackItem.Power`, printed on every card and summed on him (`UI/PackPower`) | The number that decides the arrow must be PRINTED, and the total must be a plain sum, so a swap moves it by the two cards' difference |
| "Weapons only roll offence..." | Pools per slot (`PackCore`) | A thing's job is its slot's. Asked to pick one (gloves), pick the answer that keeps the rule to ONE sentence and say why |
| "A drop button, right click by default" | `DROP` beside `EQUIP`, and the other button on a tile | Then made a HOLD (0.5 s) one round later. Anything that gives a thing away is held from the start |
| "Even more readable, even for a child" | Verdict in words, worse things dimmed, EQUIP BEST, the hotbar arrow | Below |
| "Remove DETAILS, STATS does everything" | One switch for his sheet AND the cards' numbers | ONE switch per idea. A second toggle for "show me the numbers" lasted one round |

**What "readable by a child" came down to.** None of it removed information; each moved it behind the one
switch or said it a second, simpler way:

- **Say the verdict in WORDS, big**: `BETTER +23` / `WORSE -105` / `SAME POWER` at 36 px where the numbers
  would be. The numbers come in over it when STATS is on. Do not also print the delta on the power row while
  the verdict is up: the same fact twice is noise.
- **Step back what is worse** (40%), never under the hand and never where another dim already applies (a fight).
- **One button that does the obvious thing for them** (EQUIP BEST), on screen only while it would do something,
  and its HOVER previews the press: the things it would put on light, the total reads `now > after`.
- **Tell them before the screen is open**: the same "better" picture on the thing that opens it (the pack's
  hotbar slot, `hotbarSlot`'s `Upgrade`). One picture per idea holds ACROSS screens.
- **Words on anything held**: the red that rises up a tile being dropped has DROP written in it.
- **Still owed, and said so rather than faked**: pictures for armour (two letters mean nothing to a child, and
  it needs art), a pad and touch path for the held drop.

**Ask before building, not after.** Three of the six rows were a second message correcting the first build.
The questions that would have saved them: *is this for someone who reads cards?* (decides whether numbers are
the default), *can this action lose the player something?* (decides press or hold), *is there already a switch
for this idea?* (decides whether a new toggle is allowed at all).

**What it cost in the code, so the next one costs less:**

- **A card has a HEIGHT BUDGET and it is already spent.** Before adding a row, add up the fullest thing the
  bench opens on in `lune` (head + 28 a property + 20 + 32 a line + 56 a verb) against the card's room. The
  Epic Shotgun ended exactly on it, so a 36 px power row was impossible and the row went INTO the rule (8 px),
  with 9 px taken from the card that had slack. Legendary and Mythic weapons still overflow; that is owed.
- **A new row that needs a mark needs ART.** With none to hand, a WORD (`POWER`, `BETTER`) is right and an
  existing icon borrowed for a second idea is wrong.
- **A payment into a number must ADD from the first version.** Written as "restart from what the readout
  shows", it worked for one equip and cut every burst but the last the moment EQUIP BEST fired eight. Each chip
  carries an amount; the last one home lands the number on what is owed; only a fall calls chips off.
- **A CanvasGroup the size of a tile CLIPS the tile's light.** A thing fading as one piece goes in a group the
  size of the canvas, re-placed in canvas shares first.
- **A getter that reads the HOVER runs for every tile on every step of the hand.** Keep what it derives per
  revision (`verdictFor`), or forty tiles rebuild their comparison each time the pointer crosses a gap.
- **Things used by a function defined EARLIER must be forward-declared** (`dropUid`, `holdToDrop`): `tileFor`
  is 800 lines above the code that drops. And `merge` takes TWO tables; a third is silently ignored.
- **`PackUI`'s `build` is at about 175 of 200 locals.** Count before adding (names on `local` lines plus
  `local function`s at one tab). New state goes in a table (`pay`, `pressed`); the next feature should be a
  child module (`PackUI/init.luau` plus plain children), not more of the same function.
- **A bench's rolls must be checked for duplicates when a pool shrinks.** Strides that walked ten lines landed
  three times on one line in a pool of seven. Take the first off the seed and the rest in order.

**Checking it (what worked, in order):**

1. `lune` for every number: powers, card heights, landing times, duplicate rolls. Paste the tables out of the
   story; twenty lines.
2. A client probe mounting the STORY in a playtest (§11), printing a line only when it changes: the readout's
   text with tags stripped, its ink, chips visible, groups named `Dropped`, a drawer's height in design px. It
   read back the whole climb (318, 325 ... 383) and the fall's fade.
3. **Drive with the bench's own controls first** (`Card: point at`, `Sheet: open`): they need no mouse.
   `simulate_mouse_input` can click and right-click but cannot HOLD, and if anyone is moving the real mouse in
   Studio the simulated clicks land elsewhere. Say which presses were not exercised rather than retrying.
4. A `Choose` control's `ControlValue` in a probe is not always the string the story expects (the sort came up
   in the wrong order); set such a source by hand in the probe.

### Icons in a corner: the art becomes the icon

This took four rounds and the answer is worth having first:

- **The corner's own join runs out and traces the icon.** The hairline comes in from one edge, stops on the
  icon's outline, the outline (same width, same strength, same tint) carries it round, it leaves for the other
  edge, and the icon's body is lit inside in its own colour. Laying the icon ON the join lost twice, once in two
  inks cut by the join and once on a lit corner flag: both read as "an icon on top of the art". When someone
  says an icon should blend with the art, this is what they mean. The mechanics are in §8b.
- **Only a face with NO baked corner art can do it** (`facet.Faces.SquareTableBare`, flagged `Bare`). A tile that
  draws its own corners on any other face showed two lines per corner; `itemTile` now draws corners only on a
  bare face and lays its icons plainly on any other face's own join. **Make the code refuse the doubled case**
  rather than rely on a bench default: UI Labs keeps a control's last value, so a changed default does not reach
  a bench that is already open.
- **The join's distance from the corner caps the icon's size**, because the icon is centred on the join's middle.
  At the face's 34 px a 24 px star was both too small and touching the tile's edge. The tile draws its joins at
  42 (`CORNER_REACH`) and the icons at 28.
- **At a corner's size an icon must be solid and fill its box.** A thin bar (Same) and two quarter-size
  triangles (Trade) could not be told apart. They became an equals sign of two thick bars and a diamond split
  across its middle, at about the same ink as the arrows. Check new icons at 720p, where a 28 px icon is 19
  screen px.
- **A gap through a point takes the point's tip with it.** The first star had a facet gap down its middle and
  came out wider than tall. Cut facets between points, never through them.
