- **Build per-icon pieces only where an icon can be.** The badge only ever sits top right and NEW only in a
  corner the look can name; building every piece in every corner was about three hundred hidden objects.

### Things that come and go

- **Nothing blinks out.** The NEW mark leaving on the frame the hand arrived read as a flicker. It waits 0.15 s,
  swells 7% and shrinks on `easeInBack` while fading on the soft curve, and the join closes on the same clock
  (0.65 s, driven by hand and landed on zero, §5c). Anything the player's action removes deserves the same.
- **A button for a thing he cannot do is not on the screen.** The OPEN row used to draw all three and refuse the
  ones he could not afford; it was asked to show only what he holds (none with nothing to open) and to take OPEN 10
  away when one of ten is opened. So the seal count the buttons read is LIVE (a press spends it in place before
  asking), a button that stops being held fades on the soft curve and shrinks on `easeInBack` (0.26 s) where it
  stands, and the ones left slide on a damped spring to stay centred. Each button fades inside its own
  `CanvasGroup`, since a pressButton is five layers and fading them one by one lets them disagree.
- **A re-sort is seen, not swapped.** The grid rebuilds on a new order and on opening, and every build lands its
  tiles one after another from the first cell (0.28 s each, 0.018 s apart, `easeOutBack` on a `UIScale` with the
  tile anchored at its middle). One clock per build, disconnected when the last tile lands. A re-sort after an
  EQUIP is not a build: see "An equip moves things IN PLACE" above.
- **The hand leaves a beat late.** Tiles stand a GAP apart, and crossing it dropped the hover for a frame or two:
  every step across the grid blinked the comparison and the EQUIPPED card out and back. A leave lands only if
  nothing was entered within 0.12 s (a ticket per leave, on `task.delay`, since the pack is read with the game
  paused and `TimeCore.GameClock` would stop).
- **A card that comes and goes FADES as a whole** (its chrome through `facet`'s `Transparency`, its words through
  the contents' `GroupTransparency`, its picture and its bloom by the same number), on a critically damped spring
  pinned before each new target, and it keeps drawing the LAST thing it showed while it fades out, so it does not
  empty first and then fade.
- **A card arrives when what it describes changes**: its contents rise 8 px and fade in (BuildBarUI's recipe,
  §5e), inside one `CanvasGroup` so the card fades as one piece.
- **A dim that follows the hand is eased**, and the eased value is pinned before each new target (§5g), or a
  spring returning to zero never settles.

### Pitfalls this screen hit, and the fix for each

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tiles under an open panel still lit and moved the card | `MouseEnter` fires on everything under the pointer, covered or not | Hide what is under (`gridHolder.Visible = not helpOpen()`) |
| A button built with its own `Position` sat half a button off | `facet`'s root is anchored at its middle unless told otherwise; `at()` had been setting the anchor | Pass `AnchorPoint = Vector2.zero` with any hand-made `Position` |
| `attempt to call a nil value` building a row of buttons | Each button's place read the springs of buttons built after it | Make every spring and source first, then build |
| An icon placed after a label's text overlapped its last letters (in a story) | `TextBounds` measured the fallback font before Sarpanch loaded | `followWidth`: TextBounds first, then `TextService:GetTextBoundsAsync`, which waits for the font |
| Two diagonal lines in every empty slot | A baked face plus the tile's drawn corners | Only a `Bare` face gets drawn corners |
| Stats sheet and slots stopped lining up when the air changed | The slots and the sheet had separate insets | One inset (`pad`) for everything in the panel |
| A panel looked cramped at the top with equal numbers | Air counted from the edge, not from the table line | Count from `face.Stroke` (§5e) |
| Selene `shadowing` on a new helper | Names like `plane` and `reach` are already locals in the tile | Name helpers for what they are: `cornerPlane`, `cornerReach` |
| Others' files reformatted | `stylua src` rewrites every non-conforming file in the tree, including someone's work in progress | Run `stylua` on your own files only |
| A press shrank a button into its top left corner | A `UIScale` scales toward the element's `AnchorPoint`, and `at()` hands back a top-left one | Anchor pressed things at their middle and move `Position` by half the size |
| A light band inside a tile's edge poked out past the cut, then left a bare strip | The rim was moved by the tile's parallax; a band inside an edge has nowhere to move | Parallax only what is free of the edge (the glyph, the bloom behind); the rim stays put |
| A picture meant to break out of the card was cut to the card's inner box | The card's contents are a `CanvasGroup`, and a `CanvasGroup` clips | Something that must reach the frame goes on the card's PLANE (with the card's padding laid on by hand, `Padding = 0` on the face), under the contents |
| A second, offset copy of the item under the card's picture | `toolPreview` returns the model AND a drop shadow (right on a bar slot, wrong under words) | Keep only the frame named `Art` |
| `Move Speed  18.6 > 17.2 studs/s` ran its label into its numbers | The sheet column is 233 design px; the row was ~250 | Measure the row in Sarpanch and scale by the overlap seen: `Speed`, `Pickup`. Check the WIDEST value a row can show (`now > after` with its unit), not the value on screen |
| Markers round the seals ran onto the next seal | Seals stood 0.6 of a GAP apart; a marker stands ~12 px out | Things a marker frames stand a full GAP apart; the seal row shows seven, not ten, to fit |

### How to get there in fewer rounds

- **Draw it offline before it is wired** (`Assets/ui/statusbench.py`, `sortbench.py`): the real face pictures,
  nine-sliced, with the game's arithmetic copied, at 1080p and 720p. Three of the four corner rounds would have
  been caught on that sheet.
- **Every open question is a control on the bench**, variants side by side, and the default is the current pick.
  When the verdict comes, delete the losers (their names, their controls, their code) rather than keeping them
  behind a switch.
- **Read what was asked literally, and when a word could mean two things, build the literal one first.** "The
  art becomes the shape" meant the join itself traces the icon, and two rounds went on icons laid on the art.
- **Measure what the complaint is about.** "The top has less space" was 9 px against 24 once measured from the
  table line, which is where the eye measures from; from the edge the numbers looked close.
- **When references are anime character cards, the figure is INSIDE the frame and the frame crops it.** The first
  build put the picture on the canvas breaking out past the card's corner, over the frame, and it was wrong: what
  was asked was a figure bigger than its window, cut by the window, with the words printed over it. Ask what the
  frame does to the picture (crops it / is crossed by it) before building.
- **"Inside the frame at the bottom centre" is a place, not a direction.** A button put between two cards
  because the card was full was the wrong answer; the card grows (EQUIP_ROOM) and the button goes where it was
  asked.
- **A picture under words is judged by the words.** A watermark in its own colours made the card hard to read;
  the fix was not fainter but DARKER. Offer the ink as its own control next to the placement.
- **"Go with these settings" is the verdict.** Delete the losing variants the same day (their constants, their
  lists, their controls, their art), and write down in the file what each one lost to, as the headers here do.

## 5m. The focus marker: brackets that say what the hand is on

`Components/focusMarker`, art from `Assets/ui/authormarkers.py` (one atlas, `MarkerAnchored.png`; the sheet is
`markerbench.py` -> `markers-bench.png`), wired into PackUI. Built in one session of about ten rounds. The
recipe, so the next screen only has to register its things:

- **On every device, not only a pad.** The Xbox focus guidelines ask for exactly one visible focus; a hover glow
  on a tile is not that, because the eye has to find which of forty glows. Games draw a marker on mouse too.
- **ONE marker that TRAVELS, not one per thing.** Four corner pieces on springs (`Period` 0.2, `Damping` 0.72:
  it overshoots a little and settles). On a move the corners on the side it heads for get a QUICKER spring than
  the trailing ones (`Stretch`, the leading period × `1 - Stretch · lead`, floored at a quarter), so it stretches
  toward where it goes and snaps shut on arrival. That is most of the "juice".
- **It takes the SHAPE of what it frames, corner by corner.** Ballarc's `cornerSelector` is one nine-slice with an
  L in each corner cell: one shape for all four. Here each corner is its own `ImageLabel` cut out of an atlas
  (`ImageRectOffset`): two rows of four cells, square corners and cut ones, clockwise from the top left like every
  `Cuts` table. `facet` faces carry `Cuts` (depth per corner) for exactly this. Each corner draws BOTH pieces and
  crossfades between them, so moving from a square tile to a cut seal MORPHS rather than swaps.
- **A cut piece runs PARALLEL to the face's cut at the marker's gap**, so the air is even all the way round.
  Offset outward by `o` from a cut `c` deep, the chamfer runs from `(A - o, A + c + o(1 - √2))` to its mirror,
  where `A` is where the target's corner sits in the cell (`ANCHOR`). The piece is placed by that one point.
- **A fill on a mark goes on its INSIDE, toward the target, on every corner shape.** Anchored fills the square's
  elbow; on a cut corner, which has TWO bends, it puts a small gusset in each. The cut variants that lost: the
  whole chamfer thickened (read as merely thicker), a fill outside the corner (a lump where the face has no
  corner), a tooth or a bar on the chamfer, a second hairline, and nothing.
- **Arrive from outside, leave by the same road.** It appears 12 px out and closes in while fading in (time
  constant 0.06 s). It LEAVES on a timed clock, not an eased one: drifting 10 px out on an ease-out while its light
  goes on the CUBE of the time left, so the light is gone the moment the drift ends. An eased fade has a tail,
  and the corners reached the end of their drift with a fifth of the light still on them and sat there.
- **Linger across gaps.** It waits 0.14 s on the last thing before leaving, so a sweep across a grid is one glide.
- **Breathe at rest, pinch on press.** 2.5 px out and back over 1.4 s; 3.5 px in while a press is held. The
  compared marker breathes in time and does not pinch (it does not hear a press that is not on it).
- **Register, do not hard-code.** A screen keeps a `markable` map of frame -> face getter, calls `markHover(frame,
  isOver)` from its hit buttons, walks `GuiService.SelectedObject` up to a registered frame for a pad, and sets
  every registered button's `SelectionImageObject` to an empty frame so the engine's own box never shows.
- **Costs nothing at rest.** The pass runs on `PreRender` only while it has a target or is still fading, and every
  eased value SNAPS to its goal within 0.001 (the second note below), so a marker standing still writes nothing.

### Two easing mistakes this marker made, which any hand-rolled motion will

- **`approach(value, goal, x, dt)` fed a PERIOD through `2π` makes "0.1 s" finish in 0.05 s.** It read as the
  marker blinking on. Name the argument what it is: a time constant `tau`, 95% there after `3 tau`.
- **An exponential never arrives.** At rest the fade and the cut crossfade kept writing a new, slightly different
  number every frame, and eight pieces re-set their properties for half a minute. Snap within an epsilon; a vide
  source handed the same number does nothing.

### Last Wave's marker: `cornerSelector` + `focusBrackets` (rules from the Codex rounds, 2026-11-02)

Last Wave has one client-wide marker. `focusBrackets` draws it; `cornerSelector` picks its target every
`PreRender`: the pad's `SelectedObject`, or else the newest shown `Mark` a screen set. These rules hold on every
screen:

- **Only on what the hand is on.** A screen marks the mouse's item or nothing. It never marks the picked item as a
  resting place; the picked item has its own look (a white outline).
- **Clipped by its list, and kept inside it.** Nothing clips the brackets, and they sit up to 3 units outside their
  box (2 of gap, 0.8 of breath). For a target inside a ScrollingFrame, each side the list cuts is moved to 3 units
  (`LIST_CLEARANCE_UNITS`) inside the list's edge, so the brackets frame the part the list shows. Sides the list
  does not cut are left alone, so an item that sits flush with the list's edge does not shrink. Fully scrolled
  away (no box left), it releases.
- **Two ways out.** `Clear` lingers 0.14 s, then drifts out: that is for the hand moving off. `Hide` is gone in the
  same frame: that is for when what it framed is no longer shown (`isShown` walks to an enabled layer, so a
  destroyed or hidden gui fails). A page switch is instant, and brackets fading out over the empty space read
  as left behind. Moving from a target that vanished to a new one, it `Hide`s first and arrives fresh, rather than
  gliding from where the old page was.
- `isShown(gui)` is already false for an unparented gui: do not add a `gui.Parent and` before it.
- **It takes the shape of what it frames** (BeACastleLord 5m). The framed gui carries a `FocusCut` attribute in px (its
  corners' cut on the slant); `cornerSelector` reads it from the anchor every frame and calls `SetShape`. Each corner
  is then the chamfer's stepped cells plus the two arms, parallel to the cut at the gap: depth `cut + gap (2 - sqrt 2)`
  rounded to cells. Arms shorten so two corners and their chamfers fit one edge. No attribute: the old L.
- **Frame what the eye sees as the edge, halo included.** The shop's price faces draw a white halo 2 texels out under
  the hand; framing the bare face put the brackets ON the halo and they read as inside the button. The face's
  `FocusBox` is the face plus `FOCUS_HALO` (2) texels, and the cut grows by `halo (2 - sqrt 2)` to stay parallel.
- **A thing it frames must not swell under the hand.** A price that grew 5% on hover grew into its brackets. Prices
  only rise; slabs, which the brackets frame with room, still swell.
- **What lost:** a small arc hugging each of the ticket's end notches ("the little arrows on the side"). Brackets go on
  corners; marks along a side read as arrows.
- **It draws every frame it breathes**, so its draw makes no closures: the cell maths are module functions
  (`cellLeft`, `cellTop`) and `put` takes the mark's index. Marks (each with its shadow) are made the first time a
  shape needs that many and hidden past the count in use.

## 5n. The pack's screen in the game: opened out of a thing in his hands

`Client/Controllers/PackController` puts `PackUI` on screen when the pack's open clip reaches its `UiAt`
(Animations.md §9). What that took, beyond the screen itself (§5l):

### How it comes up

On the clip's beat the page is built inside `Components/screenOpen`'s window, the window fades in (0.24 s) and the
panels rise onto it one after another: the pack's **Stagger** entrance, §5o. The close fades the window out (0.18 s)
and the page is taken down only once it has.

- **Cap a hand-driven clock's step at one frame.** Building the screen is a hitch, and the old open's first frame,
  handed all of it, came out already 59% open (measured). Capped at 1/60 it started at 19%. Every clock in §5o
  (window, panels, shatter, ground) carries the same cap.
- **A snapshot screen is rebuilt, the window is not.** Each open builds the page afresh inside the one window;
  a pack leaving his hands drops window and page at once, with no fade.

### The doll draws a BODY BUILT FOR IT, never the live character

A live character in the middle of a hold is not a picture of him. Cloned, it carried the tool hold's
`IKControl`s, which went on bending the doll's arms round a pack it was not holding. `rigPreview` now strips
`IKControl` along with scripts. The pack builds a clean body: `Players:GetHumanoidDescriptionFromUserId` (his
avatar as saved on his account), falling back to `Humanoid:GetAppliedDescription()` where there is no account to
read (a Studio test player), and then `Players:CreateHumanoidModelFromDescription(description, rigType)`. It is
built when the pack comes out, so the screen never waits on it.

- **A body fresh from `CreateHumanoidModelFromDescription` is NOT ASSEMBLED.** Measured in a playtest: no joints
  between its limbs at all (only a coat's `AccessoryWeld`), its limbs about the origin, its head 66 studs off to
  one side and the coat 33 off another. `BuildRigFromAttachments` does nothing before it is in a world. The joints
  get built once it is in the viewport's `WorldModel`, so the PICTURE comes out right, but a fit measured before
  that is framed on a box 69 studs wide, and he stood in it the size of a thumbnail. Twice: a first fix walked the
  joints, and there were none to walk.
- **So `rigPreview` assembles a model before it measures one**, the way Roblox itself does: from joints (C0 and
  C1), from pairs of `*RigAttachment`s of one name on two body parts, and from an accessory handle's attachment
  matched to the body's of the same name. Measured afterwards: a box of 4.55 x 5.09 x 2.04 studs with the head
  1.22 above the torso, the camera 17.6 studs off, and the body about two thirds of the picture's height.
- **The doll does not turn** in the pack (`rigPreview`'s `CanTurn = false`); a drag to turn was the bench's idea
  and the player did not want it.
- **EVERY ViewportFrame needs the black fringe colour**, not just `modelPreview`'s. A viewport blends the
  half-covered pixels along a silhouette toward its own `BackgroundColor3`, transparent or not, and the default is
  white, so the lord in the doll wore a thin white line round him that the build bar's pictures had lost long ago.
  `rigPreview` now sets `FRINGE_COLOR` too. Any new component that draws a model in a viewport starts with it.

### A picture of a tool with a FRONT is not laid corner to corner

The hotbar, the craft card and the gift reveal pose every tool the same way (`PreviewPose.ToolOptions`): the
camera on the model's thin side and the picture rolled so grip to tip runs corner to corner. That is right for a
pointed thing and wrong for a box: the pack came out on its side, back to the lens. `PreviewPose.FRONT_ON_TOOLS`
lists the tools drawn upright and front three-quarters on instead (a model faces its own -Z, so the yaw is
180 + 30, and 22 degrees down so the lid reads), and `toolPreview` now takes its whole pose from `ToolOptions`
rather than restating it.

### What he carries is on the doll before the pack has anything in it

The gun and the blade are the doll's Ranged and Melee slots (`PackCore`), so the screen reads them off his
body rather than waiting for items to exist: `HeldWeapon.ForSlot` for the bar's two weapon slots, and each
weapon's own data made into a card the way Stories/Pack makes one (damage per bullet or swing, rate, crit, reach).
**A screen given no `OnEquip` / `OnUnequip` puts nothing on and takes nothing off**, button and tile press alike:
with no server path behind it, moving a thing on screen that stays on him would be a lie.

### A button for a thing he cannot do is not on the screen

See §5l, "Things that come and go": the OPEN row shows only the counts he holds, off a LIVE count a press spends
in place, and a button that stops being held fades and shrinks where it stands while the others slide over.

## 5o. Opening a whole screen: modern, staged, and in one piece

Eight round trips went into how the pack and the skill tree come on screen. Read this before giving any screen an
entrance: it is the same arithmetic every time, and the same taste call.

### Doing it again in two rounds, not eight

What each round trip was, and the check that would have caught it before the user had to:

| # | What came back | What would have caught it first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | "Retro or cartoonish" (the window grown out of a point on a back curve, every tile bouncing) | The taste is already known: **no overshoot on an entrance** (below). Start from it. |
| 2 | Three new styles; one liked, "make more variants, look on the web" | **Research the references FIRST** (Fluent, Material 3, OS modals, game menus) and draw the variants off them in round one |
| 3 | "They appear instantly and disappear instantly" | **A frame-by-frame table in lune of every channel you animate** before anything is shown. The fade was solid by frame 4 of 18; the table says so in one run |
| 4 | "Rise first the inventory, then the equipment and description", "the screen itself shattered" | **"Juicier" means SEQUENCE, not bounce.** Stage the pieces from the first round |
| 5 | "I didn't say glass shards" | **Read the words literally.** "The screen shatters" is the screen breaking, not something drawn over it |
| 6 | "Use blur, make the sounds underwater like Ballarc" | **A screen that takes the eye takes the ear too.** Blur the world and muffle Effects and Ambience with the screen, from the start (below) |
| 7 | "The change feels instant rather than gradual like the UI" | **Ease what is PERCEIVED**: decibels and blur radius are not linear to the eye or ear. Same lune table as #3 |
| 8 | "Make the actual shards of the shard tool go where the UI shards are" | **Ask whether the world already has the thing** before drawing a UI picture of it. The shard's shell was already 48 real plates |

**The checklist for a new screen entrance**, which is all of those in order:

1. **What is the screen FOR?** That piece arrives first (the pack's inventory). Context arrives after it.
2. **Is there a real thing in the world this opening IS?** (The shard's plates.) Use it before drawing a picture of it.
3. **Stage it**: pieces in sequence, 60-100 ms apart, each rising or homing on the decelerate, never past its mark.
4. **Fade every piece on its own clock** (`screenOpen.Ease.Fade`), never tied to its move.
5. **Take the world back with it**: blur behind (`TweensController.SetBlur`) and muffle the Effects and Ambience buses
   (`SoundsCore.SetMuffled`), both eased over the entrance's own length on a sine in-out, both held by a reason, and
   the screen's own sounds on the UI bus.
6. **Table every channel in lune, frame by frame at 60 fps**, before showing it: opacity, travel, blur, decibels. A
   channel that is done in the first quarter of its time will read as instant, whatever its duration says.
7. **Bench the variants on the real screen**, pick, **delete the losers the same day**, and write down what each
   lost to (the table below).
8. **Play it in a playtest with a probe that prints numbers** (last subsection), open and shut, twice.
9. **Say what was NOT seen**: anything in 3D (the plate wall) cannot be benched in a story and has to be played.

**What shipped.**

- **The pack: Stagger** (`PackUI`'s `ENTRANCE`). The backdrop fades in under `Components/screenOpen`'s window
  (0.24 s), and the three panels rise onto it one after another: the Inventory first (what he opened the pack
  for), then the Equipment 90 ms later, then the Description 90 ms after that, each 48 px up over 0.4 s on the
  decelerate, fading in on its own clock. The tiles start landing 0.1 s in, as the inventory settles.
- **The skill tree: the shard's own plates cover the eye, then the screen builds itself** (`SkillTreeController`'s
  THE WALL, `SkillTreeBody`'s `Reveal`, `SkillTreeUI`'s cascade). The shell's forty-eight real pieces, thrown off by
  the burst, home into a wall over the whole picture round the crystal, nearest first, cooling to the tree's own
  sky; the page fades in over them onto an empty ground; the ground's fractures run out, its planes of light come
  up, its dust arrives speck by speck; and 0.32 s in the map lands ring by ring out of the seed. The close stands
  the wall back up, fades the page off it, and the plates fly home onto the shell and slam.

**The rounds, and what each loser taught.**

| Round | Drawn | Verdict, and why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `Pop`: a window grown out of the point on `easeOutBack` 1.7 (sailing to 1.10 of the screen), every tile and square landing past its size | "retro or cartoonish". Two overshoots stacked on one gesture read as a toy, whatever §5c says about a back curve on a movement |
| 1 | `Glide` (Pop with the overshoot taken out), `Slit` (a lit hairline across the screen that parts onto it), `Settle` (no window: a fade up from 96%) | Settle liked. A window growing out of a point is itself the old gesture, with or without the bounce |
| 2 | Settle and the ways OS and web references vary it: `Rise` (Fluent's page entrance, up 40 px), `Zoom` (out of the point from 85%), `Drop` (down from 106%), `Dim` (a black veil first), `Cascade` (Settle with the pieces after) | Rise kept. Zoom and Rise first blinked on and off: see "a fade runs on the clock" |
| 3 | Each screen staging its own arrival. Pack: `Stagger`, `Converge` (all three in toward the middle), `Unfold` (side panels sliding out from behind the pack), `Deal` (dropped in left to right). Tree: `Shatter`, `Burst` (every piece thrown out of the point), `Crack` (lit in place by a running crack, dropped on the close), `Fall` (built up like a wall from the bottom) | Stagger and Shatter. Rise is gone with the rest: neither screen moves its page as a whole any more |
| 4 | Shatter's pane rebuilt out of the shard's own 48 plates, thrown off by the burst and homed into a wall over the eye | Kept. A UI picture of shards loses to the real shards whenever the world has them |

### What "modern" came down to

- **Nothing in an entrance passes its mark.** Not the window, not a panel, not a tile, not a square. The skill tree's
  squares used to land on the map's underdamped spring and the pack's tiles on `easeOutBack`; both now grow out of
  nothing onto their size on the decelerate. The one flourish left on the tree is the PURCHASE (§5c), which is a
  different moment from the open.
- **Decelerate in, accelerate out, and the exit faster than the entrance** (20-50%, which Fluent and Material 3
  both say). The published tokens, used as published through `screenOpen.Ease.CubicBezier` (checked against CSS's
  own `ease`: 0.8024 at the midpoint): Fluent's decelerate `(0, 0, 0, 1)` for anything arriving, Material 3's
  standard accelerate `(0.3, 0, 1, 1)` for anything leaving. Material's emphasized accelerate `(0.3, 0, 0.8, 0.15)`
  was tried on a close and held the screen still for half of it.
- **A FADE RUNS ON THE CLOCK, NOT ON THE MOVE IT GOES WITH.** Fluent's decelerate is 45% of the way in a tenth of its
  time. A fade tied to it was solid by frame 4 of 18, and going out on an accelerate it stood still and then
  vanished in the last two frames: "they appear instantly and disappear instantly". Ease the move and the fade
  apart off one linear clock: in, the fade on `1 - (1 - t)²` over 80% of the time; out, an even fade from the first
  frame. That is `screenOpen.Ease.Fade`, and every clock in this section uses it.
- **Stage the arrival, and lead with what the screen is FOR.** The pack opens on the inventory because that is
  what he opened it to look at; the equipment and the card are context and come after. The skill tree opens on
  its ground because the ground is the inside of the shard he just broke, and then on the map.
- **Juice without bounce is sequence and density**: things arriving one after another (90 ms between panels, the
  tree's rings accelerating outward), many small things at once (168 pieces, 593 specks of dust), and a handover
  that lands on one frame. None of it needed an overshoot.
- **Blur is not available on the screen itself.** Every OS modal softens its page as it arrives; a GuiObject cannot
  be blurred. Lighting's `BlurEffect` blurs the 3D world behind, which a bench in a widget cannot show.

### The world steps back: blurred, and heard under water

While either screen is up, the world behind it is **blurred** (`TweensController.SetBlur`: 20 behind the pack, whose
backdrop lets the world through; 24 behind the tree, which covers it) and **heard as if under water**
(`SoundsCore.SetMuffled`, Ballarc's `MusicController` duck on the same numbers: an `EqualizerSoundEffect` on the
bus, `HighGain` -80, `MidGain` -15). Both come on with the screen and go as it closes, so the screen and the world
trade places together.

- **EASE WHAT IS PERCEIVED, AND OVER THE WHOLE ENTRANCE.** The first cut of both "felt instant rather than gradual
  like the UI opening", and the arithmetic said why. A high cut sounds fully muffled by about -30 dB, so a 0.4 s
  ease-out straight onto -80 was at -19 dB in three frames and spent the rest of itself on changes nobody hears. The
  muffle now eases one AMOUNT on a sine in-out (0.6 s in, 0.45 s out) and maps it: 80% of the amount walks the cut
  to -30 dB, and only the last 20% sinks it to -80, so the audible part takes 0.4 s in and the last 0.3 s out. The
  blur had the same fault on the window's 0.24 s ease-out (14 of its 18 steps in six frames) and now runs a sine
  in-out over 0.5 s, the length of the Stagger entrance, and 0.35 s back. Anything with a perceptual scale that is
  not linear (decibels, blur radius, brightness) wants its curve checked frame by frame in lune, not picked.

- **The Effects and Ambience buses are muffled, never UI.** The screen being read is the one thing that should still
  sound close. There are exactly three buses in `SoundService` (`Effects`, `Ambience`, `UI`), and every Sound is
  authored onto one of them.
- **A screen's own sounds belong on the UI bus, whatever their template was authored onto.** The skill tree's cues
  fall back to gift, XP and prompt sounds that live on Effects, and would have gone dull with the world;
  `SkillTreeSounds` puts every copy it makes on UI.
- **The muffle is held by REASONS, not a flag** (`"Pack"`, `"SkillTree"`): two screens overlapping on the way in and
  out each hold their own, and the world only comes up out of the water when the last lets go.
- **Only let go of a blur you took.** The pack is reset every time it leaves his hands; a reset that put the blur
  back unconditionally would cancel the skill tree's or a gift flash's. `PackController` keeps whether it holds it.

### Staging panels: a CanvasGroup only while it moves

`PackUI` builds each panel as a LAYER the size of the whole canvas, so everything in it keeps the place `at` gave it,
and during its entrance lifts that layer into a `CanvasGroup` so the panel, its words, its doll and its tiles fade
as ONE picture (a panel is dozens of layers; faded one by one they disagree). The frame it lands, the layer is put
straight back into the canvas and the group destroyed: a CanvasGroup resamples what it holds and re-renders every
frame the doll's idle moves, and neither is a price for a screen standing still.

- **Panels are stacked by layer now**, so ZIndex decides between whole panels, not between their pieces: the pack is
  drawn over the two side panels, and a side panel rising under its edge passes behind it.
- **The window under staged panels is a bare fade.** A window that moved as well moved every panel twice.
- **The first build is the open and every build after it is a re-sort**, told apart by the build effect's own
  `last` (`""` on the first run): the entrance says when the tiles start on the open, and a re-sort lands them at
  once. Both on the decelerate.
- **An entrance clock must survive its screen being destroyed under it.** A probe that destroyed the screen with the
  entrance mid-flight, without ending the Vide root first, had the clock land and put the panels back into a canvas
  whose Parent was locked (`The Parent property of Equipment is locked`). The game and the bench end the root first,
  but the clock checks `canvas.Parent` anyway, and so does the settle.

### The screen shattering: the SHARD'S OWN PLATES become the screen

"The screen itself being shattered" meant the SCREEN, not glass drawn over it. The first answer was a UI pane:
triangles of the page's own ground, flying together over the world. It shipped for one round and was replaced at
the next ask: **"make the actual shards of the shard go into the places where the UI shards would be, so the actual
world shards are the ones that cover the screen instead of a UI image."** The shell was already authored as
forty-eight real plates (`Models.Tools.ShardPlates`, the same cut the held mesh wears) that the burst threw past the
eye and let fade. Now they are the pane (`SkillTreeController`, Tune's THE WALL):

1. **The burst throws them off as ever, then each homes into a cell** of an 8 x 6 grid hung 3 studs in front of
   the eye, turning face-on and growing as it comes. The throw keeps running underneath and the plate is eased off
   it onto its cell (cubic, fast off the throw, settling in), so the gesture is one flight, not a stop and a start.
2. **The page fades in over them** (`screenOpen`'s window) onto an EMPTY ground, and the ground builds itself with
   the map landing after it. The plates are let go of once the page is up.
3. **The close stands the wall back up under the page**, whole on one frame, fades the page off it, and the plates
   fly from their cells onto the shell (shrinking back onto their cut, warming from the sky to the shell's colour)
   and slam.

- **A piece's face normal is the axis its offset is furthest along.** Every plate is a thin triangle (0.06 thick,
  about 0.5 across) lying flat on one face of the cube, so no orientation is stored: the dominant axis of its offset
  is its normal, and its narrower side across that face is what the wall scales against.
  `CFrame.fromRotationBetweenVectors(normal, zAxis)` turns it face-on to the camera; a random spin about the view
  axis keeps the wall from reading as a grid.
- **A triangle fills half its box, so it is drawn well over two cells across.** At the pushed FOV (70.2 with the
  flash's punch) the picture is 7.5 x 4.22 studs at 3 studs, a cell 0.94 x 0.70, and each plate's narrow side is
  drawn 2.25 studs (`WALL_COVER` 2.4 cells): each covers about 3.8 cells' worth of area and the 48 overlap the
  picture several times. Worked in lune, not yet seen in a playtest.
- **Pair plates with cells by DIRECTION**: the cells are read round the crystal's point on screen and the plates
  round the way each is flying, and the two lists are matched in order, so a plate thrown up and left lands up and
  left instead of crossing the picture.
- **Nearest the crystal first** (`WALL_STAGGER` over the screen's half-diagonal), so the wall is seen to close in round
  the thing in his hand.
- **The wall hangs off THIS frame's camera**: the plates step at `RenderPriority.Camera + 1`, and read the FOV every
  frame, because the crack is pushing the FOV while they come in.
- **The wall lands in the page's own sky** (`SkyGradient` at each cell's height), so the page fading in over it is
  the stone's inside arriving over the stone's pieces, with no colour jump.
- **The crystal stays in front**: it rises to 1.45 studs, 0.86 across, against a wall at 3.
- **The Lighting blur softens the plates too**, because it softens everything in 3D. At 24 the wall's cut edges were
  one smear, so the eye comes back sharp the frame the close begins (`restEye`: blurred only while `Open`).

**What the UI pane taught, kept for any screen that does need one:** a SQUARE with a hard step in a 45-degree
`UIGradient` keeps one half on a true diagonal (turn 45 keeps the top left, 225 the bottom right, 135 the top right,
315 the bottom left), so a grid of squares cut at random is a field of right triangles with no art uploaded; a piece
flies from its TRIANGLE's middle, a third of the way into its corner; a motion's length is found by stepping it, not
kept by hand; pieces are placed in scale; and a story opens before its frame has a size (cut against 1920 x 1080
until it has one).

### A screen that builds itself

`SkillTreeBody.Build` hands back `Reveal(seconds)`, which puts the ground that far into building itself and answers
whether it is whole. The screen drives the clock; nothing in the body keeps one. The order is the one asked for,
"the lines and stars coming first":

| Layer | Starts | Takes | How |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fractures | 0, then 0.07 s apart | 0.3 s | each runs out of its MIDDLE on the decelerate: its length rides a source the Size binding multiplies in |
| Planes of light | 0.12 s, then 0.06 s apart | 0.4 s | fade up to their own transparency, on the clock |
| Dust | each speck at its own moment, 0.2 to 0.65 s | 0.22 s | fade up to its layer's transparency |

- **New rolls get their own Random.** The dust field is seeded (`BODY_SEED`), and one more roll in that sequence
  would have shifted every speck after it. The build's delays come off `Random.new(BODY_SEED + 1)`, so the authored
  field is untouched.
- **Write directly while a build runs; bind only what is already bound.** 593 specks with a binding each would be
  593 effect nodes kept for the whole session to animate half a second. `Reveal` writes their transparency straight,
  and only the four fractures, whose Size was already a binding, got a source.
- **A ground nobody builds is whole from the start**, so everything else that shows the body (and any bench) is
  unchanged.

### Benching a screen a story cannot mount

`SkillTreeUI` cannot be mounted in a story: it reads the rules off `SkillTreeCore`, and `SkillTreeCore` requires
`DataCore` (§10e). `Stories/SkillOpen` benches its open anyway, by being honest about what is real:

- **Everything being judged is the game's own call**: the window, the ground (`SkillTreeBody.Build`, which requires
  nothing heavy), the curves, and the order they are called in.
- **What lives in the WORLD is not on the bench, and the bench says so**: the shard's plate wall is parts in front of
  a camera, and a story has no world. The bench's backdrop is the wall's colour (the page's sky) instead, and its
  header names the wall as the thing it cannot show. A 3D gesture is checked by playing it.
- **The map is a stand-in built from the real data**: the squares at their real cells off `Data/SkillTree`, on their
  real faces and arm colours, the rings walked off the links the way `SkillTreeCore.Depth` is. No shard, no glyphs,
  no lights.
- **Every constant copied from the screen is named in the header** as the second place to hear if it is retuned.
- **A turned frame turns about its MIDDLE, whatever its AnchorPoint says** (§3). The stand-in's wires were anchored at
  one end and turned, and every diagonal swung off both its squares. Place a turned line by its midpoint.

### Pitfalls this round hit

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The screen blinked on and off (Rise, Zoom) | The fade followed a steep decelerate's progress | Fade on the clock (`Ease.Fade`) |
| The close stood still, then the screen vanished | Material's emphasized accelerate holds for half its time | Standard accelerate `(0.3, 0, 1, 1)` on a move leaving; an even fade |
| `attempt to index nil with 'Size'` in a story, at line numbers that match no line in the file | Studio synced the module halfway through an edit that changed a signature in two places | Nothing to fix: the next sync loads. Line numbers that do not match the file are the tell |
| The first shatter showed no pieces | The pane was cut against a parent with no size yet | Cut against 1920 x 1080 until the real size arrives |
| A shatter's pane stayed up over the page | An open that was not a shatter never hid it | Every other open hides it (moot once Shatter was the only open) |
| The wall's plates a soft smear through the close | The Lighting blur is on everything in 3D, the plates included | Blur only while `Open`; the eye comes back sharp the frame the close begins |
| Wires off their squares on the bench | A turned frame turns about its middle, not its anchor | Position a turned line by its midpoint |
| `Parent property is locked` after a screen was destroyed | The entrance clock outlived its screen | The clock and the settle check `canvas.Parent` |
| A top-level constant would have pushed `SkillTreeUI` over 200 locals | Its top level was at 193 (§5g) | New numbers go in ONE frozen table (`BUILD`) |

### Checking it: a probe that plays every variant

UI Labs only runs in edit mode, and there is no way to run code there from outside, so every variant was played in
a PLAYTEST by a client probe (§11) that mounts the story, flips its controls and prints what it finds. What paid
for itself:

- **Read the controls' defaults off the story**: a UI Labs control is a table whose default is `ControlValue`, so
  `if type(c) == "table" and c.ControlValue ~= nil then c.ControlValue else c` builds every source a story needs
  without copying its list.
- **Print counts and transparencies, not pictures**: pieces cut and pieces showing, the window's and the pane's
  `GroupTransparency`, how many entrance groups are still alive. Two bugs (the empty first pane and the pane left
  up) and one crash (the clock outliving its screen) showed as a wrong number, not as anything a screenshot of a
  moment would have caught.
- **Sample at a moment inside the gesture and at one well past it** (0.1 s and 1.7 s), open and shut, twice: the
  second pass is where state left over from the first shows.
- **To play the REAL flow** (the pack out of the hands, the shard cracked): wake the world and hand him the tool from
  the server (`AwakeningService.Pull(player, true)`, `EquipService.GiveTool(entity, HotbarCore.ShardTool)`, see the
  Tripwire playtest memory), then click, with a client probe logging parts under the camera by name
  (`ShardPlate`): their count, depth, spread on screen, size and colour.
- **The Studio and the Tripwire daemon are SHARED.** A playtest here once came up running another session's probe
  (`PACKPROBE`) and the server bridge timed out. When output shows probes you did not write, stop, delete your own
  probe, and say the check was not done, rather than driving someone else's playtest.
- **Wait for the game to settle before sampling** (`task.wait(10)` from the probe's start). A tween sampled in the
  first seconds of a playtest read as not moving at all, because the loading frames stall; settled, it read exactly.

### What it costs, and what was cut

Everything here runs for well under a second, but it runs on the frame a lord is waiting for, so the per-frame work
was cut to what changes:

- **The plate wall moves in one `BulkMoveTo` per group** (reused lists, no garbage), not 48 `CFrame` writes a frame.
  A property write is a reflection call; `BulkMoveTo` is the engine's own batch for exactly this.
- **A standing wall writes its sizes only when the cell size changes** (the FOV), and the camera alone moves it.
- **A plate's face-on rotation is worked out once** when it is given its cell (`Facing`), not every frame.
- **The ground's build writes a speck only when its own share changed**: of 593 specks, a frame writes the few
  arriving, not all of them. The fractures ride vide sources, which already ignore a value they hold.
- **A panel is lifted into a `CanvasGroup` only while it moves** and put straight back the frame it lands (see
  Staging panels).
- **The muffle is one `NumberValue` tweened**, mapped onto both buses' equalizers in its `Changed`: one tween, not
  one per bus per band.
- **New top-level numbers go in one frozen table** in a file near Luau's 200-locals limit (`SkillTreeUI`'s `BUILD`).

## 5p. A screen's keys, its backdrop, and what a press falls through

What wiring the pack screen to real items cost (2026-10-09). `Client/UI/PackUI.luau` and
`Client/Controllers/PackController.luau` are the code to read beside it.

### A card that follows the hand needs KEYS, and wears them

The pack's card shows the thing under the hand. So on a mouse the road to the card's EQUIP button crosses
the pack, over other things, and each one takes the card as the hand passes: the button a player set out
for is describing something else when he arrives. A key acts on the thing the hand is on without the hand
leaving it.

- **The cap is drawn ON the button** (`pressButton`'s `Key`), at its left end, with the word centred in what
  is left. That is how a player learns there is a key at all. A refusing button dims its cap with its word.
- **Ask `InputTypeController`, never work the device out again.** `GetKeyImage(keyboard, gamepad)` already
  knows the device, the pad's brand, and the layout of the board, and its `Changed` fires on the one case a
  hand-rolled version misses: a PlayStation pad answers with Xbox labels until its first button press. The
  first cut of the caps tracked `UserInputService:GetLastInputType()` inside `PackUI` and would have drawn
  the wrong pad's art until something else redrew it.
- **Require it through `script.Parent`**, as `PromptUI` does. The absolute `StarterPlayer` path lands on a
  second copy of the controller that Ignis never registered, with its own state, and that copy writes the
  mouse icon.
- **A touch screen gets no cap.** `GetKeyImage` answers `""` there; hide the label on an empty image.
- **Pick keys against what is already bound.** E and X are the world's interact, Q is a weapon's special,
  and **Y on a pad rings the target** (`WaveController`), which is why the pack's drop is the left shoulder.
- **The key is heard where the thing is known.** EQUIP and DROP are heard inside the card (it knows which
  thing it shows); CLOSE is heard by the controller that owns the screen.

### Closing a modal: Tab, Escape, the menu, and the backdrop

- **Escape cannot be taken from Roblox.** It opens the engine's menu whatever a script does. `InputBegan`
  still fires for it (already marked processed, so check it before the `gameProcessed` return), and
  `GuiService.MenuOpened` covers the same press by the other road and the touch menu button too. Close on
  both; the close function guards against running twice.
- **The backdrop is one invisible `ImageButton` behind everything** (`ZIndex = 0`, `Selectable = false`),
  whose `Activated` closes. Ballarc's `CodesUI` is the shape.
- **A PANEL NEEDS A BUTTON TO STOP A PRESS. `Active = true` on a Frame does not.** The first cut marked every
  panel's frame `Active` and a press went straight through to the backdrop: clicking the doll closed the
  screen. What stops it is a second `ImageButton` with no handler, laid over the whole panel (padding and
  all, `ZIndex = 0` inside it, `Selectable = false`), under everything the panel holds. `PackUI`'s `panel`
  parents one into every panel it builds.
- **Things drawn OVER a panel but not IN it are covered too**, as long as they are not buttons themselves:
  the doll's viewport sits on the character panel as a sibling, and a press on it lands on that panel's sink.
- **What is still open:** a light drawn outside a card's edge (the rarity bloom) is not a panel, so a press on
  it closes the screen.

### A hold on a destructive press was tried and taken out

DROP on a tile was once a half-second hold with a red fill, against a slip. It was removed on request: the
wait was felt on every drop that was meant. What makes the instant version safe is what a slip now costs,
which is nothing: the thing lands six studs ahead and is walked back onto. **Before adding a confirm or a
hold, ask what the mistake costs and make THAT cheap instead.**

### A screen that predicts a move needs one honest answer from the server

The pack moves a tile the moment it is pressed. The server answers every request with the WHOLE pack, stood
or refused, and the controller compares one string (`PackCore.Signature`) against what it predicted with the
same rule functions the server ran (`PackCore.Equip` / `Unequip` / `Drop`). A match costs nothing; a
mismatch rebuilds the screen from the answer. Two details that bit:

- **Count the answers still owed.** EQUIP BEST sends several requests a beat apart, and the first answer
  arrives describing a state the screen has already moved past. Answers are passed over while more are
  out; the last one is the truth.
- **Compare by what a thing IS, not by table.** A client builds its things afresh from every packet, so
  identity never matches; a thing carries a `Key` (base, rarity, lines) for this.

## 6. The face

**Sarpanch** (`rbxasset://fonts/families/Sarpanch.json`). Its letterforms carry flat, chamfered terminals —
the same cut the panels have. It replaced Press Start 2P, an 8-bit arcade face that was the last thing on
screen still speaking the old language.

### The family string is in TEN files, not one

`UITools.PIXEL_FONT_FAMILY` plus nine that hardcode their own copy: `rollingCounter` (its default),
`defaultListItem`, `defaultBar`, `LoadingScreen.client`, and the settings controls `dualToggle` / `slider` /
`keybind` / `toggle` (×2). The comment in `UITools` claiming to be the only place was **already false** before
the swap. **Grep the family string; do not trust that comment.** Centralising them is still worth doing.

The constants are still called `FONT_PIXEL` / `FONT_PIXEL_BOLD` although the face is not a pixel one — 36
references across 25 files, left alone deliberately.

### Sarpanch draws ~20% smaller at the same TextSize

| Face          | Caps as a share of TextSize |
| ------------- | --------------------------- |
| Press Start 2P | 0.550                      |
| Sarpanch      | 0.445                       |

**Multiply text sizes by 1.236** to get back to what a layout was tuned to look like. Applied to the skill
tree (`TIP_TITLE_SIZE` 32→40, `TIP_BODY_SIZE` 28→35, `TIP_ROW_HEIGHT` 34→42, `POINTS_VALUE_SIZE` 36→44).
**Every other screen still carries its old, now-too-small sizes.** Do this per screen and look at it, not as a
blind sweep — some layouts are tight and want re-tuning rather than a multiply.

### Roblox's TextSize is NOT the em

Never compute a font ratio from the outline. Asked of the engine at Size 100, Sarpanch's `0` is 50 wide and
Press Start 2P's `M` is 55; the same faces measured in a font library give 0.699 and 1.000. Always measure
with `TextService:GetTextBoundsAsync`.

### Verifying a family actually resolved

A missing family does not error, it silently falls back — but it **does** warn
(`Font family ... failed to load`). To be sure, compare its advance ratio against a family you know is bad.

### A drop shadow in PIXELS is not one shadow

The skill screen drew `TEXT_SHADOW = 2` under every label it has, and the shadow on an upgrade still read
more than twice as heavy as the one on the button beside it. Both were 2. What differed was the letter:

| Label | Letter | Gap | Share of the letter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A square's glyph | 22.80 px | 2 | **8.77%** |
| The way out | 50.27 px | 2 | **3.98%** |
| Tooltip title | 40 px | 2 | 5.00% |
| Tooltip body | 35 px | 2 | 5.71% |
| The hint line | 22 px | 2 | 9.09% |

A count of pixels is only a shadow if every label it lands on is the same size, and on a screen with a
zoomable map and a fixed control that is never true. **`textShadow` takes a SHARE of the letter now**, and
the share is `SHADOW_SHARE = 0.0625`, which is not a new number: it is the HUD's own, already spelled out in
`AmmoUI` and `WaveUI` as "2 at 32". Every label above is 6.25% now.

It resolves three ways, best first:

1. **`TextSeparation` pins it** in design px and wins outright. Pin when the label is drawn at one fixed
   size and you want a specific number, and pin when the label **wraps**, because everything below reads
   `TextBounds.Y` and that is the whole block on a multi-line label, not one line.
2. **The measured share**, `TextBounds.Y / AbsoluteSize.Y`, written as a `Scale`. A ratio, so it survives the
   map's zoom (§3).
3. **The caller's own `TextSize`**, which is right on the first frame for a label that names its size. A
   `TextScaled` label before its first layout draws with **no gap for one frame** rather than a wrong one.

**Do not add a guard against re-measuring.** Both `TextBounds` and `AbsoluteSize` fire every frame of a zoom,
and the ratio comes back the same number each time; vide's `source` drops a write equal to what it already
holds (0.4.0 `source.luau`), so the effect never re-runs. The guard is already in vide.

**The outline is still pinned px** and still reads heavier on a small letter. Making it proportional needs
the `UIStroke` / `UIScale` answer nobody has (§3).

**Every caller pinned before this**, which is why switching the default changed nothing anywhere but where it
was asked for. Check that before changing a component's default: if the callers all pass a value, the default
is dead code and moving it is free.

**A picture drops one too, and it is the same number.** `Components/imageShadow` is this component for an
ImageLabel and carries the identical 0.0625, so a word and a mark on one screen drop the same shadow
relative to themselves. It differs in one thing: a letter fills an unknown part of its box and has to be
MEASURED, where a mark is authored to fill its box, so the box is the picture and no measurement is needed.
**And the fault above came back in a new costume while that was being dialled** - the mark's shadow was
picked against other marks, landed at 0.035 of itself against the letters' 0.0625, and read as less shadow
while being LARGER in pixels. Same lesson, one level up: a share is only a share of the right thing. §8b.

---

## 7. Proportional text: what broke and what did not

Two components claimed to need a monospace face. **The claim was false for one and true for the other. Check
each on its own.**

### `rollingCounter` — never needed it

It measures the advance at runtime (ten zeroes at Size 100, divided by 1000), cuts each slot to that and
**centres the glyph in it**, which is exactly what a tabular figure is. Sarpanch's digits are genuinely *not*
tabular (its `1` is about 55% of its `0`) and it still reads correctly, because `0` is its widest digit so
every other one has room.

Its seed `DEFAULT_ADVANCE_RATIO` is 0.5. It used to be `1`, which was **wrong for Press Start 2P too** (0.55),
so every counter in the game briefly drew about twice too wide before the async measure landed.

**The counters are Sarpanch BOLD**, taken from `UITools.FONT_PIXEL_BOLD` rather than spelled out again (one
of the ten copies of the family string in §6, now nine). No caller passes `FontFace`, so the module's default
is every counter in the game: the wave number, the resource readouts, the skill tree's points, both ammo
reels. Measured at Size 100, ten zeroes:

| Weight | Advance ratio |
| --- | --- |
| Regular | 0.4900 |
| Medium | 0.4900 |
| **Bold** | **0.5000** |

So the seed of 0.5 was already the **bold** number before the swap, and is now exactly right instead of 2%
wide for the frame or two before the async measure lands. `0` is the widest digit at both weights (all ten
checked), which is what the slot is cut to.

### `typewriter` — genuinely needed it, and now does not

It places glyphs on a grid and measured the cell off `"M"`, the widest letter, so under a proportional face
every narrow letter got an M-wide cell and tooltips printed with holes in them. It now measures **every**
character once at load (one `GetTextBoundsAsync` per character, ~95 calls, off the critical path) and gives
each glyph a cell of its own advance; wrap and centring work in pixels instead of columns.

Two things to know:

- **A space must be asked for as `width("M M") − width("MM")`.** The measure trims a run of spaces off both
  ends and comes back with nothing.
- Until the table lands every glyph is `M` wide, so the first frames are loose rather than overlapping, and
  they relayout once through the source.

On a monospace face every one of those measurements is the same number, so the old grid behaviour is
unchanged.

### The reading pace is ONE number, and it lives in the component

`typewriter.BASE_SPEED` is **0.0125 s/glyph — 80 glyphs a second, so the catalog's 63-to-76 character
sentences land in 0.79s to 0.95s.** Neither caller states a `Speed` any more; both take it.

**How it went wrong is the part worth keeping.** The default was `0.03` and *no caller had ever taken it*:
the skill tree's tooltip asked for 0.0125 and the build bar's card for 0.018, each set on its own screen by
its own eye. That is the same sentence reading in 0.95s on one and 1.37s on the other — **a difference a
player feels and cannot name**, and three copies of one number all free to drift. A default that every caller
overrides is not a default; it is a third place for the value to be wrong.

**`DialogueController` keeps its own `BASE_SPEED` (0.04) and should.** A card somebody is *speaking* and a
tooltip that appeared under a cursor are read at different speeds, and that is a real distinction rather than
two screens never having been compared. The test for whether two numbers should be one: **can a player see
both in the same session and expect them to match?**

---

## 8. Authoring new art

Two scripts, and `Assets/` is gitignored like the rest of the raw source material.

- **`Assets/ui/authorart.py`** writes the default `Cut` face's four images (`FacetFill`, `FacetEdge`,
  `FacetGlow`, `FacetCrystal`).
- **`Assets/ui/authorshapes.py`** writes every other FACE: a fill, an edge and **one bloom per light**, for
  each entry in its `SHAPES` — plus **one rim per silhouette** (`INNER_SHAPES`, §5f). It imports the first
  script's constants rather than copying them, and its control reproduces the shipped pair **byte for
  byte**, which is the check that the pipeline is still the same pipeline. Do that whenever you touch
  either file: author the shipped shape and diff it. (Adding the rim was checked this way — all 28 shipped
  pictures came back with unchanged checksums.)

- Authored at **3 source px per design px** so diagonals stay clean when Roblox minifies them.
- The corner cell is the **whole bevel** — that is what keeps the bevel absolute through a stretch. The
  bloom's cell is the cut **plus the whole reach of its blur**, for the same reason.
- Supersample ×4 and box down, or a 45-degree cut comes out stair-stepped.
- `ImageColor3` **multiplies**, so it can only darken. A bevel *lighter* than the face cannot come from the
  fill image — which is why the bevel lives in the **edge** image, tinted with the hue, so the facet join
  catches the same light the cut edge does.
- The crystal field is authored at a **bar's shape and stretched**, not tiled — see §5d.

**Every image is a Decal upload and the id you get back is the wrong one.** Open Cloud `asset_type: "Decal"`
returns the Decal's id; `ImageLabel.Image` wants the Image inside it, and handed the wrapper it silently
draws nothing. Three ways in, in the order to try them:

1. **`insert_model` the decal and print `Decal.Texture`** from a throwaway script in a playtest. Needs
   Studio. `get_instance_properties` does **not** return `Texture`, so it has to be a print.
2. **Let a STORY resolve them and print them.** A story runs at plugin identity in edit mode, where
   `InsertService:LoadAsset` and `game:GetObjects` both work, so a bench can hold **decal** ids, open them
   once at mount, cache them at module scope and print each `decal -> rbxassetid://image` line it finds.
   `Stories/SkillNodes` does this, and it is how twenty-four ids were recovered in one paste with the Studio
   bridge down. Worth building into any bench that carries candidate art: the ids are wanted anyway the
   moment one wins.
3. **The REST routes are dead ends.** `GET apis.roblox.com/assets/v1/assets/{id}` returns name, type,
   moderation and state and no link between the pair, even with `readMask=*`; `assetdelivery.roblox.com` is
   403 for a group's own assets; and the headless Luau execution API needs a scope this key does not have.

**Uploading does not need the Studio bridge either.** A multipart `POST` to `apis.roblox.com/assets/v1/assets`
with the `x-api-key` from `.env`, a `request` part naming `assetType: "Decal"` and the group, and a
`fileContent` part, returns an operation to poll at `assets/v1/{operation path}`. That is the whole of what
the MCP tool does, and it is the way through when the bridge is held by another process.

If you change `CUT` or `CELL` in `authorart.py`, `facet.luau`'s `SOURCE_SCALE`, `SLICE`, `CELL` and `CUT`
must move with them. (`EDGE` and `HAIR` are thicknesses inside the art and `facet.luau` never names them.)
The faces in `authorshapes.py` carry their **own** cell, and `facet` derives every slice from it with one
`sliceOf`, so a new face there is one line here and no hand-copied `Rect`. A changed image is a **new
upload**, so §3's Decal-vs-Image warning applies again.

**The square's face.** The skill tree's squares pad by 18 rather than the default 20: the old chrome left 52
of the cell's 96 units for the glyph, and 18 hands most of that back (60 units of face) without letting the
letters touch the cut.

---

## 8b. Authoring a MARK, the icon a square wears

A **mark** is the picture on a skill square: one flat silhouette, white, with an alpha channel and nothing
else in it. `Assets/ui/authoricons.py` authors the set and `Assets/ui/iconbench.py` draws it on the real
squares. They are a third art family beside the faces (§8) and the blooms (§5d), and they are the simplest
of the three: no slice, no cell, no falloff, no tint baked in.

**They replaced two capitals per square** (`node.Glyph`, "AG", "SP"). Two things were wrong with that and
only one was taste. The taste one: a pair of capitals is READ, letter by letter, and a map is looked at. The
other was a rule - the letters wear a near-black `UIStroke` to hold them off the sheet, which made the
loudest object on the map the one thing rule 2 forbids. A silhouette does not need it: the palette already
checks `Glyph` against its own dimmed sheet at 4.5:1, and a shape carries that contrast on area where a
letter has only a stem. **The mark arriving is the outline leaving with it.**

The style is the one Bills Must Be Paid uses: one solid shape, no outline, no shading, no second tone. Three
things it does NOT copy, and each is the cut face asking for something back.

### 1. Corners are CUT, so every vertex goes through `chamfer`

`chamfer(points, radius)` replaces each vertex with two, taking the corner off along both its edges.
Nothing in the set has a round join and nothing has a needle point. `CH = 0.045` of the box is the default
and every mark wears the same one - **the face's cut is absolute so a tooltip and a square share it, and a
mark is the opposite**, always drawn at one size, so its cut is a share of itself.

Round joins and organic curves are what the reference set is drawn with, and on this stone they read as a
sticker laid on it rather than a shape cut out of it.

### 2. It is a MASK, not a picture

White plus alpha, so `ImageColor3` is the whole of its colour. That is what keeps "colour is the thing being
bought" (§5) true for free: the map's drain-to-grey and the `Dim` multiply already run over the square, and
a mark carrying its own hue would be the one object on the screen not answering to them.

### 3. ONE WEIGHT, and it is measured

`ink()` reports what share of the box a mark actually covers. The set runs **24.9% to 43.7%** (Sure Shot to
Deep Pockets), which is the band a solid heart and an open crosshair can share. The reference set spans four to one (its bear against its
dumbbell), and on a lattice where every square is the same size that reads as some skills mattering more
than others. Check a new mark lands in the band before believing it belongs.

### Separation is a GAP, and there is nothing else

Rule 2 arrived at from the other direction: with no ink allowed, negative space is the only way to tell one
part of a silhouette from the part beside it. `GAP = 0.07` of the box, and it is the **thinnest feature in
the set**, so it is what decides the size the set stops working at.

### The box, and the sizes it has to survive

Authored in a square at `SRC = 3` source px per design px (`BOX` 64, so 192 px files), supersampled ×4 and
boxed down like everything else here. It is drawn at whatever size the caller gives it, which on a skill
square is 60 design units - `NODE_SIZE` 96 less `SQUARE_PADDING` 18 a side, exported as `GLYPH_INNER` and
`GLYPH_SHARE` in `SkillTreeUI`. So **every threshold below is a share of the box**, not a pixel count.

| | share | at the default zoom (57 px) | at the floor zoom (15 px) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| thinnest POSITIVE feature (the crosshair's ring) | 0.12 | 6.8 px | 1.8 px |
| thinnest NEGATIVE feature (`GAP`) | 0.07 | 4.0 px | 1.1 px |

**The floor is not a reading zoom** and nothing is meant to survive it. It is the "where am I" view, where
the map is read by colour and shape. What a mark has to do at 15 px is stay one solid thing rather than
break up, and the bench's bottom row is there so that is a decision rather than a surprise.

### A mark's COORDINATES are not its silhouette

This is the one that cost a round, and it is invisible in the source. `stroke(path, half)` mitres its
corners, and a mitre runs past the vertex it was written at by `half / sin(angle / 2)`. The double chevron,
written to sit between x 0.06 and 0.78, actually spanned **-0.024 to 0.899**: it drew left of centre with
its left edge clipped off by the image bounds, and neither fact is anywhere in the numbers that produced it.

So the box is **solved, not authored**. `fit(ops)` takes the bounds of everything a mark ADDS - a
subtraction only ever cuts a hole in that, so it cannot widen it - centres them, and scales down only if
they do not already fit. Every mark then has the same margin on both sides by construction, including the
deliberately lopsided ones: Long Shot's trail is centred on the trail and the coin together, which is what
the eye centres on anyway.

**And it is checked on the pixels, not on the arithmetic.** `margins()` reads the rendered alpha's bounding
box back, and the script prints `OFF-CENTRE` for anything more than a quarter of a design px out. A `fit`
that is right and a picture that is right are two claims.

### Making one: the loop

1. Add a function to `MARKS` in `authoricons.py`, keyed by the node's `Name` (or a run's `Prefix`). It
   returns a list of `("add" | "sub", polygon)`, built from `chamfer`, `ngon`, `star`, `rect`, `cross`,
   `stroke`, `spoke`, `shrink`, `place` and the shared `ROUND` cartridge.
2. `python3 authoricons.py` - writes `icons/Skill<Name>.png` and prints ink and margins for the whole set.
   Read the line. Ink inside the 24.9-43.7% the set already spans, and no `OFF-CENTRE`.
3. `python3 iconbench.py` - draws every mark on the real nine-sliced face art, in the arm's own colours,
   **in all three states a square is drawn in** (owned, offered, far) and at both zoom ends. A mark judged
   white on grey is a mark nobody will ever see.
4. Look at the sheet. §10c's rules apply: the eye beats the measurement, and a variant is judged against
   the one beside it rather than against a memory.

Three of the nineteen are the weakest and are the ones to redraw first if the set is ever revisited: Second
Wind (a diamond over three bars, which reads a little like a podium), Scavenger (the round is small under
its U-turn) and Long Shot (legible, least specific).

### The shadow under it: `Components/imageShadow`

`textShadow`'s trick for an ImageLabel: the same picture drawn twice, the copy underneath tinted dark and
the real one lifted off it. Not a `UIShadow`, for §3's reason - a second copy of the picture IS the
silhouette, whatever shape the silhouette is. And it is not an outline: an outline surrounds a shape, a drop
shadow is OFFSET from it.

**The gap is `textShadow`'s own share, 0.0625, and getting there is worth repeating.** It shipped at 0.035,
picked on a bench of marks alone, and read as less shadow than the letters next to it. Measured on a skill
square at the default zoom: the letters are drawn 22.0 px tall and drop 1.375 px; the mark is drawn 56.9 px
and dropped 1.99 px. **The mark's shadow was larger in pixels and still read as less**, because what the eye
compares is the shadow against the thing casting it - 0.035 of itself against the letters' 0.0625, a bit
over half. A bench of marks could not have caught that; the two had to be measured side by side. One share
for the whole interface is also the entire argument for writing either as a share rather than a pixel count.

- At 0.0625 the mark drops 3.6 px. **Past about 0.08 the shadow starts filling the holes** in an open
  silhouette: the gap between the crosshair's ring and its centre dot is 8.3 px, and the revolver's chambers
  are tighter. There is a ceiling and it is not far above.
- **`ShadowColor3` defaults to BLACK here where `textShadow` can leave it unset.** A TextLabel's default
  `TextColor3` is black, so an unset shadow there is already a shadow; an ImageLabel's default
  `ImageColor3` is WHITE, so the same omission would hang a white copy of the picture under the picture.
- **`Name` is shadow-only**, which is the one place it parts company with `textShadow`. That one mirrors the
  name onto both halves, so a caller naming its label gets the name twice and the component's own names
  never apply - a probe read the pair back as `Icon` inside `Icon`.
- It is **cheaper than the letters it replaced**: two ImageLabels against `textShadow`'s two TextLabels plus
  two UIStrokes. Counted from the source rather than measured, but §5g cares about per-square object counts
  and this moves the right way.

### A second set in this style: the wave title's END PIECES

`Assets/ui/authorends.py` authors them and `Assets/ui/endsbench.py` draws them where they are seen. It
imports `authoricons`' geometry rather than restating it — same `chamfer`, same ×4 supersample, same white
plus alpha — and it is worth reading for the **two places a wide strip parts company with a square mark**:

- **No `fit`.** A mark is solved into its box so every one of them is centred; an end piece has to be
  **flush at its inner edge**, because that edge is the thing pinned at a constant distance from the middle
  of the screen. So the box is authored, not solved, and `reach()` reads back how far in the ink actually
  starts as the check that it is.
- **The fade is baked into the alpha.** A `UIGradient` over the element knows nothing about what is under
  it, so it eats the ornament along with the tail; baked, the ramp starts past the ornament. The drawn end
  is then one `ImageLabel` with no gradient on it at all.

**One file serves both sides.** Every design is symmetric top to bottom, so the mirror is `Rotation = 180`
— the same argument the title's old flourish sprite made, and safe for the reasons §3's rotation traps are
not about this: not nine-sliced, no light direction baked in, and a half turn samples on the grid. **Place
it by its CENTRE**, though: Roblox's own answer to what `Rotation` pivots on is not a thing to bet a layout
on, and an element anchored at its middle turns about the same point under either answer.

### A third set: the pack's SORT MARKS and the tile SIGIL

`Assets/ui/authorsorts.py` authors them (imports `authoricons`' geometry) and `Assets/ui/sortbench.py`
draws them on the sort buttons at 1080p and 720p. What differs from the skill marks is the SIZE: a sort button
is its mark alone, a 44 design px square on the bare `Square` face (one hairline, no table line), with the
mark about 28 px, 19 screen px at 720p, so its `GAP` is 0.11 of the box rather than 0.07, which would close
up. Two candidates per button were drawn and both sets are uploaded; the ids live
in `PackPalette.SortMarkSets` and `SortMarks` is the set in force, swept on `Stories/Pack`'s `Pack: sort
marks`. The Gem's first draw had facet cuts running down the pavilion to the point, and at 16 px they
read as a letter V; the crown carries the cuts now.

The SIGILS (`Sigil3` to `Sigil8`, ids in `PackPalette.Sigils`) are EpicLoot's knot triangle said in this
style, one per rarity: Common's triangle of nine facets, then a side more each step, to Mythic's octagon of
32, so a tile says its rarity by SHAPE as well as by hue. Every facet is its small triangle SHRUNK by half
the gap, which parts neighbours by one gap at any angle; subtracting lines only works on a three-direction
grid. **Every polygon has the same AREA** (§8b's one weight): sized off its circle the square read small,
and sized off its outline it filled its box at 56% ink against the rest's 30. Fitted, so `itemTile` centres
the box. It stands in the floor light `itemTile` draws in the
tile's rarity, which is the hotbar socket's recess and well recoloured. **It is a mark rather than the
crystal field** because the field is a rectangle, and a rectangle laid inside a cut face shows square
corners past the cut (§3, a layer must be the silhouette).

The STATUS icons (`Status*.png`, ids in `PackPalette.Status` and `PackPalette.NewIcons`) replaced ▲ ▼ ~, a
drawn bar and the word NEW. **One picture per idea, everywhere it appears**: a tile's corner, the card's
comparisons, the sheet and the help all use the same set, and the NEW mark means both "not looked at yet" on
a tile and "a line what you wear lacks" on the card. `Assets/ui/statusbench.py` draws them on the real face.

**An icon in a tile's corner is MADE OF THE CORNER'S ART, not laid on it.** The join (the hairline a corner's
plane ends at) comes in from one edge, stops on the icon's outline, the outline carries it round, and it
leaves for the other edge, with the icon's body lit inside. Two icons laid ON the join were tried first, one
in two inks cut by the join and one on a lit corner flag, and both read as an icon on top of the art.

- **The tile draws all four corners itself**, on `SquareTableBare` (SquareTable's face with no corner art),
  because a join baked into the edge picture cannot bend. A grid tile that gets a baked face doubles them.
- **A straight piece of join is a band**: a `UIGradient` across the other diagonal of the square the piece is
  the diagonal of, stepped up and back down at 0.5, `CORNER_HAIR` design px wide (its half width over the
  square's diagonal, in gradient units). The wash is the same square stepped once.
- **Where a piece stops** is measured off the pictures: `Assets/ui/authorcorners.py` authors each icon's
  OUTLINE (the join's width, on the icon's edge) and FILL (inset a 1 px gap), and prints `ICON_REACH`, how far
  the corner's diagonal travels from the icon's centre before it first meets the icon. Re-run and re-paste it
  when an icon is redrawn. Checked in a playtest: the pieces end at the table times the box from centre.
- **The join sits at 42 design px, not the face's 34** (`CORNER_REACH`). An icon's centre is half the join's
  reach in from both edges, so the reach is what caps an icon's size: at 34 a 24 px star was too small to read
  and its outline already touched the tile's edge. At 42 a 28 px icon clears the 3 px edge by about 3 px. Every
  grid cell, empty ones too, is on the bare face, or a baked 34 px join shows beside the drawn 42 px one.
- **Icons in a corner must fill their box.** Same (one thin bar) and Trade (two quarter-size triangles) could
  not be told apart at a corner's size. They are an equals sign of two thick bars and a diamond split across
  its middle, at about the arrows' ink (38 and 45% against 36%).
- **The NEW mark leaves over a stated 0.65 s**, not the frame the hand leaves: a 0.15 s beat, then it swells
  7% and shrinks to nothing on `easeInBack` while fading on the soft curve, and the join's two pieces close on
  the same clock into one straight line. Measured frame by frame in a playtest.

### Measure text with `GetTextBoundsAsync` when something is placed after it

An icon placed after a label's text by its `TextBounds` landed on the text's last letters in a story: the
label was measured before Sarpanch had loaded, against the narrower fallback face. `TextService:
GetTextBoundsAsync` waits for the font. `PackUI.followWidth` takes TextBounds first (free, and usually right)
and corrects it with the async answer, on every change of the text, its size or its font.

### Uploading a SET, and where the id goes

The Decal-versus-Image round trip in §8 applies unchanged, and for a batch it is one playtest rather than
one each. **The fastest way needs no inserts at all**: a throwaway server `Script` holding the decal ids that
calls `InsertService:LoadAsset(id)` for each in its own `task.spawn` and prints
`FindFirstChildWhichIsA("Decal", true).Texture`, with an `ALL` line when the count is reached. Sixteen resolved
in about four seconds that way (they print out of order; poll the output until `ALL`). The older way,
`insert_model` into one folder and one script walking it, still works.

### Recipe: a new set of icons, end to end

1. **Author** in `Assets/ui` with `authoricons.py`'s geometry (`chamfer`, `stroke`, `shrink`, `render`), white
   plus alpha, fitted so the box centres the ink. Print ink share and margins; keep a set within a band of ink.
2. **Bench offline** on the real face art at the size it is drawn and at 720p (`statusbench.py` is the model).
   Judge the sheet before uploading anything.
3. **Upload** each file as a Decal (`upload_asset`, group creator) with a distinct display name.
4. **Resolve** the Image ids in one playtest with the `LoadAsset` script above. Delete the script, stop the
   playtest.
5. **Paste** the ids into the screen's palette file, one table per set, commented with what each is.
6. **Probe**: mount the story (§11), check each picture `IsLoaded`, and measure positions in design px.
7. **Keep the authoring script and bench in step with the code.** A table the code needs from the pictures
   (like `ICON_REACH`) is printed by the script and pasted; re-run and re-paste whenever a picture changes.

**The ids live in `Data/SkillTree/Marks.luau`**, keyed by node name, and each arm file says
`Icon = Marks.SpringHeels`. One file because it is one set: authored together, uploaded together and judged
together, so the ids arrive as a batch, and a batch pasted into seven files is a batch with one of them
missed. `buildRun` passes an `Icon` down to every rung of a run. `TSkillNode.Icon` is optional and a square
without one keeps its `Glyph`, so the two can coexist while a set is being drawn.

**The seed has no mark on purpose.** The square in the middle is a cell with the shard's own model turning
inside it (`SkillTreeBody.Shard`), so an `Icon` on it would be data nothing reads. The Shard mark is
authored and uploaded with the rest so the bench sheet is complete, and it is wired to nothing.

**Reading a shipped mark back** is §11's trick and it is worth doing once after an upload:
`AssetService:CreateEditableImageAsync` plus `ReadPixelsBuffer` gives the real alpha, so the size and the
four margins can be measured on the asset Roblox actually has rather than on the local file. All eighteen
came back 192×192 with left equal to right and top equal to bottom.

### What the bench duplicates by hand, and will eventually lie about

`iconbench.py` carries its own port of `SkillTreePalette`'s OKLab arithmetic, its own copy of the six arm
hues, and its own `SHADOW_SHARE`. Nothing keeps them in step with the Luau but hand. Both have already had
