to be chased once (an arm hue swap, and the shadow). It is a bench rather than shipped code, which is why it
is tolerated, but **it is the seam most likely to start quietly lying**, and a sheet drawn from stale
constants is worse than no sheet. Check them when either file moves.

---

## 9. Migrating a screen from `panel` to `facet`

1. Swap the require; `panel(...)` → `facet(...)`.
2. `ContentColor` → `FillColor`, `InsideColor` → `EdgeColor`. Drop `Gap`.
3. Delete the caller's `UIPadding` and pass `Padding` instead.
4. Fix the size arithmetic: `panel.InsetX/InsetY(gap)` → `facet.Inset(padding)`, and **remove the separate
   `2 * padding` term** the old code added on top — it is one number now.
5. Pick the edge from the hierarchy table in §5.
6. `Shadow = false` inside any `CanvasGroup` cut to the panel's own size.
7. Multiply the screen's text sizes by **1.236** and look at it.
8. Buttons: `Padding` ~14, and check the label share — the default padding will shrink the word.

---

## 10. What is not done

- **The world prompt is `Gem`, in the game** (§5k), with `Lit` and the old `Iris` kept on `Stories/Prompt`
  at the owner's word. The bench has been looked at in UI Labs, and every behaviour in §5k was read back in
  playtest probes before the switch. **The game's own path was not probed after `DEFAULT_VARIANT` became
  `Gem`**: the three controllers call `PromptUI(onTake)` with no look and lint clean, and that is all.
- **The revives are IN THE GAME** (§5i): `DownedUI` draws only the `Keystone` and `WakingUI` only the `Gem`,
  and the losers are deleted. Probed on the bench, looked at in UI Labs, and **played through the game's
  own client path** by firing the server's `Healed`, `Downed` and `Revived` at it from a probe: the bar
  held at 0 / 20, the stand ticked it to 8 / 20, no errors. A down the SERVER starts (with its Core paying
  for it) and a catch's `Hide` under the blink have not been played.
- **The special attack's badge is IN THE GAME** (§5h) on both weapon slots, driven off one number each:
  `hotbarSlot` takes `Special` / `SpecialSeconds`, `HotbarController` holds a pair of sources per weapon
  slot, and `MeleeWeapon` and `Firearm` push theirs every frame beside the stamina push, because the
  deadline lives on those modules and nothing else can see it. **Played**: the Sword's pierce counts 4, 3,
  2, 1 and the Revolver's fan counts from 8, both their authored cooldowns, and the gem rides the pick's
  grow. What is NOT done is **deleting the four variants that lost** — `Keystone` is chosen and the other
  four are still in the file and still drawn by `Stories/SpecialBadge`, against §5e's own rule.
- **The reaction is IN THE GAME** (§5f) — `SkillTreeUI` draws it, `facet.Faces` carries the rim as a third
  art family, and the bench survives as the place the three kinds are compared. It has been **played**: the
  module loads, the tree opens, and a probe read the layer ladders back off the running screen (rung, verb
  with its `Cross` and `Echo`, and the way out with none of the upgrade-only gestures, all at rotation 0).
  The purchase ring was read back the same way and wears the bought square's own outline.
- **What has NOT been done is LOOKING at it.** A playtest cannot be screenshotted, so every check so far is
  structural — the shapes are right, and how the thing *feels* is unjudged. That is the next session's
  first job, and the bench is where to do it.
- **The spring pinning and the `Visible` gates (§5g) are linted and reasoned, not played.** The settle
  arithmetic was simulated against vide's own condition rather than watched, because the playtest wedged
  before they could be driven. Re-run the cost probe when Studio is free.
- **The skill tree's four faces have not been seen running.** They were landed with the Studio bridge
  unavailable, so `facet`'s face support, the four surfaces that ask for one, the verb's de-rotation and both
  node lights are **linted and reasoned about, not played**. That is the first thing to check.
- **The marks are IN THE GAME and have NOT been seen running** (§8b). Nineteen are authored, eighteen are
  uploaded and wired (the seed keeps its model), and every one of the eighteen was read back off the shipped
  asset at 192x192 with symmetric margins. But that is the PICTURE, not the screen: the composite - a mark
  tinted, shadowed, dimmed and sitting on a lit face - has only ever been looked at on `iconbench.py`'s
  simulation of it. A playtest cannot be screenshotted, so the sheet is the nearest thing there is and it is
  drawn from constants a human keeps in step by hand. Open the tree and look.
- **`FacetGlow` is still a BLUR, not a distance field** (§5d). It lights the health bars, where corners are a
  small share of a long outline, so it is the least urgent of the family, but it is the last one carrying the
  bug that starves corners.
- **The build bar is ON the cut face, was judged on the bench over four rounds, and is SHIPPED.** `Niche` on
  `SquareTable` squares, on a `SquareCrown` sheet, opened with **right click** while the Hammer is in hand.
  The bar measures **828 × 278** design px (43% of the screen's width, 26% of its height), stands at 0.7, and
  gives 23 px of air on all four sides round a 150 px picture in each 150 × 232 slot. Every one of those is
  worked out in `lune` rather than by eye.
- **The build bar's three losing slots are deleted and the bench draws one bar** (§5e). What that screen
  still owes is a `Components/buildSlot.luau`: the file owns the row, the slot, the card, the refusal and the
  box arithmetic in one place, and `hotbarSlot` is a separate component for exactly that reason. It was not
  worth doing while there were four slots to move.
- The HUD's **text sizes** have not had the 1.236 correction (below) — only the skill tree and the build bar
  have.
- **The skill tree, the HUD chrome and the build bar wear the cut face; nothing else does.** Every other
  screen still uses `panel.luau`, which is untouched and still works. The **font** has been swapped globally

- **Only the skill tree's and the build bar's text sizes carry the 1.236 correction.** The HUD, settings and
  loading screen are all still ~20% small.
- The font family string lives in ten files; centralising is outstanding.
- `FONT_PIXEL` / `FONT_PIXEL_BOLD` are misnamed for the face they now hold.
- `UITools.WarmPixelFontMetrics` is defined and never called (pre-existing).

## 10b. What this costs

The style is cheaper than what it replaced, and the places it is not are worth knowing before you scale it.

- **A `facet` is half a `panel`.** Two ImageLabels against four, and **two** `scaleNumber` entries against
  three. Every `scaleNumber` call joins a list the viewport walks on every change, so this is per-panel and it
  adds up: the skill tree builds 55 of them.
- **One source, many readers.** The padding is one `scaleUDim` read by all four `UIPadding` properties, not
  four calls. Asked for four times it registered five entries a panel instead of two — 275 entries across the
  tree doing the work of 110. The sides are not four questions, they are one answer written four times.
- **The same applies to any run of design-px numbers on one axis.** `facetBar` registered four for its shards
  (size, speed, rise, gravity) and a fifth whose answer was always zero; they are one `scaleNumber(1, "y")`
  multiplied at the point of use, and the zero is stated as a constant. Three entries a bar instead of seven,
  which on the HUD's three bars is twelve instead of twenty-one.
- **`scaleNumber` cannot be hoisted to module scope.** It registers a `cleanup`, which vide refuses outside a
  reactive scope, so it throws at require time. Per-instance is the only option.
- **A shared component that mints its own must let a caller hand them in.** `facet.Light` minted two entries
  a light, which is fine for the hotbar's one and **212 entries** across the skill tree's 106, all holding
  the same three answers. It takes `Size` and `SliceScale` as given when they are passed, and the tree mints
  `facet.LightSize` once per light kind plus one `scaleNumber(facet.SourceScale)` for the lot: **212 → 3**.
  The general shape of this: a component that is built once may register what it likes; a component built
  per item in a list must be able to borrow.
- **A component built per slot must borrow its scales, and that includes its own measurements.** The badge
  minted SEVEN `scaleNumber` entries on one axis — its width, its height, its type size, the gap it hangs
  at, the sink, the drop of a spend and its bloom's box — which is seven entries holding one answer on
  every weapon slot in the bar. They are one `scaleNumber(1, "y")` multiplied at the point of use, which
  takes a badge from eight entries to two. Same fix as `facetBar`'s shards, one layer up.
- **Don't give every node a shadow.** The tree's squares pass `Shadow = false`; 54 extra `UIShadow`s to say a
  thing the pool of light already says is the one place on that map where chrome is worth counting.
- **A ViewportFrame re-renders every frame it is visible**, whatever you do, and the cost is the geometry. The
  seed's silhouette glow is a second frame with two cubes in it, which is affordable; the same trick on a
  200-part building is not. The only lever is `Visible` — the tree's is off with the screen.
- **Guard a per-frame write.** `SkillTreeBody` skips the shell fade and the halo when the value has not moved
  (`math.abs(want - shown) >= 1e-3`). The halo settles on 1 whenever there is nothing to spend, which is most
  of the time the tree is open.
- **`typewriter` measures ~95 characters once at load**, one `GetTextBoundsAsync` each. One-time and off the
  critical path, but text shown in the first second or so lays out on the fallback width and relayouts once.
- **A GETTER handed to a component costs an effect node per property, forever — so resolve it and branch.**
  Making `facet`'s `Face` accept a source is what lets a bench sweep the cut under a screen that is already
  up, and it is free *only* if the component checks. Handed a table, the picture and the slice are written as
  plain properties and no node is built at all; handed a getter, each is an effect that will be walked once
  and then never fire again for the rest of the run. On the build bar's five slots that was **60 nodes**
  standing over a source nothing would ever write.

  `facet.Resolve(given)` is the branch, exported so anything drawing its **own** layers on a face makes the
  same one: it returns the resolved table, plus the live getter **only if there was one**. The caller then
  writes `if live then closureOver(live) else face.Plane`. The general shape, and it is not about faces:
  **a prop that CAN be reactive should not be reactive when the caller handed a constant.** Deciding that at
  build time costs one `type()` check; deciding it per property costs a node apiece, and nothing about the
  screen tells you they are there.

  The same rule caught the build bar's own `artShare`, which asked the face for its stroke every frame to
  size a picture that could not change size: resolved once where the face is fixed, a closure only where a
  bench is sweeping.

---

## 10c. Dialling a look — build the bench, don't guess

The bloom took **five rounds** to land and four of them were avoidable. What finally worked was not a better
guess, it was a different tool. Reach for this whenever a number is a matter of appearance rather than
correctness — a glow, a falloff, a pattern's strength, a motion's damping.

### Build a slider page, publish it, and read the numbers off

An Artifact with sliders over a live render of the real thing, with **the reference sitting next to it**.
`Bloom Bench` is the worked example: it draws the same octagon, the same blur, the same compositing the
authoring script bakes, and hands back the constants to paste in. One pass settled what four rounds of
measurement had not.

**Rules for the bench, each of which cost a round when it was missing:**

1. **Model the runtime exactly, including its scaling.** The first bench had a bar-height slider while the
   glow was a fixed size, so tuning at 72px gave numbers that drew nearly twice the glow at the game's 35px.
   Whatever the game scales by, the bench must scale by. If it cannot, it must not offer the control.
2. **Put the reference in the page, scaled to a matched size**, not in another window. The comparison is the
   whole point, and it is only valid at one scale.
3. **Depend on nothing that can fail quietly.** The first bench asked the canvas for `filter: blur()` and read
   it back with `getImageData`; in a sandboxed frame that returns empty with no error, and the page showed a
   bar with no glow and nothing to say why. It computes its own blur now — three box passes, which no browser
   can refuse — over a silhouette computed arithmetically rather than rasterised.
4. **Give it a status line.** Canvas size, the brightest value it found, the numbers it derived. A page that
   fails silently is worse than no page.
5. **Emit the constants, not a screenshot.** The handoff is `GLOW_SIGMA = 12, GLOW_ALPHA = 0.52`, copyable.

### Draw the thing OFFLINE first, in twenty lines, before touching the game

`Assets/ui/badgebench.py` renders the badge the way Roblox renders it — the same distance field, the same
compositing, the same colours — and `badgesolve.py` answers "which pair of numbers holds this reach" in one
dimension along the horizontal, where a diamond's perpendicular distance is just `(x - span/2) / sqrt(2)`.
Between them they replaced five round trips through Studio with five seconds, and they are what found that
a crop keeps the flat interior and that no fixed pair of inks survives a sweeping ground.

**Everything in this style is analytic**, which is what makes this cheap: a bloom is an `erfc` of a signed
distance, a fill is a half-plane, and on a diamond every one of them is a function of `|x| + |y|` alone —
so a whole frame is a lookup table and one add per pixel. If you are about to upload art or start a
playtest to answer a question about a *shape*, write the twenty lines instead.

**And render the OPTIONS, not one guess.** A taste call answered with four panels side by side is answered
once; the same call guessed at is answered three times and rejected twice.

### A slider page has to model the STATE as well as the numbers

§10c's bench drew one variant in one state, and the first thing it earned was "that isn't what's in the
game" — because the game draws several faces at every charge and the page drew one face at full. A page
whose reference panel does not match what is on screen is worse than no page: it sends you off to fix
something that is not broken.

So the page takes the same inputs the component takes — which face, how charged, which moment of the
breath — and its "Shipped" panel carries the constants that are in the file **right now**. And when a
number in the file changes, the page changes with it in the same commit, or the next session is comparing
against a reference that has quietly gone stale.

### The eye beats the measurement, and by a lot

Three rounds were spent fitting the bloom to numbers measured off the reference — 41% of the bar's own
brightness one pixel out, 30% at 0.06 bar-heights, 20% at 0.12, 11% at 0.19, 3% at 0.29 — landing inside two
points **every time**, and it was visibly too much **every time**. What was finally chosen is flatter than all
of it: 26% at the edge, 11% at 0.29. Those figures came off a screenshot of a screenshot and their absolute
levels do not survive the trip. Two pictures side by side on one screen do.

So: **measure to find the shape of a problem, not to decide the answer.** Measurement is what proved the tail
was the culprit rather than the peak, that a rotated gradient's step was landing at 57% instead of 98%, and
that a "quiet" blur pass decided zero pixels. It is not what should pick a number a person is going to look
at.

### If you must measure a glow, measure in bar-heights

Two pictures of a glowing bar are at different scales, and the question is how far the glow reaches *next to
the thing it surrounds*. Comparing in raw pixels is what let three rounds of "this is close" survive against
a thing that was nearly twice too big.

### Say what the change actually was

Every retreat in this document — the 45° leading edge, the `Bevel` variant, the two-pass bloom, the inset
crystal — was something that sounded right and did not survive being looked at. Write those down with the
reason. The next session will otherwise have the same good idea.

---

## 10d. Five rounds of "still happening", and the habits that would have saved four of them

Picking the node faces took five rounds, and **every round found a real bug**. That is the trap: each fix
was correct, and each one was partial, so every round ended with the same three words. None of the bugs was
hard. The methods below are what found them, in the order they should have been reached for.

### The CONTROL is where the bug shows

The last bug was a halo poking past the cut at every corner. It was **invisible on the shape it was blamed
on** (an octagon, where the halo's cut is merely too shallow) and **obvious on the plain square being used as
a reference** (which has no cut, so nothing disagreed and it looked right). The report that cracked it was
"just compare a normal square with one without corners".

So: when something looks wrong on one shape, **draw the simplest shape you have beside it**. If the simple
one is right, the difference between them is the diagnosis. A bench that shows one specimen cannot do this,
which is half of why every bench here draws a row.

### Measure the screenshot; do not look harder at it

Not one of these rounds was settled by looking. All five were settled by sampling pixels, and the sampling is
always the same three lines: a scanline **perpendicular to an edge**, one **diagonally out from a corner**,
and the same pair on the shape next to it. Print the numbers.

| What the numbers said | What it proved |
| --- | --- |
| fill `32/66/65`, a join at `58/102/101` nine px inside a tip, nothing outside the silhouette | the tip's second line was **in the art**: not a seam, not a shadow, not resampling |
| one px out: edge **21**, corner **8**; corner gone by 4px, edge still going at 6 | a blur **starves corners** |
| the face's cut begins 6px along the diagonal, the halo's at 2 | the halo's cut was **k times** the face's |
| edge `67,62,58,53,49,45…` against corner `67,63,59,54,50,45…` | the distance-field fix **landed** |

A difference you cannot put a number on is a difference you cannot tell you have fixed.

### Reproduce the pipeline offline BEFORE uploading

Roblox's nine-slice is about twenty lines of PIL: corners drawn at their own size, edges stretched on one
axis, middle on both, and all four corners **shrunk together** when two of them will not fit. With that in
hand, "is this the art or the renderer?" is one command, and so is "does the halo's silhouette land on the
face's?". Three rounds of authoring and uploading happened before that existed. Write it first.

The same goes for the art itself: **render it, look at it, and measure it locally**, then upload. Every
upload is permanent and the round trip through Studio is the slow part of the loop.

### "Still happening" means a SECOND cause, not a failed fix

Twice the fix was right and the complaint survived it. The discipline: after a fix, **re-measure the exact
number that was wrong**. If it is now right and the complaint stands, stop defending the fix and start
looking for the next cause. Saying "the fix did land, and here is the number" costs one command and stops
both sides re-arguing a settled point.

### Do not guess twice at a taste call

The verb's facet was guessed twice and rejected twice. The third time it went out as five rendered options
side by side with the thing they had to match, and was answered in one line. **Rendering the options is
cheaper than one wrong guess**, and a taste call is the owner's, not yours.

### A bench opens on what you want JUDGED

Showing the control first is right everywhere except when the control has a known artifact. While `full` put
a bar across every turned node, opening on it meant six of seven specimens wore the same bug and the shapes
could not be compared through it. Open on the candidate; leave the control one button away.

---

## 10e. The bench that lives in the repo: a UI Labs story with controls

§10c's bench is an Artifact in a browser, which is the right tool for a number that is a matter of
appearance. This is the other kind: a **story**, a `*.story.luau` module that the UI Labs plugin mounts
inside Studio, drawing the **real component** rather than a drawing of it. Reach for it when the thing being
judged is the component's own behaviour — a spring, an entrance, a state change, a layout against the other
things on the screen — because that is what a browser bench cannot model.

`src/FeedTheCore/Client/UI/Stories/Hud.story.luau` is the worked example and is the one to copy: every fixed
HUD readout at the position and size the game draws it at, plus the build menu standing over the hotbar it
springs up on top of, with a setting for each thing that moves. `Stories/BuildBar` is the other shape the
same tool takes — one object drawn four ways at once to pick between them — and between them they are the
two reasons to write a story at all: **does this piece read against the others**, and **which of these
pieces is right**. The plugin is [UI Labs](https://ui-labs.luau.page/docs/); everything below is its
behaviour, learned the hard way or read out of its source.

**A COMPOSITION BENCH AND A TAKE-IT-APART BENCH MUST NOT MERGE.** `Hud.story` draws the shipped build bar
and nothing else — no face dropdowns, no settings of its own for it — because the question it asks is where
the bar lands among everything else on screen. `BuildBar.story` sweeps the faces, walks the stores, replays
the entrance and does not care what else is up. Growing either toward the other costs both.

It held while `BuildBar` drew **four** bars to choose between, and it still holds now it draws one: the
question has changed from *which of these* to *does this one behave*, and neither is *does it sit right
beside the ammo readout*.

### There are two story formats, and only one of them can have controls

The older stories here (`Settings`, `Chrome`, `SkillNodes`, `SkillReact`, `SpecialBadge`) are **function
stories**: `function(target) ... return cleanup end`, the Hoarcekat shape. UI Labs runs them, and they can
never have a settings panel — a function story has nowhere to declare one, which is why every one of them
draws its own row of `TextButton`s instead.

`Hud`, `BuildBar` and `CoreBars` are **table** stories with controls. `BuildBar` is the one to read for a
bench that compares *variants* — or rather for what one looks like afterwards: it drew four whole bars 2×2
with every setting driving all four on the same frame, which is the only way the losers get judged against
the winner rather than against a memory of it (§5e), and it draws **one** now that the choice is made. A
bench that outlives its round should shrink to the thing that won, or it goes on inviting a comparison that
is over.

`CoreBars` **carried candidate art for two rounds and then gave it back.** A face that is uploaded but not
yet in `facet.Faces` cannot be drawn from a data table, because an upload hands back a Decal id and the Image
inside it is only discoverable by opening the decal (§3, §8) — so the bench held the **decal** ids, opened
them once per Studio session, cached them at module scope and printed every `decal -> rbxassetid://image`
line plus the block `facet.Faces` wanted. That is the way through when the Studio bridge is held by another
process, and it is worth building into any bench carrying candidate art, because the ids are wanted anyway
the moment one wins. **The moment they were wanted, all of it came out**: the opener, the candidate table,
the status line and the paste block were 295 lines, and the two winners are two entries in `facet.Faces`.

**Past six rows it runs a second column** rather than closing the pitch up: a readout is 0.075 of the screen
tall, so ten of them down one side would have to sit at a pitch of 0.074 and the panels would touch. The
sheet is 0.24 wide, so two columns stand clear with a third of the screen between them. It drew a **mode**
for one round, when seven faces and four marks were open at once and twelve would not stack — both sets
built, one set `Visible`, taking the same slots so nothing moved when the mode changed. The mark round closed
and the mode went with it.

`CoreBars` is the shape a round takes while it is still **open**, and on a question the other two do not
ask: not *which variant of one object*, but *which of the faces that already exist* each surface of one
readout should be drawn on. It draws the real `CoreHealthUI` once per entry in `facet.Faces`, all three of
its surfaces on that one cut, stacked down the screen and driven off one set of numbers — plus one copy in
the readout's own slot whose sheet, shield strip and HP bar are three separate dropdowns, because a sheet
0.24 of the screen wide and a strip a third the height of the bar under it do not have to be cut alike. Each
copy gets a full-size frame of its own that the bench slides, rather than a Position written into the panel:
the panel's own Position is bound to the drop it arrives on and would shove any such write straight back.

`WaveTitle` ran four rounds on the last thing on the HUD still wearing the old chrome — the CAMP / WAVE N
title, two mirrored sprites hard against the words with four px of pure black round every letter. **It is
shipped**: the word small and spaced over the number, centred as one thing on a dissolving cut-face plate
with a hollow diamond at each end, wiping open from its own middle while the whole of it settles onto its
line. The plate, the ends, how the two lines sit and how it arrives and goes were each their own round, and
the bench drew the real module once per candidate, announced on the same frame off one wave number, because
everything not being chosen is then literally the same code rather than several things dialled alike.

**What it taught about MOTION is in §5c** — the three curves and which layer takes which, size-versus-
transparency, the window and the group. What it taught about running a round on a *bench*:

- **Two rounds on one object are two FIELDS, not one list of drawings.** What a thing stands on and how one
  part of it is drawn are questions about different parts, and crossing them is rows nobody can stack. Carry
  **two row sets, one `Visible`, taking the same slots** — `CoreBars`' mode. **When a round closes, the field
  goes with it**: one ground is not an axis. All four have closed here and `WaveUI` has no variant word left.
- **A bench for MOTION wants one at a time and a TIME SCALE, not a row of them.** Six gestures playing at
  once is six things moving, and a gesture is judged by watching one. The setting that makes the round
  judgeable is the scale: an arrival is 24 frames, which is not enough to form an opinion on, and at a tenth
  speed it is 240. **Slow the component's whole clock** — the sweep, the hold, the beat before a counter
  turns and the turn itself — or what is watched is a different gesture with its parts re-timed against each
  other. That means the component keeps its own `elapsed`, never reads `os.clock`, and divides any duration
  it hands to something with a clock of its own (`rollingCounter`'s roll is wall time).
- **The set that is NOT being swept has to be live, or the two rounds cannot meet.** Candidates that can only
  stand on one ground need that ground to change under them — so the swept field takes **a name or a getter**,
  exactly as `Face` does. A name builds one and a getter builds them all and shows the named one: the game
  names its pick and pays for one, the bench pays for all of them.
- **A plate that dissolves wants no edge PICTURE at all** — or rather, it wants it under a **second, harsher
  ramp**. Transparent for the first and last 9% of the width (68 design px against a 34 px corner cell and an
  11 px table-line inset) kills every *vertical* thing in that picture — the outline's two ends, the lit
  corner art, a crown's table line where it turns — and leaves the long horizontal runs. Two drawn lines give
  a plain face's top and bottom and nothing else; the picture gives a crown face its table line as well.
- **A gap between two LINE BOXES is not the gap you see.** Stacking a caption and a number in a list put
  **30 design px** between two lines asked to touch, on a `Padding` of 2 — a 58px number sits in an 81px line
  box. Cut the boxes the layout stacks to the **ink** and the padding means what it says: 4 buys 7.25. Both
  lines then overflow their boxes, which is free — a list centres a child taller than itself — with one
  catch: **a `TextLabel` clips its line to its own rect**, so a label needs its full line box even when the
  layout only gives its row the ink.
- **When two lines sit wrong against a fixed thing, move the TYPE, not the thing.** The ends are the
  announcement and the caption is the label on it; dropping the *ends* to meet a low number reads as badly as
  it sounds.

**A setting that picks one of a set must be a `Choose`, not a string.** `BuildBar`'s two face settings were
literal strings for one round, and a string control is a bare text box: a reader cannot tell what is valid,
a typo silently draws the default, and the list has to be printed somewhere on the screen to be usable at
all. They are dropdowns built from `facet.Faces` itself now (§10e's advanced controls), so the list cannot
go stale and a wrong name cannot be typed. **Build the options from the table they come from**, never from a
second copy of the names.

A story that wants controls is a **table**:

```lua
return {
    summary = "One sentence, shown in the preview. Rich text is allowed.",
    vide = Vide,          -- required: the library UI Labs should mount with
    controls = CONTROLS,  -- optional
    story = function(props) ... end,
}
```

`name` is accepted and **ignored** (the module's name is always used). `vide` is what makes it a Vide story
rather than a React or Fusion one; the story function is then called **once**, inside a stable scope.

### Controls come in two families, and only one of them is free

**Primitive controls are literals.** Put a `string`, `number`, `boolean` or `Color3` in the table and UI
Labs builds the matching widget: the value *is* both the declaration and the default.

```lua
local CONTROLS = {
    ["Core: HP"] = 41,              -- a drag field with a number box
    ["Ammo: gun in hands"] = true,  -- a tick box
    ["Wave: number"] = 1,
}
```

**Advanced controls are constructors**, and they come from the UI Labs **utility package** — which the repo
now carries: `UILabs = "pepeeltoro41/ui-labs@2.4.2"` in `wally.toml`, required as
`ReplicatedStorage.Packages.UILabs`. Signatures read off the installed 2.4.2 rather than off the docs, which
are a version behind (they still show a `widen` argument neither `Choose` nor `EnumList` takes):

| Constructor | Story receives |
| --- | --- |
| `Slider(def, min, max, step?)` | `number` inside the range; **errors if `max <= min`** |
| `RGBA(def, transparency?)` | `{ Color: Color3, Transparency: number }` |
| `Choose(list, def?)` | the selected **entry** of the array; `def` is an INDEX, and errors past the end |
| `EnumList(list, key)` | the **value** of the selected key of a record; the key is required and must exist |
| `Object(className?, def?, predicator?)` | an `Instance`, or `nil` |

The same package exposes the primitives as constructors (`String`, `Number`, `Boolean`, and `Color3` under
`Datatype` to dodge the name collision), which is the only way to give a number a **min, max or step** —
`Number(def, min, max, step, dragger, sens)`.

**And `Ordered(control, order)`, which is the one that retires a papercut below.** It takes a control *or a
bare literal* — it runs `ConvertControl` first, so `Ordered(true, 6)` is a boolean control at order 6 — and
stamps the `Order` field a literal cannot carry. `ControlGroup(controls)` nests a set of them under one
heading.

`Stories/BuildBar` is the worked example: two `Choose` dropdowns over `facet.Faces` read off the table rather
than typed out, three `Slider`s bounded to the real length of the row, and every entry wrapped in `Ordered`
so the panel reads top to bottom.

**Still clamp the reads.** A slider cannot hand back anything outside its range, so the clamps stop being
load-bearing — but a bench should not trust a widget to be the only guard on an index into a table.
`Hud.story` keeps every one of its clamps for exactly that reason.

**Reach for a slider whenever the number has a real ceiling**, which on these benches is nearly always: six
chambers, five hotbar slots, forty shield, one slot per building. The range is then a statement about the
game as well as a way to drive it. Where one has to be invented, **derive it and say so** — `Hud.story`'s
Core ceiling runs to 550 because `BastionCore`'s `HP_PER_LEVEL` is 250 and that is the crystal at three
fortress levels, not because 550 looked roomy.

**A range that could collapse needs a floor**, because `Slider` and `Choose` throw at MODULE scope: a count
taken off a folder wants `math.max(n, 1)` behind it, or an empty folder hides the story from the list
entirely (see "Small things that cost a run each").

**Never hand-build a control table.** UI Labs passes one through untouched, so it *would* work, and it would
be a copy of an internal shape — use the constructors, which are now available.

### A control arrives as a `Vide.Source`, so read it in an `effect`

UI Labs builds one source per control and writes to it when the panel changes. `props.controls["Core: HP"]`
is therefore a getter, and it can be handed straight to a property:

```lua
Visible = props.controls.Visible
```

`props.target` is the frame to mount into, and returning an instance from the story parents it there.

### EVERY EFFECT RUNS TWICE, so a "fire on change" effect has to remember

Vide's strict flag is on whenever the module is compiled below `-O2`, and strict mode **evaluates every
effect twice per update**. An effect that fires an event — a sting, an announcement, a sound — fires it
twice unless it compares against something the second pass has already seen.

`effect` hands the callback **its own previous return value**, which is exactly that memory:

```lua
effect(function(last: Vector2): Vector2
    local hp = math.clamp(coreHp(), 0, untrack(coreCeiling))
    local shield = math.clamp(coreShield(), 0, CORE_MAX_SHIELD)
    core.SetCurrent(hp, shield)
    if hp < last.X or shield < last.Y then
        core.Show()
        core.Sting()
    end
    return Vector2.new(hp, shield)
end, coreStart)
```

Pass 1 sees the old pair and stings; pass 2 is handed the pair pass 1 returned and does not. An effect that
instead tracks its previous value in an upvalue works too, as long as it **writes that upvalue**, which is
how the stores walk in `Hud.story` stays single-fire. An effect that decided on a comparison it does not
update will fire on both passes, every time.

### UNTRACK EVERY PUSH INTO A COMPONENT — its setter may READ its own sources

This is the one that cost a session, and it is not obvious from either side.

A component's setter is free to read the sources it owns. `facetBar`'s `SetCurrent` throws shards and reads
the bar's scale to size them. `BuildBarUI`'s `Select` calls `pinAll`, which writes every slot's `emphasis`
and `dimmed` **springs** a position — and to write "the position it is already at" it has to **read** each
one first (that pin is itself a fix, for §5g's spring-that-never-settles).

A read inside an effect subscribes that effect. So calling a setter while tracking silently wires your
effect to the component's internals, and **when one of those is a spring, the effect re-runs on every frame
that spring ticks** — pushing again, which re-pins, which keeps the spring off its tolerance, forever.

What it looks like on screen is not a stutter or a stall. It is the thing being **re-triggered**: the build
bar's picked slot sat there playing its pick — the kick, the glint, the flash — over and over, a frame at a
time, while every other slot drew correctly.

**The shape that is safe:** read the settings tracked, then push inside `untrack`.

```lua
local push = untrack -- `untrack` under a name that says why

effect(function(last: number): number
    local index = math.clamp(math.floor(pickedSlot()), 1, slotCount)
    if index == last then return index end
    push(function()
        local id = bar.GetIdAt(index)
        if id then bar.Select(id) end
    end)
    return index
end, -1)
```

Both halves are load-bearing and they fix different things. **Untracked** stops the subscription, so the
effect no longer runs every frame. **Remembered** stops an unchanged index from re-firing a pick, which
matters because `Select` is an *event* — it is not idempotent, it strikes a flash every time it is called.

Do it uniformly rather than auditing which setters happen to read today: a setter that reads nothing this
week can grow a shard throw next week, and nothing will point at your effect when it does. Writing your
**own** sources needs none of this — a write is not a read — so the sources a bench owns (a sweep, a glow,
an active slot) can be set straight from an effect.

And note what this means for the story BODY: a source read there is outside every effect and subscribes to
nothing, so seeding a component before the effects is free and needs no `untrack`. Same for a click handler,
which runs with no scope on the stack.

### A control is not a button, and that is usually an improvement

There is no button control. Two ways round it, and the first is almost always right:

- **Make the event fall out of the state.** Dropping a health number *is* the blow; changing the wave number
  or the phase *is* the announcement. `Hud.story` has no "damage the core" button — it has `Core: HP`, and
  dragging it down is the damage. The setting then does double duty: it is the trigger *and* it is the
  resting value, which a button can never be.
- **A boolean whose every flip fires once**, for the handful of things that are genuinely momentary and have
  no state behind them — pulling the trigger on an empty gun, replaying an announcement without changing it.
  Same previous-value shape as above.

### A SETTING NEVER DRAWS ANYTHING; it calls what the controller calls

The point of a story over a screenshot is that it exercises the real path. So a control's effect should end
in the same call the controller makes — `core.Show()` then `core.Sting()`, `resources.Add` for a gain and
`Hold` + `Release` for a spend — and never in a property write of its own. A bench that sets `Visible` or
nudges a `Position` to show a state is testing the bench.

Where a number cannot be required (below), **copy it and name the file it came from**, the way
`Stories/BuildBar` copies `BuildablesCore`'s refusal lines. A bench fed invented numbers is testing a state
the game cannot reach.

### THE TARGET IS A FRAME IN A PLUGIN WIDGET, so it cannot hold a `ScreenGui`

Every screen in this game returns one. A story's target is not a `PlayerGui`, so the gui has to be taken
apart: lift its children into one plain `Frame` and destroy it.

```lua
for _, gui in guis do
    for _, child in gui:GetChildren() do child.Parent = holder end
    gui:Destroy()
end
```

The lift is free — everything is positioned against its parent, and the holder fills the target exactly as a
`ScreenGui` fills the screen — and **the order of the lift is the stacking order**, since the HUD's guis all
sit at `DisplayOrder` 0 and sort as siblings.

### Vide's root frees STATE, not INSTANCES

`vide.mount`'s unmount tears down the reactive graph and leaves everything it built on screen, and UI Labs
does not destroy the mount frame's children either. So `cleanup(function() holder:Destroy() end)`, or every
re-run leaves its bench standing on top of the last one. (`Vide.cleanup` is also how a story learns it is
being unmounted at all.)

### MODULE state outlives the story, so put it back

A leaf state module — `CrosshairState`, `AmmoState` — is a module and not a scope, so whatever the bench
wrote into it is still there for the next story that mounts the same component. Clear it in `cleanup`.

The mirror of this is worth knowing too: **UI Labs caches a story's requires per load**, so two requires of
one ModuleScript inside a story hand back the *same* table. A bench and the component it mounts really do
share the leaf module, which is what makes writing to it work.

### A module-level connection that is never disconnected leaks ONCE PER RE-RUN

`CursorUI` hung its per-frame work on `RunService.PreRender` and never disconnected it. That cost the game
nothing, since the game mounts the crosshair once and never takes it down, and it cost a story one idle loop
every single re-run, which a tuning session does dozens of. It is wrapped in `cleanup` now, because
`Stories/Revive` mounted one per cell while its round was open, and four leaks a re-run was the point at
which writing it down stopped being enough.

So: **a story is what exposes a missing `cleanup`**, because it is the only thing that unmounts. When a
component is going into a bench, check that its connections are wrapped; when one is not, either wrap it or
write the leak down where the next person will read it. Wrapping is safe whenever the component is only ever
built inside a `Vide.mount`, which is where `cleanup` is allowed.

### A story cannot require `DataCore`, and therefore cannot require most Cores

`DataCore` requires **every weapon module** at load to register the abilities hanging off them, and a weapon
names its behaviour module through `Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild(...)`. There is no LocalPlayer in the
Studio **edit** session a story plugin runs in, so one require of one Core takes the whole bench down on a
line about swords before a single pixel is drawn. That rules out `DataCore`, `BuildablesCore` and
`ResourcesCore`.

What is safe:

- **The data modules themselves.** `ReplicatedStorage.Data.Buildables`, `.Resources`, `.Tools` — enums and a
  type, nothing that reaches for a player. Walk the folder and require the children.
- **`ReplicatedStorage.Models`**, which is instances, and instances are always there.
- **Cores that require nothing heavy.** `HotbarCore` (TData plus the four clean `Data/Tools` modules),
  `AwakeningCore`, `DownedCore`, `FirearmSpread`. Check the require chain before adding one.

**Mirror the Core's own ordering rather than borrowing it.** `Hud.story` sorts the resources by `Order` then
`Name` because that is what `ResourcesCore` does; `BuildBar.story` mirrors the buildables' sort the same way.
Both note that the rule now lives in two places.

### Two things about a widget that are not the game

- **Pixel sizes come off the real viewport.** Everything positioned in **scale** lands exactly where it
  should at any widget size, but `scaleNumber` measures design px against
  `Workspace.CurrentCamera.ViewportSize` — so a small widget draws slots and type sized for a full screen.
  **Maximise before judging any spacing.** This is the same trap as §11's "a playtest's ViewportSize lies",
  reached from the other side.
- **`UserInputService` does not work inside a plugin widget.** Take the pointer off the GUI's own
  `MouseEnter` / `MouseMoved` / `InputBegan` events, which is what §5f says to do anyway and for a better
  reason (the event only fires while the cursor is actually over the element). The utility package's
  `Environment.InputListener` is the way to get a real global listener if one is ever needed; the same
  `Environment` is also how a story reaches `plugin`, the widget itself (the only place a `Sound` will play
  in edit mode), a janitor, and `Unmount` / `Reload`.

### Seed off the settings, not off a constant

A bench that seeds a component at some tidy default and then lets the first effect push the panel's value in
fires an event on frame one that nobody asked for: `Hud.story` opened on the Core taking a hit, because it
was seeded at full and the panel said 41. Read the controls **in the story body**, seed from those, and hand
the same values to the effect as its initial previous-value. A source read outside every `effect` does not
subscribe to anything, so this is just a read.

### Open on a state that STAYS

§10d's rule, with a second edge on it. `CoreHealthUI` is built to take itself off the screen when the Core
is at full, correctly — so a bench that opened at full showed its largest readout for four seconds and then
had to be poked before it could be looked at again. The defaults put it part way down, which is both a real
mid-fight state and the one that holds still.

### Control ORDER: `Ordered`, or the names carry it

A literal control carries no `Order` field, and UI Labs' default sort mode *is* `Order` — which means every
control sorts as 0 over a `pairs()` walk, and the panel comes out in hash order. The plugin's other two modes
are `Name` and `ControlType`.

**`UILabs.Ordered(control, n)` is the fix** now that the package is carried, and it takes a bare literal as
happily as a constructed control. Number them so the panel opens on what the bench was opened to look at:
`Stories/BuildBar` puts its two face dropdowns first, then the row, then the three settings that are events.
`Hud.story` numbers them in the order the readouts are BUILT, which is roughly the order they are read on
screen — the Core at the top, then the phase, the stores, the lord, the gun, the bar, the build menu, the
down — so the panel and the picture are walked the same way round.

**Name them for it anyway.** `Core: HP`, `Hotbar: lit slot`, `Face: the sheet` — the thing each one moves as
the first word groups them under a Name sort too, and leaves every one readable wherever it lands, which
matters because the sort mode is the reader's setting and not the file's.

### Small things that cost a run each

- **A story must not yield.** UI Labs warns, and the mount has already gone past you.
- **A throw at MODULE scope hides the story from the LIST**, where a throw inside `story` at least says so
  in the Output. Everything above the story table runs while UI Labs is enumerating the folder — the
  `controls` table included, and `Slider` and `Choose` both throw on a bad range — so anything up there that
  reads the place must be able to fail softly: `FindFirstChild` rather than a dot, `math.max(n, 1)` on a
  count that bounds a slider, and no `require` of a module that might not be there. Both `Hud.story` and
  `Stories/BuildBar` count their catalogs off `GetChildren()` without requiring anything, for this reason
  alone.
- **An error in the story is CAUGHT, not raised.** UI Labs runs a Vide story's function inside its own
  handler and warns, so the plugin keeps going and the unmount is still handed back — but everything built
  before the error is already parented and nothing will take it down, because the root frees state only
  (above). A story that half-mounted leaves its half on screen. Read the Output window, not the widget.
  (A **function** story is worse: an error there means the cleanup function is never returned at all, and
  the docs say a Studio restart is the way out.)
- **Only `stylua` and `selene` can be run against a story from outside Studio**, plus a compile check
  (`luau.compile` under Lune parses it without a DataModel). Nothing on this side can drive the plugin:
  Tripwire's `run_luau` is the published place headless and `run_luau_live` is the playtest server, and a
  story runs on the client in edit. **Say so** rather than implying it was opened.

---

## 11. How this gets checked

There are no automated tests. The two that actually work:

- **Lint.** `stylua --check src` must pass; run `selene` on the files you changed, not all of `src` (the tree
  already fails on old code, so only new warnings in your files count).

  **Read selene's WHOLE output, not the warnings.** It reports an undefined global as an **error**, and
  `selene file | grep '^warning'` is blind to exactly that — which is how a refactor here deleted a
  constants block, left three undefined globals behind, and passed its own check. `[table index is nil]` at
  mount was the first anyone knew. Check the `Results:` line, or grep `-E '^(error|warning)'`.

  **And neither linter can see a scope's 200-local limit, a spring that never settles, or a local read
  inside its own initializer** (§5g). Lint is necessary and it is not sufficient; those three only fail
  when the thing runs.
- **A playtest probe.** Studio screenshots are **edit-mode only**, so a running screen cannot be captured —
  the way to check UI is a temporary `.client.luau` that mounts the thing, reads properties back and prints
  them, driven with Tripwire's `start_playtest` / `get_playtest_output`. That is how the glyph advances, the
  node rotations, the image loads and the button's label box in this document were all confirmed. Delete the
  probe afterwards.

### Put a probe in `ReplicatedStorage` as a `Script` with `RunContext = Client`

A `LocalScript` in `StarterPlayerScripts` is the obvious place and it **silently did not run** twice in one
session: the playtest came up, the game's own scripts printed, and the probe's first line never appeared. A
`Script` in `ReplicatedStorage` with `RunContext = Client` ran every time. Prefer it, and if a probe prints
nothing at all, suspect where it is parented before you suspect what it measures.

**A font question needs no client at all.** `TextService:GetTextBoundsAsync` works on the live **server**, so
`run_luau_live` answers advance ratios, cap heights and "which digit is widest" in one call with no probe,
no `.client.luau` and no cleanup. Every measured font number in this document can be re-checked that way.

### A probe can MOUNT A STORY, with plain sources for its controls

A client probe can `require` a story module and call `story.story({ controls = ..., target = frame })`
inside `vide.mount`, with each control a `vide.source(value)` named exactly as the story names it. That runs
the bench, with the real HUD, inside a playtest, and flipping a source is pressing the control. Put the
target frame in a ScreenGui of the probe's own, and call the returned unmount and destroy that gui at the end.

**Every control the story declares needs a source**, or the story indexes nil. Do not copy the list: read it off
the story. A UI Labs control is a table whose default is `ControlValue` (a bare `true` or a number is its own
default), so `if type(c) == "table" and c.ControlValue ~= nil then c.ControlValue else c` over `story.controls`
builds every source it needs and never falls behind the story. §5o's probe is the worked example: it mounted two
stories, flipped their controls and printed counts and transparencies, and caught three bugs no screenshot would.

**Measure in DESIGN px, not screen px.** A screen laid out on a 1920 x 1080 canvas (PackUI) divides every
`AbsolutePosition` and `AbsoluteSize` by `canvas.AbsoluteSize.Y / 1080`; the numbers then compare directly
with the constants in the code ("slots 31 from the panel top, 20 above the rule"). Useful reads beyond
positions: `TextFits` (false on any visible label means cut text), `IsLoaded` on each picture, a
`UIScale.Scale` sampled every frame for an animation's peak and rest, a `GroupTransparency` after it settles.

### Tripwire's simulated mouse CAN hover, in a probe's own ScreenGui

It did not in an earlier session, and it did for the focus marker: a probe mounted the Pack story into a
`ScreenGui` of its own (`IgnoreGuiInset = true`, `DisplayOrder = 100`) under `PlayerGui`, and
`simulate_mouse_input` `move` fired `MouseEnter` on the tile under it. **The coordinates are SCREEN px:
`AbsolutePosition` plus the top bar inset** (58 in Studio), so print each target's AbsolutePosition and
`GetGuiInset()` first and add. If a hover still does not fire, fall back to driving the state the hover would set
(mount the component alone with that state as a source, flip it, sample every frame), as the NEW mark's exit was.

**Log motion by printing only on CHANGE.** A `Heartbeat` probe that prints a piece's transparency and position
only when the formatted line differs gives the whole curve of a fade or a glide in a dozen lines: that is how the
marker's leave was shown to reach zero on the frame its drift stopped.

### To play a screen the SERVER drives, fire the wire from a server probe

A `Script` in `ServerScriptService` that requires `ServerScriptService.GlobalServer.Network` and calls an
event's `FireAll` with the ids the client expects drives the client's real controller path, without
touching game state. `ReplicatedStorage.GlobalShared.Utils.Functions.getCharacterIdFromPlayer` gives the
character id. **Do not require a game Service from it**: that hung silently when tried. The revives were
played this way: `Healed(60)` and `Downed(10)`, then 10 s later `Healed(8)` and `Revived(8)`, with a client
probe reading the game's own `DownedGui`. A down fired this way costs the Core nothing, so the server's own
path still needs a real down.

### Measure an ORDER in frames, off one thing each side writes

"Does A happen on the frame B does" is answered by a frame counter in a client probe's `PreRender` and one
observable per side: here the humanoid's `CameraOffset` coming back up (the revive) and the first explosion
light turning visible (the blast). The answer was frames 599 and 600, which timestamps printed at two
decimals would have hidden. Remember the probe's own `PreRender` runs after the game's (it connected later),
so anything the game's step writes is already visible to it that frame.

### A playtest stops SLOWLY

`stop_playtest` returns before the teardown is done, and Studio does not answer for 15 to 20 seconds while it
tears down. Wait about 45 s, check `list_studios` for `playtestActive: false`, and only then delete the probe
or start the next run.

### Settling a COORDINATE SPACE takes one probe, and it must print all the candidates

The two mouse spaces in §3 were settled by one script that printed, on a single mouse move: the event's own
args, `GetMouseLocation`, `Mouse.X/Y`, `GetGuiInset`, and `AbsolutePosition` of one button under **two**
ScreenGuis, one ignoring the inset and one not. Every relationship falls out of that one line, and the
question never has to be asked again.

**The trap is printing only the two numbers you are comparing.** They will differ by 58 and you still will
not know which one is wrong, or whether the gui setting matters. Print the whole family.

### A probe that SAMPLES will catch the previous event; POLL

Checking the purchase ring, a probe bought a square and read the ring 0.35s later. It reported a verb
wearing a rung's outline — because the map holds a purchase until the chips have flown to the square, so
every read caught the **previous** purchase's ring. The fix is to wait for the old one to die, then poll
each frame until the new one appears.

**The tell that it is a timing bug and not a real one:** the answers did not line up with the sequence —
two "nothing there" followed by one wrong answer, rather than three wrong answers. A result that is
inconsistent across identical cases is measuring the clock, not the code.

### After a BULK edit, check what else moved

Deleting a comment block by matching its first and last lines swallowed a table declaration and two
constants that happened to sit between them. It lints (they became globals), and it fails at mount. After
any edit that removes a *range* rather than an exact string, grep back for the things that were supposed to
survive — and read the linter's errors, not its warnings (above).

### A probe measures the LAYER and ASSUMES the picture — so measure the picture too

Every probe written for the badge read back the element: its size, its slice, its transparency. All of them
passed while the thing on screen was wrong, because none of them ever asked what was actually **inside the
image**. When the geometry checks out and it still looks wrong, the next question is whether the art is the
art you think it is.

It can be read directly. `AssetService:CreateEditableImageAsync(Content.fromAssetId(id))` opens an asset the
place's creator owns, and `image:ReadPixelsBuffer(Vector2.zero, image.Size)` hands back **8-bit RGBA, four
bytes a pixel** (`buffer.readu8(buf, (y * width + x) * 4 + 3)` is the alpha — not a float32 read, which is
the first thing to get wrong). A scanline through the middle then gives the peak and, at half of it, where
the silhouette's boundary sits.

That is how the badge's light was cleared of suspicion in one run: 360×360 source px, peak 0.518, boundary
at **0.200** of the width, which is an Offer light exactly (a Pool is 720 at 0.339). Worth doing before
re-authoring anything, and worth doing to `facet`'s own ids the first time a face is used in anger — a
light that nothing had drawn before could have been wired to the wrong id for a year without anyone seeing.

### A playtest's ViewportSize lies, so never trust raw pixels

A Studio playtest can report `Workspace.CurrentCamera.ViewportSize` as **1×1**, which makes `scaleMin`
1/1920 and collapses every design-px value to something that prints as zero. Worse, `scaleNumber` captures
`CurrentCamera` **at module load** while a probe reading `Workspace.CurrentCamera` fresh may get a *different*
camera — so the UI can be laid out against a real viewport while your probe reads the stale one and tells you
everything is zero. This cost a round of chasing a bug that was not there.

**So: print `ViewportSize` alongside anything measured in pixels, and check ratios rather than absolutes.** A
padding of 18 design px reads as `Offset = 17` at a 0.94 scale, not as 18 — the useful check is that the four
sides agree and that `Offset / scaleMin` lands on the design number.

**At 1×1 every design-px number reads as literally 0.** Checking `textShadow`, the control case (a gap
pinned at 2) printed an offset of **0** and looked like a broken component; it was `scaleNumber(2)` against a
1×1 viewport. The share-based case in the same run printed `0.4375` (which is `0.5 - 0.0625`) and was right,
because a **ratio does not care what the viewport lied about**. Design a probe so its answer is a ratio and
the lie cannot reach it.

### When the Studio bridge is unavailable

It goes down, and on a long UI session that is most of the loop. What still works, and none of it needs
Studio to be reachable from the agent:

- **Author and look at the art locally.** Simulate the nine-slice and measure it (§10d). This catches
  geometry bugs, which is most of them.
- **Upload through Open Cloud directly** (§8), so the round trip is not blocked either.
- **Have a bench print the ids it resolves** (§8), so a paste from the Output window replaces a playtest
  probe.
- Check what is holding the port before touching it: `ss -lptn 'sport = :44331'`. A bridge with **established
  connections from Studio is not stale**, it is another session's, and killing it takes their Studio with it.

### A LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts ran fine this time

The focus marker's probes were `LocalScript`s created with `create_instance` under
`StarterPlayer.StarterPlayerScripts` and all ran. The advice above stands as the fallback when a probe prints
nothing, not as a rule that the other place never works.

### A playtest can wedge, and only a human can clear it

`start_playtest` twice in a row leaves Studio with *"Failed to start the test because a previous one is
still in progress"*, and every later call returns `No live server peer`. Nothing on this side clears it —
it wants Stop pressed in Studio. **Stop after every playtest**, and if two starts in a row fail, say so
rather than retrying.

**It happened again on the focus marker, and this is how.** A probe errored, the playtest was stopped and a new
one started three seconds later, before the teardown (above: 15-20 s) had finished. Every start after that
returned `No live server peer` for the rest of the session, across five later rounds of work that then went
unverified. **After `stop_playtest`, wait the full 45 s, confirm with `studio_status` / `list_studios`, and fix a
broken probe by editing its source while stopped rather than restarting in a hurry.**

Say what was actually verified. "Not playtested" is a fine answer; leaving it out is not.

---

## Last Wave: the retro run UI (round 2, built 2026-10-29, unjudged)

> **Parked.** Everything in this section up to "The vitals" lives on the `retro-ui` branch, not on `main`: the user had
> it rolled back because it changed the whole HUD at once. The files it names (`RetroStyle`, `pixelPlate`, `retroBar`,
> `motion`, `Stories/Hud`) do not exist on `main`. What shipped from it is the lesson in "The vitals" below.

Everything above this section is BeACastleLord's and is kept as reference. Last Wave is on **Fluid**, not Vide, and
its look is **modern retro**: shapes and type are pixel-hard (Press Start 2P, Pixelated nine-slices), light and motion
are modern (a soft glow, springs, sweeps, bursts). Icons (weapons, passives, minimap, skull, soul) are NOT redrawn;
only the chrome around them is.

### The kit (`src/Global/Client/UI`)

- **`RetroStyle`** holds every look still being judged (panel, health length, timer, counters, card entrance, ability
  slot, panel entrance) and the two text-shadow switches. The game reads it at build time; the bench flips it and
  rebuilds. A pick is one line there, then delete the losing branch.
- **`pixelPlate`** is the SLAB, after SpecialDelivery's 3D border: face, a two-pixel LIP baked into the bottom of the
  block, a top light, an optional inset ring ("Framed") and an ink outline. **Depth is the lip, never a shadow
  floating under the box** - the first plate had an offset shadow whose depth was a per-look setting, and the Bare
  bar came out with half again the shadow of the Cells bar at the same size. `Pressed` swaps to the flat plate
  dropped by the lip's height, which is a button going into the screen.
- **The pixel scale is a WHOLE number** (`pixelPlate.SliceScale`): at 2.6 some source rows draw two px tall and some
  three, so an outline thickens and thins along one edge.
- **`pixelText`**: SpecialDelivery's Press Start 2P, a mitred outline and a hard drop shadow in the outline's colour.
  `Boxed = true` text follows `RetroStyle.TextShadowInBoxes` (off: a box already stands the words off the screen),
  free text follows `TextShadowFree`. Rich-text colour tags are stripped from the shadow so a green "+10" does not
  cast a green shadow. TextSize in design px; `MaxTextSize` + TextScaled only for wrapped text of unknown length.
- **`motion`**: springs (`Kick` adds velocity, **`Pop` raises it without stacking - use it for anything fired per
  event**), shakes with a ceiling, timed curves (`Play` with `Ease.Decelerate`/`Accelerate`/`OutBack`/`OutBounce`,
  which unregister themselves when they land), and one `TimeScale`. **Measure a punch** (spring value = the visible
  amount, kick = velocity): the first tuning peaked at 3% where 22% was wanted.
- **`pixelBurst`** (unrotated squares and sparks), **`retroButton`** (a thing you OPERATE), **`retroPanel`** (a
  panel that sizes to its words, arrives, leaves and is struck).

### The rules carried over from BeACastleLord (UI.md 5c, 5f)

- **A thing you TAKE rises and is lit from outside; a thing you OPERATE holds still and is lit from within.**
  `retroCard` lifts 14 design px and lights its frame and a glow behind it in its hue; `retroButton` never moves,
  its face walks toward white, and a press goes IN (face into the lip, 0.965 squeeze, ~0.09 s, no overshoot).
- **The rise and the light are two springs at two speeds** (~0.28 s critically damped, ~0.12 s).
- **Press-in and pop are separate springs.** Only the pick earns an overshoot and a burst.
- **An entrance is a timed curve, not a spring**, and a screen of overshooting pieces reads as a toy, which is why
  the card entrance is a look to judge ("Deal" decelerates, "Drop" bounces, "Pop" overshoots).
- **A refusal is one hard knock that stops dead.**
- **An alarm breathes; it does not strobe.** The low-health bar walks its outline toward red and breathes a glow
  (1.15 s cosine), BeACastleLord's facetBar alarm. A lub-dub outline flash was tried first and taken out.

### What is on it

| Piece | File | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Health, shield | `Components/retroBar` | BeACastleLord's facetBar in pixels: quick + slow springs with the band between (white taken, green given back), the slow one thrown back by the bite, a flash, chunks thrown from the cut, the breathing alarm, overshield tail. "Grows": the health bar's length is max health. |
| XP | `Components/xpBar` | The same full-width strip on the bottom edge, no level box: smooth fill, lit leading edge sparking on gains, a level runs to the end, flashes and bursts, rainbow while picking, red when locked. |
| Clock | `Components/timerPlate` | "Bare" letters (default) or "Plate"; a drop each second, punches on a pick countdown, shakes when urgent, beats red in overdrive. |
| Counters | `Components/counterPlate` | "Split": number box and a separate square icon box (how they were before), or "Tab"; roll, punch, icon hop, heat. |
| Level up, augments | `UpgradeUI`, `RewardUI` on `Components/retroCard` + `pickActions` | Cards dealt in, hover rise + glint, pick flash + sparks + pop, losers dim; banish lights everything red and shakes an X over the hovered card. |
| Abilities | `Components/abilityComponent` | "Slab" (shade sweeps down) or "Socket" (well fills with light); cast squeeze + flash, ready pop + sparks, active breath. |
| Objective, quest, warning | `QuestsUI`, `QuestActiveUI`, `QuestLockWarningUI` on `retroPanel` | Arrive ("Slide" / "Unfold"), struck on change, timer ticks. |
| Announcements | `AnnouncementsUI` | Slab edged in the header colour, pop on arrival, pop on pulse; fly-to kept. |
| Keybind hints | `KeyBindsUI` | Slab keycaps that go in and light while their key is held. |
| Streak | `StreakUI` | Punch per kill, heats toward white, burst every fifth, red drop when broken. |

### The art and the bench

- **Art**: `Assets/ui/authorslab.py` (the slab), `Assets/ui/authorretro.py` (flat plate, glow, spark), uploaded with
  `Assets/ui/upload.py` (group Decals through Open Cloud, ids in `Assets/ui/retro/ids.json`). The decal-to-image lookup
  is 403 over HTTP, as it was in BeACastleLord, so the bench resolves the ids in Studio and prints the block for
  `RetroArt.Images`. Until it is pasted every plate draws as a square frame with an outline.
- **Bench**: `src/Survivors/Client/UI/Stories/Hud.story.luau`, a UI Labs *generic* story (no Fluid mode): screens
  (HUD, Level up, Augments, Panels), every `RetroStyle` look as a dropdown, auto play, time scale. It puts
  `scaleNumber` into canvas mode at the widget's own height while it builds, because the camera viewport in edit mode
  is the 3D view and has nothing to do with the widget - which is what made the first bench's pixels come out tiny.
- **Not reworked yet**: ChestUI, WinBoxUI, FinalStatsUI, PlayersInfoUI, InteractableUI, PassiveChangesUI, SelfReviveUI,
  RestartRadialUI, PauseUI and the lobby. TimerBarUI (the pick countdown's screen glow) is already the modern half and
  is left as it is.

### Round 3 (2026-10-29): what the round-2 bench got wrong

- **Pixels were too small everywhere.** There is now one multiplier, `RetroStyle.PixelScale` (1.5), on every slab,
  and `RetroStyle.TextScale` (1.25) on every letter; the bench has a slider for each. A slab's pixel size is capped
  by its own height (ten source px of corner art must fit), so a big multiplier never crushes a thin bar.
- **Numbers on a box are sized off the box**, not a fixed TextSize: a bar's number is half its trough's height, a
  counter's 0.4 of its box, an ability's timer 0.4 of the slot. `pixelText` takes a function for that.
- **A plate cannot be a scale-sized child of an auto-sized frame**: the objective panel ran to the bottom of the
  screen. `pixelPlate.Behind(content, props)` hangs the slab from a zero-size holder, sized in pixels to the content.
  And nothing scales such a panel (a UIScale over a pixel-sized plate scales it twice): panels jolt and slide.
- **The ability slot keeps its own frame art.** The slab around it read as a panel inside a panel; the slot's
  picture is back, the charges back at its bottom middle, and the juice is laid on the old frame.
- **Counters are JOINED**: number box and icon box touching along one outline, the icon box in the counter's colour.
- **A bench card list must use `for_values`**: a plain reactive child runs in a reactive node, and a card makes
  effects, which Fluid only allows under a stable one, so the bench drew no cards at all.
- **The bench needs the minimap's footprint** (a square 0.3 of the screen's height, top right): the objective hangs
  under it and the counters pin to its left edge, exactly as MinimapUI and SelfStatsUI place them.

## Last Wave: the vitals (`vitalBar`, shipped 2026-10-29)

The health and shield bars, redone on their own after the whole-HUD round was rolled back. **Do one element per
round.** The retro round touched every screen at once, so no one piece could be judged or kept; this one touched two
bars and shipped in three passes.

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `src/Survivors/Client/UI/Components/vitalBar.luau` | The bar. `Style = "Slab"` (health) or `"Neon"` (shield). |
| `src/Survivors/Client/UI/HealthPlayerUI.luau`, `ShieldPlayerUI.luau` | The game's two bars, built on it. |
| `src/Survivors/Client/UI/Stories/Vitals.story.luau` | The bench: the old `defaultBar` beside the new pair, or the pair alone where the game puts it. |

`defaultBar` is now used only by `Stories/Vitals` as the control: `GreatshieldClient` and `ConvoyClient` moved to
`worldBar` (below), `PlayersInfoUI` to `teammateCard`. The API is `defaultBar`'s (`SetMax`, `SetCurrent`, `SetOvershield`, plus an optional `instant`), so swapping one
of those over is a require and a props table.

### How the round ran

1. **Bench first, game second.** Round 1 was four presets (Slab, Cells, Arcade, Neon) plus the shipped bar as the
   control and a "Mix" built from four dropdowns (Frame, Fill, Hit, Chip), all hit by one fake fight so one blow lands
   on every bar in the same frame. The game was not touched until a pick was made.
2. **The user picked per bar, not one look for both**: Neon on the shield ("more of a shield look"), the Mix on
   health. **Ask what a Mix was set to**: the bench cannot report the dropdowns back, and the Mix opens on the Slab
   preset, so "the Mix" may mean an unchanged default (it did: Slab / Solid / Shatter / Chase).
3. **Then the losers were deleted** (Cells fill, Blocks / HitStop / Glitch-on-health hits, the Hold chip band) and the
   look axes collapsed to one `Style` word. The bench shrank to before/after plus an event per gameplay moment.
4. **The second pass was the events the first bench never fired**: the max going up, overshield granted / hit /
   broken, and the shield break. A bench has to fire every way the number can change in the game, not just hit and
   heal. List them from the controllers and the server before building it.

### Drawn in Frames, snapped to a pixel unit

- **No uploaded art at all.** The retro round's slabs were nine-slices whose Decal ids had to be resolved in Studio
  and pasted back, and until then they drew as squares. Frames draw on the first run, in any story, with nothing
  to paste. For pixel-hard chrome (outlines, rows of light and shade, stepped glows) Frames are enough.
- **One pixel unit `p`** = `scaleNumber(PixelSize, "y")` rounded to whole screen px, capped at a sixth of the bar's
  height so the well always keeps four rows. Every position and size is a multiple of it. **The fill is snapped
  too** (`pixelsOf`): it steps a unit at a time like an old bar, anything above zero shows at least one unit, and
  full is the whole well even when the width is not a multiple of `p`.
- **A glow is stepped rings, not a blur**: three solid Frames behind the bar, each a unit bigger, at falling opacity
  (`AlarmRings`, `NeonRings`). They stack, so the inside is brightest. This is the retro answer to a bloom and
  needs no art. Neon's glow hangs off the FILL, so the light shrinks as the shield drains.
- **A diagonal is a staircase of rows, never a turned UIGradient.** The heal sheen was first a 45-degree gradient on a
  square the bar's height. Its band ran into the square's own side before it reached the bar's bottom, so the stripe
  ended on a hard vertical cut (measured off the user's screenshot: the bottom five rows all stopped at one column).
  Now it is one Frame per row, each one unit left of the row above, crossing from wholly off the fill's left to
  wholly off its right. Rendered as ASCII offline before shipping (`lune`), it is a clean 45 degrees to the last row.
- **Particles are unrotated squares that blink out** (visible every other 0.05 s over the last 30% of their life)
  instead of fading. Pooled, 48 a bar, placed on the frame they spawn.
- **Text**: Silkscreen bold (`UITools.FONT_SILKSCREEN_BOLD`, the game's pixel face), `TextSize` = 0.7 of the
  WHOLE bar's height, a miter-joined ink `UIStroke` of 0.1 of the TextSize (at least 1 px, not rounded). Not `TextScaled`.
  **A stroke is a share of its LETTERS, never of the pixel unit.** It was two thirds of a unit at first, the same 2 px
  on both bars, and on the shield's smaller number that is twice the weight: measured off a screenshot, ~0.17 of the
  letter's height on health against ~0.3 on the shield. The old bar's `ScaledSize` stroke kept the share, about 3 px
  on 17 px letters, and 0.1 of TextSize matches it. Rounding would bring the mismatch back (1.4 px to 1, 2.5 to 3).

- **Numbers are Silkscreen; WORDS are still open.** SpecialDelivery's lettering was benched against Silkscreen on
  both bars and lost for numbers; the user wants to judge it again for letters (labels, titles). It was taken out of
  `vitalBar`, so its recipe lives here: Press Start 2P, built into the engine
  (`rbxasset://fonts/families/PressStart2P.json`, nothing to upload), drawn TWICE (SpecialDelivery's `textShadow`):
  a solid ink copy of the text with the same outline underneath, and the coloured text lifted off it, so every letter
  wears a hard drop shadow as well as its outline. SpecialDelivery sets the drop and the outline at 2 px each on 28
  px text, so take both as 2/28 of the TextSize. Round the drop to whole px (half a pixel of offset is a blur), not
  the outline. Its capitals are ~half its TextSize like Silkscreen's, and it is on a pixel grid, so snap its TextSize
  DOWN to a multiple of 4. Lift the text by half the drop so the pair stays centred.
- **Size text off the bar, not the well, and measure the letters.** Both faces draw their capitals at about HALF
  their TextSize (measured on bench screenshots: Silkscreen 10 px at 19, Press Start 8 px at 16). Sized at a share
  of the well, the thin shield's number came out 6 px tall in Silkscreen and 4 px in Press Start, which its outline
  ate to 2 px of white. At 0.7 of the whole bar the letters are ~0.37 of it (the old bar was ~0.4): 16 px on health
  and 10 to 12 px on the shield at 1080p.
- **...and then cap it to what fits INSIDE the well.** 0.7 of the bar was right for health and too big for the thin
  shield: its ink (letters and outline, ~0.77 of the TextSize; Press Start's with its drop measured the same) filled
  all 12 rows of a 12-row well and touched the edges. The TextSize is now the smaller of 0.7 of the bar and what
  leaves half a pixel unit (at least 1 px) of air above and below the ink. Silkscreen sits 1 px low in its line box at
  TextSize 13, so it is raised by 0.075 of its size. The user's words: the text "should be inside", not touching.
  **Check text against the well it sits in, not only against the bar's height**; a thin bar is where it breaks.

### Fluid applies STATIC properties on a `task.defer`

> **Fluid only.** Ballarc moved to Vide on 2026-10-30 (`GlobalShared.Utils.Vide`, notes in
> `performance/vide-migration-2026-10-30.md`). Vide applies static properties when `create` runs, so the `isReady`
> defer below is gone from the pixel components; keep the rule only for any Fluid code still around.

`Fluid.create` does not set a plain property when the table is evaluated: `bind` queues it with `scheduler.defer`
(`task.defer`), and only reactive (function) properties and `Parent` are applied at once. So **a component that writes
Instance properties imperatively right after creating them is overwritten a moment later by its own static props**,
and a property written only once (a `Visible` set in a layout pass) stays wrong. `vitalBar` holds an `isReady` flag
set by its own `task.defer`, which is queued after Fluid's, and lays out and draws nothing until then. Either do
that, or never give a static value to a property you also write by hand.

### The motion: its own clock

Fluid's spring only pulls toward a target, and a hit wants a value SHOVED past its rest. `vitalBar` runs plain
spring tables (semi-implicit Euler at 1/240 substeps) on ONE module-level `PreRender` connection that exists only
while some bar is moving: each bar's `tick` returns whether it is still busy and is dropped when it is not. Every
duration is scaled by `vitalBar.TimeScale`, so the bench slows the bars and its fake fight together. The bars draw
imperatively in one `draw()` per frame, not through dozens of reactive bindings.

**Measure every punch** (`lune`, the spring pasted out of the module). Numbers that shipped:

| Spring | Frequency / damping | Kick | Peak |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Number punch on a hit | 3.6 / 0.32 | 8 | +22% |
| Number punch on a heal | same | 3.6 | +10% |
| Bar thump on a break | 2.9 / 0.4 | 3.2 | +10% (the first 1.6 gave +5%: too weak for a break) |
| Bar thump on a refill | same | 1.4 | +4% |
| Bar thump on a raise strike | same | 2.9 | +9% |
| Reading (quick) | 4.1 / 0.72 | | |
| Memory (slow) | 1.1 / 1.0 | +2.2 per share taken | |

### What every hit, heal and change does

- **Hit** (more than 0.2% of the bar): white flash over the fill (0.75, decays at 14/s), the memory spring kicked back
  so the white chip band opens wider than the hit, number punch, a hard-position shake (30 jumps a second, decays,
  0.7 to 3 units by bite). Slab throws chunks of the bar's own colours off the cut; Neon splits the fill into red and
  cyan copies a few units apart, flares its glow, and spits sparks. Under 1.2% nothing is thrown: a tick is a number
  moving, a hit is an event.
- **Heal**: the band runs green ahead of the fill, sheen, motes rising. At most every 0.35 s, because regen and
  lifesteal heal many times a second. **Refilling to full** also "dings": outline to white, sheen, sparkles along
  the bar, +4% thump.
- **Low health** (under 30%, health only): the outline warms toward red and three red rings BREATHE (1.15 s cosine).
  It never strobes. A shield has no alarm, since it refills on its own and an alarm would be on more than off.
- **Shield break, and overshield break**: both repulse enemies on the server (`CharacterService.overshieldBreak`), so
